teile.einleitung: Direct democracy means that the people do not only elect politicians but also vote themselves on specific issues. Switzerland is known for this around the world, because here people vote several times a year on laws and constitutional amendments. The most important tools are the referendum and the popular initiative.
wichtigste: In direct democracy the people themselves decide on specific issues.
Every change to the Federal Constitution needs a popular vote, which is the compulsory referendum.
Against new laws you can collect signatures for an optional referendum within 100 days.
With a popular initiative the people can propose a change to the Federal Constitution.
In votes on the constitution the double majority of people and cantons is needed.
At federal level you may vote and elect from the age of 18.
In Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden the Landsgemeinde still exists today.

abschnitte.text: In a **direct democracy** citizens vote themselves on specific issues. In a purely **representative democracy**, by contrast, only elected representatives decide. Switzerland combines both: Parliament makes the laws, but the people often have the last word. In Switzerland there are usually four voting Sundays a year for this.

The **compulsory referendum** applies to every change to the Federal Constitution, and then the people must always vote. With the **optional referendum**, 50,000 eligible voters or eight cantons can demand a vote on a new law within 100 days. The optional referendum was introduced at federal level in 1874. As early as 1831 St Gallen had created a forerunner with the veto.

With a **popular initiative** the people can themselves propose a change to the Federal Constitution. For this 100,000 valid signatures are needed, which must be collected within 18 months. This right has existed for partial revisions since 1891. An initiative is accepted only if the **double majority** is reached, that is, the majority of the people and of the cantons.

In the 19th century the **Democratic Movement** in cantons such as Zurich demanded more direct popular rights instead of pure representation by deputies. Zurich received a very democratic cantonal constitution in 1869. For a long time only men were allowed to vote, and women's suffrage at federal level was accepted only on **7 February 1971**. Appenzell Innerrhoden had to be forced by the Federal Supreme Court in 1990 to introduce it at cantonal level too.

The **Landsgemeinde** is an open-air assembly at which the eligible voters of a canton come together. Votes are taken by a show of hands. Today at cantonal level it exists only in **Glarus** and **Appenzell Innerrhoden**. In Glarus even 16-year-olds may vote.

At federal level Swiss citizens may vote and elect from the age of 18. Before every vote they receive a **voting booklet** with explanations and arguments. You can vote at the ballot box, by post or, in some cantons, in other ways. Often only about half of eligible voters go and vote, and on important topics it is more.

begriffe.erklaerung: A popular vote on a law or a constitutional amendment.
A proposal from the people to change the constitution.
A proposal needs the majority of those voting and the majority of the cantons.
An open-air assembly of all eligible voters of a canton.
The right to take part in votes and elections.

gewusst: Since 1848 the Swiss have voted on more than 600 proposals at federal level.
The voting age of 18 was introduced at federal level only in 1991, before that it was 20.
No other country in the world holds as many popular votes at national level as Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Women's suffrage allows women to take part in elections and votes. In Switzerland women received this right at federal level only in 1971, much later than in most countries of Europe. The road there was long and took a lot of patience and commitment.
wichtigste: On 1 February 1959 Swiss men rejected women's suffrage with about two thirds voting No.
In 1959 Vaud was the first canton to introduce women's suffrage.
On 7 February 1971 men accepted women's suffrage at federal level with about 65.7 per cent.
In 1971 eleven women were elected to the National Council.
Appenzell Outer Rhodes introduced women's suffrage in 1989.
In Appenzell Inner Rhodes it was only the Federal Supreme Court that forced women's suffrage in 1990.
On 14 June 1981 the equality article was added to the constitution.

abschnitte.text: With **women's suffrage** women may vote in ballots, and with the right to vote in elections they may elect and be elected. For a long time only men could take part in political decisions in Switzerland. Because every change to the constitution needs a popular vote, the **men** themselves had to give women this right. That was one reason why it took so long.

On **1 February 1959** Swiss men voted for the first time at federal level on women's suffrage. About two thirds said No. But in the same year **Vaud** became the first canton to introduce women's suffrage at cantonal level, and Neuchâtel and Geneva soon followed. Already in 1958 Iris von Roten had set off a fierce debate with her book “Frauen im Laufgitter” (“Women in the Playpen”).

Many women kept fighting in associations and on the streets. On **1 March 1969** the “March on Bern” took place, a large rally in front of the Federal Palace. On **7 February 1971** the men finally said Yes with about 65.7 per cent. In autumn 1971, eleven women were elected to the National Council and one woman to the Council of States.

In some cantons it took even longer to introduce cantonal suffrage. **Appenzell Outer Rhodes** decided in favour at the Landsgemeinde of 1989. In **Appenzell Inner Rhodes** the men kept saying No. Only a ruling of the Federal Supreme Court of 27 November 1990 forced the canton to let women take part in decisions.

On **14 June 1981** the people and the cantons accepted the **equality article**, which demands equal rights and equal pay for work of equal value. Ten years later, on 14 June 1991, hundreds of thousands of women took to the streets in the **women's strike**, because equality had not yet been achieved. In 1984 Elisabeth Kopp was elected as the first woman to the Federal Council. In 2019, too, a large women's strike took place again on 14 June.

begriffe.erklaerung: The right to take part in deciding in votes.
The right to elect people and to be elected oneself.
The aim that women and men have the same rights and opportunities.
A gathering of many people who show a demand together.

gewusst: In New Zealand women were allowed to vote as early as 1893, almost 80 years before Swiss women.
In Europe, after Switzerland only Liechtenstein introduced women's suffrage, namely in 1984.
7 February is often celebrated today as the anniversary of women's suffrage.

teile.einleitung: Elisabeth Kopp was the first woman to be elected to the Swiss Federal Council, in 1984. Her resignation in early 1989 was a major political event.
wichtigste: Elisabeth Kopp belonged to the FDP, the Radical Liberals.
From 1974 to 1984 she was municipal president of Zumikon in the canton of Zurich.
From 1979 she sat in the National Council.
In 1984 she was elected to the Federal Council as the first woman.
She headed the Department of Justice and Police.
Because of a telephone call with her husband she resigned on 12 January 1989.
Her successor was Kaspar Villiger.

abschnitte.text: Elisabeth Kopp began her career in the municipality. From 1974 to 1984 she was **municipal president of Zumikon** in the canton of Zurich. She was one of the first female municipal presidents in Switzerland. From 1979 she represented the **FDP** in the **National Council**. There she made a name for herself as a committed politician.

In 1984 the Federal Assembly elected Elisabeth Kopp to the **Federal Council**. She was the **first woman** in the national government. This was an important step, because women had had the right to vote and stand for election at federal level only since 1971. Kopp took over the **Department of Justice and Police**, FDJP for short. There she was responsible, among other things, for **asylum matters**.

At the end of 1988 Kopp came under pressure. She had warned her husband by telephone and advised him to resign from the board of a company. That company was under investigation. Because she at first kept this quiet, she lost a lot of trust. On **12 January 1989** she resigned. She would actually have become **President of the Confederation** in 1990.

Kopp was succeeded by the Lucerne Radical Liberal **Kaspar Villiger**. Criminal proceedings were brought against Kopp for breach of official secrecy. The **Federal Supreme Court** acquitted her in 1990. A parliamentary investigation of her department also brought the **files scandal** to light. Politically her resignation remained a deep turning point.

gewusst: Elisabeth Kopp had still been elected vice-president of the Federal Council in December 1988.
The investigation after her resignation led to the discovery of the files scandal.

teile.einleitung: The Fête des Vignerons is a huge festival of winegrowers in Vevey on Lake Geneva. It takes place only about every 20 to 25 years and is therefore an experience that many people see only once or twice in their lives.
wichtigste: The Fête des Vignerons takes place in Vevey in the canton of Vaud.
“Vignerons” means winegrowers in English.
The festival takes place only about four or five times a century.
The last Fête des Vignerons was in summer 2019, the one before in 1999.
At its centre are the grapevine and the work in the vineyards.
Since 2016 the festival has been on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.

abschnitte.text: The word **“Vignerons”** means **winegrowers**. The Fête des Vignerons honours their work in the **vineyards**. At its centre is the **grapevine**, whose grapes are made into wine. It is organised by an old association of winegrowers, the **Confrérie des Vignerons**. It honours the best vine growers of the area.

The festival takes place in **Vevey**. The town lies in the **canton of Vaud** on the shore of **Lake Geneva**. Nearby lie the steep vineyards of the **Lavaux**. They climb in terraces from the lake up the slope. The Lavaux is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The Fête des Vignerons is very **rare**. It takes place only about every **20 to 25 years**, so four or five times a century. The last was in summer **2019**, the one before in **1999**. Many people experience the festival only once or twice in their lives. That is why the anticipation is huge each time.

For the festival a huge **arena** is built on the market square of Vevey. Thousands of volunteers from the region take part. They sing, dance and act in costumes. The performances show the **year in the vineyard**, from the work in spring to the harvest. Also famous is the song **“Ranz des vaches”**, an old song of the alpine herdsmen.

In **2016** **UNESCO** added the Fête des Vignerons to the list of the **intangible cultural heritage** of humanity. It was the first Swiss tradition on this list. Intangible cultural heritage means customs, festivals and knowledge passed on from generation to generation. The Fête des Vignerons is a good example of this.

gewusst: The Fête des Vignerons was the first Swiss tradition on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.
For the festival a huge arena is built in the middle of Vevey.

teile.einleitung: The Jungfrau Railway is a rack railway in the Bernese Oberland. It runs from the Kleine Scheidegg up to the Jungfraujoch. There, at 3,454 metres above sea level, lies the highest railway station in Europe.
wichtigste: The Jungfrau Railway runs from the Kleine Scheidegg to the Jungfraujoch.
At 3,454 metres, the Jungfraujoch station is the highest in Europe.
The idea came from the Zurich entrepreneur Adolf Guyer-Zeller.
On 1 August 1912 the railway reached the Jungfraujoch.
The railway runs for the most part in a tunnel through the Eiger and the Mönch.
The Jungfrau lies in the Bernese Oberland.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century many mountain railways were built in Switzerland. The Zurich entrepreneur **Adolf Guyer-Zeller** had a particularly bold idea in 1893. He wanted to build a railway all the way up to the **Jungfrau**. With the **Eiger** and the **Mönch**, the Jungfrau is among the best-known mountains in the **Bernese Oberland**. In 1896 construction work began.

The railway runs for the most part up in a **tunnel** through the Eiger and the Mönch. The workers blasted and drilled their way laboriously through the hard rock. The work in the altitude and the cold was dangerous, and there were fatal accidents. Guyer-Zeller died in 1899 and did not live to see its completion. On **1 August 1912** the railway ran for the first time all the way to the **Jungfraujoch**.

The Jungfrau Railway begins at the **Kleine Scheidegg**. To get there you travel on other railways from Grindelwald or Lauterbrunnen. Because the line is very steep, the Jungfrau Railway is a **rack railway**. In the tunnel there are stops with windows in the rock wall. There you can look out onto glaciers and down into the valley.

The **Jungfraujoch** station lies at **3,454 metres above sea level**. It is the **highest railway station in Europe** and is therefore also called the “Top of Europe”. Up there are viewing terraces, an ice palace and a research station. You see the **Great Aletsch Glacier**, the longest glacier in the Alps. The region is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: The line is about 9 kilometres long, of which about 7 kilometres lie in the tunnel.
On the Jungfraujoch stands the Sphinx Observatory, in which experts research the weather and the air.

teile.einleitung: In the area of the present-day canton of Graubünden three leagues came into being in the late Middle Ages. They joined together in the Free State of the Three Leagues, which lasted until joining Switzerland in 1803.
wichtigste: The League of God's House arose in 1367 from the subjects of the Bishop of Chur.
The Grey League was sworn in 1424 in Trun under a maple.
The League of the Ten Jurisdictions arose in 1436 after the death of Frederick VII of Toggenburg.
In 1524 the federal charter united the three leagues into the Free State.
The Ilanz Articles limited the bishop's secular power.
The League Diet met in turn in Chur, Ilanz and Davos.
Jürg Jenatsch shaped the Graubünden Troubles and was murdered in 1639.

abschnitte.text: The oldest league is the **League of God's House**. It arose in **1367** from the subjects of the Bishop of Chur. The diocese was then called the **House of God**. The people wanted to limit the bishop's power and have more say themselves. The main town of the League of God's House was **Chur**.

abschnitte.titel: The Grey League and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions
abschnitte.text: The **Grey League** was, according to tradition, sworn in **1424** in **Trun** under a **maple**. The maple of Trun is still an important symbol of Graubünden. In 1436 **Frederick VII of Toggenburg**, the last of his family, died. Thereupon the jurisdictions in the Prättigau and around Davos joined together as the **League of the Ten Jurisdictions**. Its main places were **Ilanz** and **Davos**.

In **1524** the **Federal Charter of the Three Leagues** united the three leagues permanently. It was the basis of the **Free State of the Three Leagues**. The communities had a lot of power in it. The shared **League Diet** met in turn in **Chur, Ilanz and Davos**. With the **Ilanz Articles** of 1524 and 1526 the communities limited the secular power of the bishop and the monasteries and were allowed to choose their own faith.

The Three Leagues ruled the **Valtellina**, a valley in present-day Italy. In the 17th century Spain, Austria and France fought over influence in the region, and to this came the dispute between the denominations. This period is called the **Graubünden Troubles**. In July 1620 Catholic Valtellinese, with Spanish support, killed numerous Reformed, which is called the **Valtellina Massacre**.

A defining figure of the Graubünden Troubles was **Jürg Jenatsch**. He was first a Reformed **pastor**, then became a military leader and fought on the Reformed side. Later he changed his denomination and worked together with Spain to win back the Valtellina. In 1639 he was murdered at a feast in Chur. In 1803 the Three Leagues became part of Switzerland as the canton of **Graubünden**.

gewusst: The name Graubünden recalls the Grey League.
The coat of arms of Graubünden still shows the arms of all three leagues today.

teile.einleitung: John Calvin was a reformer who worked for many years in Geneva. He made the city a centre of the Reformation in Europe. His teaching shaped the Reformed churches in many countries.
wichtigste: Calvin came from France and arrived in Geneva in 1536.
Guillaume Farel persuaded him to stay in Geneva.
In 1538 he had to leave Geneva, and in 1541 he returned.
He preached in the cathedral of Saint-Pierre.
In 1559 he founded the Geneva Academy, from which the university grew.
Geneva received the nickname “Protestant Rome”.
Calvin lived in Geneva until his death in 1564.

abschnitte.text: John Calvin was born in **Noyon** in France in **1509**. He studied law and engaged with the ideas of the **Reformation**. Because the Reformed were persecuted in France, he left his country. In 1536 his most important book appeared, the **“Institutes”** (“Institutio”), an explanation of the Christian faith.

In **1536** Calvin actually wanted only to travel through **Geneva**. The preacher **Guillaume Farel** had introduced the Reformation there. He persuaded Calvin to stay and help build the new church. But already in **1538**, only two years later, the Geneva council sent both out of the city. Calvin went to Strasbourg. In **1541** he was called back to Geneva.

Calvin preached in the **cathedral of Saint-Pierre** in the old town of Geneva. His **chair** can still be seen there today. He gave the church strict rules, the **church ordinances**. People were to live simply, diligently and devoutly. Calvin stayed in Geneva until his death in **1564**.

In **1559** Calvin founded the **Geneva Academy**, a school for scholars. Pastors and teachers from many countries were trained there. The academy later became the **University of Geneva**. The students carried Calvin's teaching to their homelands, for example France, Scotland and the Netherlands. Geneva became as important for the Reformed as Rome for the Catholics. That is why it was called the **“Protestant Rome”**.

In the **Parc des Bastions** in Geneva stands the **Reformation Wall**. It is a long wall with large **stone figures**. In the middle stand Calvin, Guillaume Farel, Theodore Beza and John Knox. The monument was begun for the 400th birthday of Calvin. It stands right next to the university that grew out of Calvin's academy.

gewusst: The Reformation Wall is about 100 metres long.
Calvin's grave in Geneva is not known for certain, because he wanted a plain burial without a gravestone.

teile.einleitung: The Burgundians were a Germanic people who founded a kingdom of their own in the 5th century. It stretched from Lake Geneva into the Rhone valley and left a lasting mark on western Switzerland.
wichtigste: In 436 Hunnic auxiliary troops of Rome destroyed the Burgundian kingdom on the Rhine.
In 443 the Burgundians were settled in the Sapaudia, from which the name Savoy came.
Gundobad was a commander-in-chief in Italy and in 473 raised Glycerius to emperor.
The princess Clotilde married the Frankish king Clovis.
For the Romans the Lex Romana Burgundionum applied.
King Sigismund was taken prisoner in 523 and killed in 524.
In 524 the Burgundians defeated the Franks at Vézeronce.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of the 5th century the Burgundians had a kingdom on the **middle Rhine** around **Worms**. In 436 Hunnic auxiliary troops in Rome's service destroyed this kingdom. This defeat entered the **Nibelungen legend**. King **Gundahar** corresponds to Gunther in the Nibelungenlied. The song, however, arose only many centuries later and is not an accurate historical source.

abschnitte.titel: A new start in the Sapaudia
abschnitte.text: In 443 Rome settled the surviving Burgundians in the **Sapaudia**, an area around **Lake Geneva**. From this name the name **Savoy** later developed. The Burgundians were to secure the area for Rome. Soon they extended their kingdom as far as the Rhone valley. Important cities were **Geneva** and Lyon.

**Gundobad** was a nephew of the powerful general Ricimer. He became **commander-in-chief** of the Western Roman Empire, that is, supreme commander. In 473 he raised **Glycerius** to emperor, but then returned to Burgundy and became king there. His niece **Clotilde** was Catholic and married the Frankish king **Clovis**. She is regarded as the driving force behind his conversion to Christianity.

In the Burgundian kingdom **personal law** applied. That means it depended on which people someone belonged to. The Burgundians lived by their own law. For the Roman population the **Lex Romana Burgundionum** applied, a selection from Roman law. In this way both groups could live by their own customs.

The sons of Clovis attacked Burgundy. In 523 they took King **Sigismund** prisoner and had him killed with his family in 524. Later he was venerated as a saint. In the same year the Burgundians under **Godomar** defeated the Franks at **Vézeronce**, and King Chlodomer fell. The victory delayed the end by only ten years, however: in 534 Burgundy came under Frankish rule.

gewusst: The name Burgundy lives on today in the French region of Bourgogne.
King Sigismund founded the Abbey of Saint-Maurice in the Valais in 515, and it still exists today.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Switzerland shows a white cross on a red background. What makes it special is its square shape, because almost all other national flags are rectangular.
wichtigste: The Swiss flag is square.
It shows a white cross on a red background.
The red probably goes back to the flag of Schwyz.
Since 1815 the Swiss cross has been the coat of arms of the Confederation.
The arms of the cross are one sixth longer than they are wide.
Swiss ships at sea sail under a rectangular flag.
The Red Cross uses the reversed colours.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss flag shows a **white cross** on a **red background**. The red probably goes back above all to the red flag of **Schwyz**. The name Switzerland also comes from Schwyz. Already in the Middle Ages, Confederate warriors wore a white cross as a sign of recognition. The national flag later grew out of this.

The Swiss flag is **square**. This is very rare for national flags. Only the **Vatican** also has a square flag. At **sea** it is different: Swiss ocean-going ships sail under a **rectangular** flag. On land the flag stays square.

In **1815** the white cross on the red field became the **coat of arms of the Confederation**. The federal state took over the flag in 1848. Since **1889** it has been laid down exactly what the cross looks like. All four arms are **equally long**. Each arm is **one sixth longer than it is wide**.

The **Red Cross** was founded in **Geneva**. In honour of Switzerland it chose the **reversed colours** as its sign: a red cross on white. Today this sign is known all over the world. It protects helpers, hospitals and the wounded in wars. For that reason it must not simply be used for advertising.

On **1 August** Switzerland celebrates its **national day**. Then many people decorate their houses, balconies and gardens with flags. At sporting events, too, you see many Swiss flags. The Swiss cross also appears on many products as a sign of Swiss origin. There are strict rules for this.

gewusst: Only Switzerland and the Vatican have square national flags.
At sea, Swiss ships sail under a rectangular Swiss flag.

t13xxv4b.t: International Committee of the Red Cross

teile.einleitung: The International Committee of the Red Cross, ICRC for short, is a humanitarian organisation based in Geneva. It helps people affected by wars and armed conflicts. It was founded in 1863 by five citizens of Geneva.
wichtigste: The ICRC was founded in Geneva in 1863.
The idea came from Henry Dunant, who had witnessed the Battle of Solferino in 1859.
The first president was the Swiss General Guillaume-Henri Dufour.
Gustave Moynier led the ICRC from 1864 to 1910.
Since 1876 it has borne the name International Committee of the Red Cross.
Henry Dunant received the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.
The Swiss Red Cross was founded in 1866.

abschnitte.text: In 1859 the Geneva businessman **Henry Dunant** happened to arrive in northern Italy just after the Battle of **Solferino**. Thousands of wounded soldiers lay on the battlefield without help. With women from the area, Dunant organised the care of the wounded, no matter which side they came from. After that he wrote the book “A Memory of Solferino”. In it he proposed founding relief societies for the wounded in all countries.

In 1863 the **Geneva Society for Public Welfare** set up a commission to examine Dunant's proposals. This **Committee of Five** included Henry Dunant, Gustave Moynier, General Guillaume-Henri Dufour and the doctors Louis Appia and Théodore Maunoir. The first president was **Dufour**, whose good reputation gave weight to the committee. From 1864 the jurist **Gustave Moynier** led the organisation for almost half a century, until 1910. At first the committee was called the International Committee for Relief to the Wounded, and since **1876** it has borne its present name.

Already in 1864 several states signed the first **Geneva Convention** in Geneva. It laid down that wounded soldiers and the personnel who help them are protected. As protective sign a **red cross on a white background** was chosen, that is, the reversed colours of the Swiss flag. Later further agreements were added, for example for the protection of prisoners of war and civilians. These rules are called **international humanitarian law**.

Henry Dunant had businesses in **Algeria**, which failed. He fell into **bankruptcy** and had to leave the Geneva committee in 1867. After that he lived for a long time impoverished and almost forgotten, finally in **Heiden** in the canton of Appenzell Outer Rhodes. In 1901 he received, together with the Frenchman Frédéric Passy, the **first Nobel Peace Prize**. He died in Heiden in 1910.

On the model of the Geneva committee, the **Swiss Red Cross** came into being in Bern in **1866**. It helped as early as 1871, when thousands of French soldiers were interned in Switzerland. Today almost all countries have national Red Cross or Red Crescent societies. The ICRC itself still has its seat in **Geneva** and works neutrally, impartially and independently.

gewusst: The ICRC has received the Nobel Peace Prize three times: in 1917, 1944 and 1963.
The protective sign is the Swiss flag with swapped colours, as an honour to the founding country.
In Geneva there is an International Red Cross and Red Crescent Museum.

teile.einleitung: The Geneva Convention is an international treaty meant to protect people in war. The first convention was signed in Geneva in 1864. It is regarded as the beginning of modern humanitarian international law.
wichtigste: The first Geneva Convention was signed on 22 August 1864.
Twelve states signed it at that time.
The Swiss Federal Council had called the conference.
The wounded, field hospitals and medical personnel count as neutral.
The protective sign is a red cross on a white background.
In 1949 four new Geneva Conventions were adopted.

abschnitte.text: The Genevan **Henry Dunant** witnessed the Battle of Solferino in Italy in 1859. He saw how thousands of wounded were left without help. In his book “A Memory of Solferino” he called for help for all the wounded. In 1863 a group in Geneva founded a committee, from which the **Red Cross** came. This committee also wanted a treaty between states.

At the wish of the Geneva committee, the **Swiss Federal Council** invited the states to Geneva. On **22 August 1864**, **12 states** signed the convention on the wounded in the field. These included Switzerland, France, Prussia, Italy and Spain, among others. Many more states joined later. Since then Switzerland has played a special role for **humanitarian international law**, that is, the rules for the protection of people in war.

The core idea is simple: the wounded, **field hospitals** and **medical personnel** count as **neutral**. A field hospital is a hospital for soldiers. Anyone who cares for the wounded must not be attacked. The wounded of both sides are looked after. The first convention had only ten articles.

The protective sign is a **red cross on a white background**. It is seen as a reversal of the colours of the Swiss flag and as an honour to Switzerland. It is not a religious symbol, but a neutral protective sign. From 1876 the **Ottoman Empire** used the **red crescent** instead. Today it, too, is recognised as a protective sign.

After the Second World War, **four Geneva Conventions** were adopted in 1949. They protect the wounded on land, the shipwrecked, **prisoners of war** and **civilians**. They build on the convention of 1864. Additional protocols were added later. Today almost all states in the world have recognised the Geneva Conventions.

gewusst: The first Geneva Convention of 1864 had only ten articles.
Switzerland keeps the originals of the Geneva Conventions and is responsible for accessions.

teile.einleitung: The Eight Old Places is the name for the eight members of the Confederation between 1353 and 1481. To the three forest cantons of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden were added Lucerne, Zurich, Glarus, Zug and Bern. Out of this loose alliance of rural places and cities, Switzerland slowly grew.
wichtigste: The Eight Old Places were Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Lucerne, Zurich, Glarus, Zug and Bern.
Lucerne joined the alliance in 1332 as the first city.
Zurich came in 1351, and Glarus and Zug followed in 1352.
Bern joined in 1353 as the last of the Eight Old Places.
The places sent envoys to the Diet to discuss shared matters.
In the Old Zurich War, Zurich and the other Confederates fought one another.
The time of the Eight Old Places ended in 1481 with the admission of Fribourg and Solothurn.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning stood the three **forest cantons** of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, who according to the Federal Charter of 1291 promised each other help. In 1332 the first city, **Lucerne**, joined. In 1351 the rich trading city of **Zurich** followed, and in 1352 Glarus and Zug came in. With **Bern** in 1353 the last and soon most powerful of the eight places joined. These alliances were often made one by one, so not every place was directly allied with every other.

The eight places were very different. Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Glarus and Zug were rural, and there the **Landsgemeinde**, the assembly of free men, decided. Lucerne, Zurich and Bern were **city places**, governed by a council of rich citizens. The cities traded and conquered subject territories, while the farmers of the rural places lived mainly from cattle farming. These contrasts led again and again to tensions.

The dukes of **Habsburg** wanted to win back their power in the region. At the Battle of Sempach in 1386 the Confederates defeated a Habsburg army of knights, and in 1388 the people of Glarus won at Näfels. The **Sempach Letter** of 1393 then regulated the conduct of troops in war. It forbade, for example, plundering before the end of the battle and protected churches and women. It was one of the first shared laws of all the places.

In 1415 the Confederates conquered the Habsburg Aargau, and in 1460 Thurgau. Such territories became **common lordships**, ruled jointly by several places. The places took turns sending a **bailiff**, who administered the territory for two years at a time. The people there were subjects and had no say. But the shared territories also held the Confederates together, because everyone profited from them.

In 1436 the last Count of Toggenburg died without heirs. Zurich and Schwyz quarrelled fiercely over the **Toggenburg inheritance**. In the **Old Zurich War** from 1440 to 1450 Zurich even allied with the Habsburgs against the other Confederates. In 1444 the Confederates fought at the Battle of St Jakob an der Birs near Basel against the French **Armagnacs**, who were meant to help Habsburg as mercenaries. In the end Zurich had to give up the alliance with Habsburg and become part of the Confederation again.

The envoys of the places discussed shared matters at the **Diet**, which met in changing places such as Lucerne or Baden. There was no government that could give orders to everyone, and each place stayed largely independent. In 1481, with the **Convention of Stans**, Fribourg and Solothurn were admitted, and the time of the Eight Old Places was over. By 1513 the Confederation had grown to 13 places. The eight old places are still regarded as the core of Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: This was the old name for a member of the Confederation; today we say canton.
An assembly at which envoys of the Confederate places met and held discussions.
A territory that several places ruled together.
An official who administered a subject territory on behalf of the places.
French mercenary troops against whom the Confederates fought near Basel in 1444.

gewusst: Bern was the last of the Eight Old Places, but soon became the largest and most powerful city state north of the Alps.
At St Jakob an der Birs only about 1,500 Confederates fought against a huge superior force, and almost all of them fell.
Unterwalden counted as one place, although it consisted of the two parts Obwalden and Nidwalden.

teile.einleitung: The alphorn is a long wooden wind instrument. In the past herdsmen used it to signal to each other over long distances, and today it is one of the best-known instruments of Swiss folk music.
wichtigste: An alphorn is made of wood, usually spruce.
It is usually about 3 to 4 metres long and curves upwards at the bottom.
You blow with your lips into a mouthpiece.
It has no finger holes, keys or valves.
When playing, the lower end rests on the ground.
At folk festivals alphorn players often perform together with yodellers.

abschnitte.text: An alphorn is made of **wood**, usually **spruce**. In the past people looked for trees that had grown crooked on the slope. That way the wood already had the right curve. Today alphorns are built in several parts that can be fitted together. Inside, the tube is hollow.

An alphorn is usually about **3 to 4 metres** long. At the top is the **mouthpiece**, and at the bottom the wide **bell**, curved upwards. Because the instrument is so long, the lower end rests on the **ground** while playing. The player stands upright in front of it and holds the horn only at the top.

The alphorn has **no finger holes**, no keys and no valves. All the notes come from the player's **lips**. The tighter he tenses his lips, the higher the note. That is why you can play only certain notes on the alphorn, which are called **natural notes**. One of them sounds somewhere between two normal notes. It is called the **alphorn F** and gives the alphorn its special sound.

abschnitte.titel: From herdsman's signal to folk music
abschnitte.text: In the past **herdsmen** used the alphorn to signal to each other over long distances. The sound carries far over valleys and mountains. Later it was almost forgotten. At the **Unspunnen Festival** near Interlaken in 1805 it was promoted again. Today you hear the alphorn at many folk festivals, often together with **yodelling**.

gewusst: In good weather you can hear the sound of an alphorn for several kilometres.
Today alphorn players play not only folk music but sometimes also jazz or music with an orchestra.

teile.einleitung: In the 1860s many people in several cantons demanded more say. This Democratic Movement won important popular rights in the canton of Zurich and elsewhere that still apply today.
wichtigste: In Zurich the movement was directed against the “Escher system”.
It began in 1867 in Winterthur.
An important mouthpiece was the newspaper “Der Landbote”.
The Zurich constitution of 1869 brought the compulsory referendum on laws.
The movement demanded among other things the founding of cantonal banks.
It was carried by the middle classes of the countryside and small towns.
In Basel-Landschaft and Thurgau it also prevailed early.

abschnitte.text: In the canton of Zurich a small group had a lot of power. At its head stood **Alfred Escher**, a politician and entrepreneur. Linked with him were industrialists and bankers. Critics called this the **“Escher system”**. Instead of this concentration of power, the **Democratic Movement** wanted more **direct say** for the people.

In 1867 the movement began in **Winterthur**. Winterthur was the centre of the opposition to the liberal elite of the city of Zurich. From there a **new cantonal constitution** was demanded. The newspaper **“Der Landbote”** spread the demands, as did, for example, the Bülacher Volksfreund. The NZZ, by contrast, stood close to the liberal camp.

The movement was carried mainly by the **middle classes of the countryside and small towns**. They included craftsmen, farmers, small manufacturers and workers. The leadership often came from **teachers**, pastors, doctors and editors in the country. They felt insufficiently heard by the elite in the city of Zurich.

In 1869 the canton of Zurich received a new constitution. It brought the **compulsory referendum on laws**: all laws had to be put to the people for a vote. In addition the **Executive Council** was now elected directly by the people. The movement also demanded **cantonal banks** that were to give farmers and trades cheap credit. Further demands were progressive taxation, free schools and factory laws.

The movement had success not only in Zurich. In **Thurgau** and **Basel-Landschaft** it also prevailed early. In Basel-Landschaft the revision movement around **Christoph Rolle** won far-reaching popular rights in the 1860s. The Catholic-Conservative cantons remained untouched by it. The ideas later influenced popular rights at federal level too.

gewusst: The Zurich Cantonal Bank was founded shortly after the new constitution and still exists today.
Many popular rights that are typical of Switzerland today were first tried out in the cantons.

teile.einleitung: The Burgundians were a Germanic people who settled in what is now French-speaking Switzerland in the 5th century. Later the Kingdom of Upper Burgundy arose there. Both realms strongly shaped Romandy.
wichtigste: In 443 the Romans settled the Burgundians in the Sapaudia.
Around 500 King Gundobad had a book of laws written down.
The Burgundians adopted the Latin of the locals.
In 534 the Franks conquered the first Burgundian kingdom.
In 888 Rudolf I became king of Upper Burgundy in Saint-Maurice.
Queen Bertha lives on in legends as a diligent spinner.
After the death of Rudolf III in 1032, Burgundy fell to the Holy Roman Empire.

abschnitte.text: In **443** the Roman general **Aëtius** assigned land to the Burgundians in the **Sapaudia**. This area lay in today's French-speaking Switzerland and in Savoy. The Burgundians were to protect the border there as allies of the Romans. Soon they founded a realm of their own. Important places were Geneva and Lyon.

Around **500** King **Gundobad** had the laws of the Burgundians written down. This book of laws is called the **Lex Burgundionum** or Lex Gundobada. It regulated the coexistence of Burgundians and Romans. Romans here means the local people who spoke Latin. The law shows that both groups lived side by side.

The Burgundians were only few. They lived among many locals who had long been shaped by Rome. So they gave up their **Germanic language** little by little. They spoke the **Latin** of the locals. From it later developed the French of **Romandy**. In **534** the sons of the Frankish king Clovis conquered the realm, but the name Burgundy remained.

In **888** **Rudolf I** of the family of the Welfs had himself crowned king in the abbey of **Saint-Maurice** in Valais. His realm was called **Upper Burgundy** and covered large parts of today's French-speaking Switzerland. His son **Rudolf II** was married to **Queen Bertha**. In French-speaking Switzerland she is remembered as a good and diligent queen. The saying “au temps où la reine Berthe filait” means “in the time when Queen Bertha was spinning” and refers to the good old days.

King **Rudolf III** had no heirs. When he died in **1032**, the German emperor **Conrad II** took over the Kingdom of Burgundy. With this, French-speaking Switzerland also belonged to the **Holy Roman Empire**. So the German-speaking and French-speaking areas of today's Switzerland came under the same rule.

gewusst: Romandy probably speaks French also because the Burgundians adopted the language of the locals.
The abbey of Saint-Maurice in Valais has existed for over 1,500 years and was the place of coronation of a king.

teile.einleitung: Alberto Giacometti was a Swiss sculptor and painter from the Bregaglia valley. His long, very thin bronze figures are famous all over the world.
wichtigste: Alberto Giacometti was born in 1901 in Borgonovo in the Bregaglia valley in Graubünden.
His father Giovanni Giacometti was a well-known painter.
For many years Alberto worked in a small studio in Paris.
His human figures are very long and thin.
His best-known figure is “Walking Man”.
He appeared on the 100-franc note of the eighth series.

abschnitte.text: Alberto Giacometti was born in 1901 in **Borgonovo**. The village lies in the **Bregaglia**, a valley in the canton of Graubünden on the border with Italy. People speak Italian there. His father **Giovanni Giacometti** was a well-known painter. From him Alberto learned to draw and paint as a child.

As a young man Giacometti moved to **Paris**. There he learned from sculptors and lived among many artists. For decades he worked in a small, cramped **studio**. His brother Diego often helped him. Most of his famous works were created in this studio.

A **sculptor** shapes figures from stone, clay, plaster or metal. Giacometti first shaped his figures from clay or plaster and then had them cast in **bronze**. His people are very long and quite thin, and you recognise them at once by this. The figure **“Walking Man”** takes a big step forward. It became one of the best-known works of art of the 20th century.

Giacometti died in 1966 in Chur and was buried in his home village of Borgonovo. On the blue **100-franc note** of the eighth series his face could be seen, together with one of his figures. In Swiss museums, for example in Zurich, you can look at many of his works. In the Bregaglia too, people remember the Giacometti family of artists.

gewusst: A figure of “Walking Man” is among the most expensive works of art ever sold at auction.
Not only Alberto but also his father Giovanni and other relatives were well-known artists.

teile.einleitung: Today many people move to Switzerland. In the past it was the other way round: in the 19th century tens of thousands left Switzerland because they were poor or hungry at home. Most went to America.
wichtigste: In the 19th century most emigrants went to the USA.
Important reasons were poverty, hunger, failed harvests and unemployment.
The “year without a summer” of 1816 set off a great famine.
In 1819 emigrants, mainly from Fribourg, founded the town of Nova Friburgo in Brazil.
In 1845 families from Glarus founded the settlement of New Glarus in Wisconsin.
Around 1890 Switzerland changed from a country of emigration to a country of immigration.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century many people in Switzerland were very **poor**. There were **failed harvests**, too little work and, in some years, hunger. It was especially hard in the **mountain regions**. Many hoped to find a better life elsewhere. So they left their homeland.

In 1815 the volcano **Tambora** erupted in Indonesia. Its ash darkened the sky around the world. As a result **1816** was very cold and wet in Europe, and it is called the **year without a summer**. The harvest failed, and many people went hungry, especially in eastern Switzerland. After that many emigrated.

Most emigrants went to the **USA**. There was cheap land and work there. In **1845** poor families from the canton of Glarus founded the settlement of **New Glarus** in Wisconsin. To this day the place keeps up many Swiss customs. Already in **1819** about 2,000 people, mainly from the canton of Fribourg, travelled to Brazil. Their settlement is called **Nova Friburgo**, after their homeland.

At that time the **municipalities** had to care for their poor. That was expensive. So some municipalities paid for poor people's passage to America. A single journey often cost them less than years of **poor relief**. For the emigrants the journey was long and dangerous, and many never saw their homeland again.

abschnitte.titel: The turning point and the Fifth Switzerland
abschnitte.text: Towards the end of the 19th century **industry** and **railway building** brought enough work. Around **1890** for the first time more people came to Switzerland than left. Since then Switzerland has been a **country of immigration**. Even so, many Swiss people live abroad. They are called the **Fifth Switzerland**, and in 2024 there were more than 800,000 of them.

gewusst: The “Fifth Switzerland” is so called because it comes symbolically on top of the four language regions.
In New Glarus in the USA people still celebrate Swiss festivals and keep Swiss customs alive.

teile.einleitung: The Basel Fasnacht is the biggest carnival in Switzerland. It begins on the Monday after Ash Wednesday at 4 o'clock in the morning with the Morgestraich and lasts exactly three days. The people of Basel call it “die drey scheenschte Dääg”, the three most beautiful days.
wichtigste: The Basel Fasnacht begins with the Morgestraich at 4 in the morning.
It lasts exactly 72 hours, that is, three days.
The cliques play mainly piccolo and drum.
The masks are called “Larven”.
Confetti is called “Räppli” in Basel.
The Waggis with a big nose and yellow hair is a typical figure.

abschnitte.text: The Fasnacht begins on the Monday after **Ash Wednesday** with the **Morgestraich**. At exactly **4 o'clock in the morning** all the lights go out in the old town. Then the **cliques**, that is, the carnival groups, set off with glowing, painted **lanterns**. It is dark, and only the lanterns shine. Thousands of people watch.

Typical of the Basel Fasnacht is the music with **piccolos** and **drums**. A piccolo is a small, high flute. The cliques walk through the narrow lanes playing. There are also **Guggenmusik** bands, which play loudly and cheerfully on brass instruments. For three days the whole city is full of music.

The masks are called **Larven** in Basel. They are often large and brightly painted. Every year the cliques choose a **Sujet**, that is, a theme. Often they use it to poke fun at events in politics and everyday life. A well-known figure is the **Waggis** with a big nose, wild yellow hair and wooden clogs.

Confetti is called **Räppli** in Basel. After the Fasnacht it lies everywhere on the streets. On Monday and Wednesday afternoon the big parade, the **Cortège**, moves through the city. From the floats the carnival-goers throw Räppli, oranges or sweets. In the evening groups sing funny verses, the **Schnitzelbänke**.

gewusst: Since 2017 the Basel Fasnacht has been part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.
The Basel Fasnacht starts later than most other carnivals, namely only after Ash Wednesday.

teile.einleitung: The Burgundians were a Germanic people who lived in present-day western Switzerland about 1,500 years ago. They adopted the language of the Romans, and that is why French is spoken there today.
wichtigste: The Burgundians were originally a Germanic people.
They lived in western Switzerland around Lake Geneva.
Geneva was an important city of the Burgundians.
They adopted the Latin language.
From this Latin the French of western Switzerland later developed.
The Burgundians were Christians.
King Sigismund founded the Abbey of Saint-Maurice in the Valais in 515.

abschnitte.text: The Burgundians were originally a **Germanic people**. They came from the north and wandered for a long time. In the 5th century the **Romans** gave them land in the west of present-day Switzerland. There they lived together with the people who already lived there. They founded a **kingdom** of their own.

The Burgundians settled around **Lake Geneva**. Later their kingdom became much bigger and reached far into France. **Geneva** was an important city, and the kings lived there at times. Many place names in western Switzerland still recall this time.

The people in the area spoke **Latin**, the language of the Romans. The Burgundians were fewer in number and learned this language. Their own Germanic language was lost. From Latin, **French** developed in time. That is why French is spoken in western Switzerland today, but German in the east.

The Burgundians were **Christians**. They built churches and monasteries. King **Sigismund** founded the **Abbey of Saint-Maurice** in the Valais in the year 515. Members of a religious order still live and pray there today. Saint-Maurice is one of the oldest monasteries in the west of Europe that has existed without a break.

gewusst: The border between German and French in Switzerland also has to do with the Burgundians and the Alemanni.
The Abbey of Saint-Maurice has been inhabited for over 1,500 years.

t19jewk8.t: Division of the Canton of Basel

teile.einleitung: Until 1833 Basel was a single canton in which the city had the say. After disputes and fighting, city and countryside separated into two cantons: Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft.
wichtigste: The Basel countryside was under-represented in the Grand Council.
Stephan Gutzwiller was an important leader of the people of the countryside.
On 3 August 1833 the countryside won at the Hülftenschanze near Frenkendorf.
After that the Diet ordered complete separation.
Liestal became the main town of Basel-Landschaft.
Riehen, Bettingen and Kleinhüningen stayed with Basel-Stadt.
In 2014 Basel-Landschaft clearly rejected examining a merger.

abschnitte.text: Before 1830 the citizens of the city of Basel decided for the whole canton. The city had about 40 per cent of the population but about 60 per cent of the seats in the **Grand Council**, the cantonal parliament. People in the countryside therefore felt disadvantaged. They demanded **equal rights**, that is, an equal say for everyone.

In 1830 representatives of the countryside met in Bad Bubendorf. There a **petition** came about, a written appeal to the government. The lawyer **Stephan Gutzwiller** helped write it and became one of the most important leaders of the people of the countryside. But the city did not give in enough to the demands. So in the following years there was unrest again and again.

On 3 August 1833 troops from the city marched into the countryside. Near Frenkendorf at the **Hülftenschanze** they were beaten by the country people. After that the **Diet**, the assembly of the cantons, stepped in. It ordered the complete separation of city and countryside. Basel was now divided into two **half-cantons**.

The new canton of Basel-Landschaft chose **Liestal** as its main town, and its parliament, the Landrat, meets there today. Only the municipalities on the right bank of the Rhine stayed with the city: **Riehen**, **Bettingen** and Kleinhüningen. Kleinhüningen was later incorporated into the city of Basel. The cantonal property was divided according to population. Even the **Basel Minster treasure** was divided, and the countryside later sold its share.

Again and again people asked whether the two Basels should come together again. In 2014 both cantons voted on whether a **merger** should be examined. Basel-Stadt said yes with about 55 per cent. Basel-Landschaft clearly rejected it with about 68 per cent. So the two cantons remain separate, but work together in many areas.

gewusst: Riehen and Bettingen are still the only municipalities of Basel-Stadt besides the city of Basel.
Because the Minster treasure was divided, parts of it are now in museums outside Basel.

teile.einleitung: In the 19th century Alfred Escher was one of the most powerful men in Switzerland. The Zurich politician and entrepreneur pushed forward the building of railways, founded a bank and helped to found the ETH.
wichtigste: Alfred Escher lived in Zurich from 1819 to 1882.
For many years he sat in the National Council and in the Zurich government.
He headed the Swiss Northeastern Railway.
In 1856 he founded the Swiss Credit Institution, a bank.
He campaigned for the ETH in Zurich, which opened in 1855.
From 1871 he was president of the Gotthard Railway Company.

abschnitte.titel: A politician in Zurich and Bern
abschnitte.text: Alfred Escher was born **in Zurich in 1819**. Even when young he made a career in politics. He sat in the **Zurich government** and for many years in the **National Council**. At that time Switzerland had only just become a federal state. Escher was among the most influential politicians of the young country.

Escher wanted Switzerland to get a good **railway network**. He headed the **Swiss Northeastern Railway**, based in Zurich, one of the largest private railways. At that time private companies built the railways, not the state. Escher made sure that many lines were built.

To build railways you needed a great deal of money. So in **1856** Escher founded the **Swiss Credit Institution**, a bank. In 1857 he co-founded the **Swiss Annuity Institution**, a life insurance company. For progress you also needed well-trained engineers. That is why Escher campaigned for the **ETH in Zurich**, which opened in 1855.

Escher's greatest project was the **Gotthard Railway**, a railway line through the Gotthard. From **1871** he was president of the Gotthard Railway Company. The construction cost far more than planned. Because of these cost overruns Escher had to resign as president in **1878**. The railway opened in 1882, and Escher died in the same year.

On the **square in front of Zurich main station** stands a statue of Alfred Escher. It recalls how important he was for the railway, the economy and education. Some people, however, also took a critical view of his great power. To this day he is regarded as one of the founders of modern Switzerland.

gewusst: The bank that Escher founded was later called Credit Suisse.
Escher lived to see the opening of the Gotthard Railway only briefly: he died in the same year.

t1a4tq86.t: The Princely Abbey of St Gallen

teile.einleitung: For over a thousand years the Princely Abbey of St Gallen was one of the most important monasteries in Europe. Its abbots were not only churchmen but also imperial princes who ruled over a territory of their own.
wichtigste: The monastery goes back to the monk Gallus, who settled in the Steinach valley around 612.
Notker Balbulus, “the Stammerer”, became famous for his sequences.
Wiborada was killed in 926 during the Hungarian invasion and later canonised.
From the 13th century the abbots held the rank of imperial princes.
The Abbey Library keeps manuscript B of the Nibelungenlied.
The Abbey District of St Gallen is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Princely Abbey was dissolved in 1805.

abschnitte.text: Around **612** the Irish travelling monk **Gallus** settled in the valley of the Steinach. At this spot a **monastery** later arose. In the 8th century the monk **Othmar** founded a proper community of monks there. The monastery was named after Gallus. From the settlement around the monastery grew the town of **St Gallen**.

In the Middle Ages St Gallen was an important centre of **education**. Monks copied books there by hand and decorated them. One of the best known was **Notker Balbulus**, called “the Stammerer” (around 840 to 912). He composed **sequences**, which are chants for Mass. He also wrote stories about Charlemagne.

**Wiborada** lived as an **anchoress** in St Gallen. An anchoress is a woman who has herself shut into a small cell for a life of prayer. She warned of the invasion of the **Hungarians**, so that monks and books could be brought to safety. In the raid of 926 she was killed. In 1047 she was canonised by the pope as the **first woman**.

Abbot **Ulrich von Sax** was raised to the **rank of imperial prince** in 1206/1207. Since then people have spoken of the **Princely Abbey of St Gallen**. The abbots ruled over a territory of their own, like secular princes. Later the abbey became an **Associate Place** of the Confederacy. In 1805 it was dissolved, and its territory now belongs to the **canton of St Gallen**.

The **Abbey Library** of St Gallen is one of the oldest libraries in the world. Its magnificent **Baroque hall** attracts many visitors. It keeps valuable medieval **manuscripts**. These include **manuscript B** of the **Nibelungenlied** from the 13th century. The whole **Abbey District** is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: Wiborada was the first woman to be canonised by a pope.
In the Abbey Library of St Gallen lies one of the most important manuscripts of the Nibelungenlied.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages the Kyburgs were one of the most powerful noble families in the area of today's Switzerland. They named themselves after Kyburg Castle near Winterthur and founded several towns that still exist today.
wichtigste: The counts of Kyburg named themselves after Kyburg Castle in the canton of Zurich.
In the 13th century they owned large territories between Lake Constance and the Aare.
The Kyburgs founded towns such as Zug and Baden.
Around 1264 the Kyburgs died out in the male line.
Rudolf of Habsburg became guardian of the heiress Anna.
The great estate of the Kyburgs passed to the Habsburgs.
A marriage in 1273 created the younger line of New Kyburg.

abschnitte.text: **Kyburg Castle** stands on a hill near Winterthur in the canton of Zurich. The family of counts, the **Kyburgs**, named themselves after this castle. A count in the Middle Ages was a nobleman who ruled over a large territory. The Kyburgs became rich because they took over the inheritance of other noble families. This included part of the inheritance of the Zähringens. Today Kyburg Castle is a museum.

The Kyburgs laid out several **towns**. A town offered protection by walls and brought the lord money through markets and tolls. In Central Switzerland the Kyburgs founded the town of **Zug** on Lake Zug. Around 1230 they laid out the town of **Baden** on the Limmat. Baden had already been known in Roman times for its hot springs. Other places in north-eastern Switzerland also go back to the Kyburgs.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the old Kyburgs
abschnitte.text: In the 13th century there lived two counts who were both called Hartmann. **Hartmann V** died in 1263, **Hartmann IV** in 1264. After that there were no more male Kyburgs. It is said that the family died out in the **male line**. The only heiress was Anna, the daughter of Hartmann V. She was then still a child.

abschnitte.titel: The inheritance goes to the Habsburgs
abschnitte.text: The young Anna needed a **guardian**, that is, someone to decide for her. **Rudolf of Habsburg** took on this task. His mother came from the House of Kyburg. As guardian Rudolf administered the great inheritance and brought it to his own house. In 1273 he even became Roman-German king. In this way the Habsburgs became the strongest power in the area of today's northern and central Switzerland.

In 1273 Anna of Kyburg married Eberhard of **Habsburg-Laufenburg**, a relative of Rudolf. Their descendants again called themselves counts of Kyburg. This is called the line of **New Kyburg** or Kyburg-Burgdorf. Their possessions lay mainly in the area of today's canton of Bern. They were, however, much less powerful than the old Kyburgs.

gewusst: Without the inheritance of the Kyburgs, the Habsburgs would hardly have become so powerful so quickly.
Rudolf of Habsburg was related to the Kyburgs, because his mother was a Kyburg.

teile.einleitung: Conrad Gessner was a Zurich doctor and naturalist in the 16th century. His enormous animal book “Historia animalium” made him famous all over Europe.
wichtigste: Conrad Gessner was born in Zurich in 1516.
From 1554 he was city physician in Zurich.
He wrote an enormous work on animals, the “Historia animalium”.
The pictures in it were printed using woodcuts.
The book also includes mythical animals such as the unicorn and Dürer's rhinoceros.
In 1555 he climbed Pilatus.
In 1565 he died of the plague.

abschnitte.text: Conrad Gessner was born in **1516** in **Zurich**. He came from a modest background and still studied at several universities. From **1554** he was **city physician** in Zurich. Alongside that he researched **animals** and **plants** and collected knowledge from many books. He also wrote about languages and compiled a large catalogue of books.

Gessner's most famous work is the **“Historia animalium”**, the history of animals. In it he described all the animals he knew, from mammals through birds to fish. He collected what earlier scholars had written and added observations of his own. The work was very extensive and appeared in several volumes. It is regarded as a beginning of modern **zoology**, the study of animals.

The book contains many pictures. They were printed using **woodcuts**: the picture was carved into a block of wood, inked and printed on paper. One picture Gessner took from the artist **Albrecht Dürer**: the famous **rhinoceros**. Dürer himself had never seen the animal and drew it from a description.

Gessner also included animals that people only told stories about, for example the **unicorn**. At that time people did not yet know exactly which animals really exist. Many reports came from travellers from distant countries. But Gessner tried to separate truth from invention and often said so when he doubted a report.

In 1555 Gessner climbed **Pilatus** near Lucerne and wrote about it. At that time few people climbed mountains for pleasure. Gessner raved about the beauty of the mountains. In 1565 the **plague** raged in Zurich. Gessner nursed the sick, caught the disease himself and died in the same year.

gewusst: Gessner is regarded as one of the first people to describe and illustrate a pencil.
Because of his great catalogue of books he is also called a father of bibliography.

teile.einleitung: In the St. Alban valley in Basel a large water wheel turns at an old mill. Paper used to be made here, and today the Basel Paper Mill is a museum where you can scoop paper yourself.
wichtigste: Paper used to be made by hand in the Basel Paper Mill.
It stands in the St. Alban valley on the Rhine.
A water wheel on the St. Alban canal drives the machines.
In the past paper was made from old fabric rags.
You scoop the paper out of the vat with a sieve.
Today the mill is the Museum of Paper, Writing and Printing.

abschnitte.text: The paper mill lies in the **St. Alban valley**, an old district on the Rhine. A canal, the **St. Alban-Teich**, flows through the valley. Its water turns a large **water wheel**. The wheel used to drive many mills in the valley. It supplied the power long before there was electricity.

In the past paper was made not from wood but from **rags**. These were old scraps of linen and hemp cloth. The rags were chopped up and pounded by heavy hammers into a **pulp**. The water wheel moved these hammers. The pulp then went with a lot of water into a large **vat**.

The papermaker dips a **sieve** into the vat. He lifts out a thin layer of paper pulp, and the water drips off. The wet fibres are laid on a cloth and pressed out. After that the sheet is dried. In the museum children may **scoop** a sheet themselves and then even print on it.

Basel used to be an important city of **printers**. Many scholars had their works printed here. For the many books, an enormous amount of paper was needed. That is why the paper mills in the St. Alban valley were so important. The **Museum of Paper, Writing and Printing** shows how paper is made, how people wrote in the past and how books were printed.

gewusst: Because rags used to be collected, there was a trade of its own for it: the rag collector.
In the museum you can also write with a quill and ink and work at old printing presses.

teile.einleitung: Guillaume-Henri Dufour was an engineer, cartographer and general from Geneva. In 1847 he led the troops in the Sonderbund War and helped to build up the Red Cross. A famous map and the highest mountain in Switzerland are named after him.
wichtigste: Dufour was born in Konstanz in 1787 and died in Geneva in 1875.
He studied at the École polytechnique in Paris.
In 1847, as general, he led the troops of the Diet in the Sonderbund War.
The war lasted barely a month.
Under his direction the Dufour Map was made, at a scale of 1 to 100,000.
At 4,634 metres the Dufourspitze is the highest peak in Switzerland.
In 1863 he was one of the founders of the Red Cross.

abschnitte.text: Dufour was born in **Konstanz** in 1787, where his parents from Geneva were living in **exile**. He then grew up in **Geneva**. From 1807 to 1809 he studied at the **École polytechnique** in Paris, a famous university. After that he became an officer in the **engineers**, the troop for structures such as bridges and fortifications. Later he lived and worked mainly in Geneva.

In 1847 the **Sonderbund War** broke out between Catholic Conservative and liberal cantons. Dufour led the troops of the **Diet** as **general**. He wanted as few casualties as possible and ordered that prisoners and wounded be treated well. The war lasted only about four weeks in November 1847. After that the modern **federal state** came into being in 1848.

Under Dufour's direction the first accurate map of the whole of Switzerland was made, the **Dufour Map**. It has a **scale of 1 to 100,000**. So one centimetre on the map is one kilometre in reality. The mountains are drawn with **hachures** and shading, as if light were falling on them. In this way they look almost three-dimensional.

The highest mountain in Switzerland bears Dufour's name: the **Dufourspitze** in the **Monte Rosa massif**. It is **4,634 metres** high. The Federal Council gave it this name in 1863 in honour of the general. It lies in Valais on the border with Italy.

In 1863 Dufour was one of the founders of the Geneva committee from which the **Red Cross** came. He worked together with **Henry Dunant** in this. Dufour was the first president of the committee. In 1864 he also chaired the conference at which the first **Geneva Convention** was signed. He died in Geneva in 1875.

gewusst: The highest mountain in Switzerland is named after a man who was born in Germany.
In Geneva, on the Place Neuve, there stands an equestrian monument to General Dufour.

teile.einleitung: In 1872 the USA and Great Britain settled a serious dispute not with weapons but before a court of arbitration in Geneva. The Alabama Arbitration became a milestone of international law and strengthened Geneva's reputation as a place of diplomacy.
wichtigste: The dispute was about damage caused by warships of the Southern states that had been built in Britain.
The best-known ship was the “Alabama”, built in Birkenhead near Liverpool.
The court met in Geneva's town hall, in what is now the “Salle de l'Alabama”.
The Swiss Jakob Stämpfli was one of the five members.
Britain had to pay the USA 15.5 million dollars.
Two great powers accepted a neutral verdict instead of going to war.

abschnitte.text: In the **American Civil War** the Northern states fought against the Southern states. The Southern states had ships built in Britain, although the country was supposed to be neutral. The **CSS Alabama** was built at a shipyard in **Birkenhead** near Liverpool. As a commerce raider she captured more than sixty ships of the Northern states. In 1864 she was sunk off Cherbourg in France.

After the war the USA demanded **compensation** from Britain. The British, it said, had broken their duties as a neutral state. The dispute was fierce, and some even feared a new war. In the end both countries agreed on a **court of arbitration**: independent judges were to decide, and both sides promised to accept the verdict.

The court met in the **town hall of Geneva**. In the same hall the first Geneva Convention had already been signed in 1864. Since then it has been called the **Salle de l'Alabama**. Five judges sat on the court: one each from the USA, Britain, Italy, Brazil and Switzerland. Switzerland was represented by **Jakob Stämpfli**, and the president was the Italian Federico Sclopis.

In September 1872 the court ruled in favour of the USA. Britain had to pay **15.5 million dollars** and transferred the sum in gold in 1873. Above all it was important that two great powers settled their dispute peacefully. This strengthened the idea of settling conflicts between states in court. Geneva thereby became even better known as a city of diplomacy.

gewusst: In Geneva's town hall, the first Geneva Convention was signed and later the Alabama verdict was delivered in the same hall.
Jakob Stämpfli had earlier been a member of the Swiss Federal Council.

teile.einleitung: Carl Lutz was a Swiss diplomat. In the Second World War he saved tens of thousands of Jewish people in Budapest from deportation to the extermination camps.
wichtigste: Carl Lutz was born in 1895 in Walzenhausen AR and died in 1975 in Bern.
From 1935 to 1940 he worked in Jaffa in Palestine.
From 1942 he was vice-consul in Budapest.
With letters of protection he placed Jewish people under Swiss protection.
In the “Glass House” thousands of people found refuge.
He worked together with the Swede Raoul Wallenberg.
Only in 1995 was he posthumously rehabilitated by Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Carl Lutz was born in **1895** in **Walzenhausen** in the canton of **Appenzell Ausserrhoden**. He worked abroad for Switzerland. From 1935 to 1940 he was in **Jaffa** in what was then the British mandate territory of **Palestine**. There he got to know the situation of Jewish emigrants. At the beginning of **1942** he came as **vice-consul** to **Budapest** in Hungary.

In the war Switzerland represented the interests of many foreign states in Hungary, including the USA and Britain. This is called being a **protecting power**. Lutz headed the department for foreign interests. In 1944 Germany occupied Hungary, and the **deportations** of Hungarian Jews began. Lutz used his position to save people.

Lutz issued **letters of protection** that placed their holders under Swiss protection. The authorities often respected them and did not deport these people. Officially, it was permitted to make the emigration of 8,000 Jews to Palestine possible. Lutz interpreted the number 8,000 as **families** instead of individuals and numbered letters of protection several times. In this way he could protect far more people than intended.

The **Glass House** was the seat of a glass firm in Budapest. In 1944 the Swiss legation used the building. **Thousands of people** found refuge there. Lutz also worked together with the Swedish diplomat **Raoul Wallenberg**. Wallenberg came to Budapest in July 1944 and adopted the method of the letters of protection.

After the war the Swiss authorities at first criticised Lutz. They accused him of **exceeding his authority**, because he had acted on his own. Only in **1995**, twenty years after his death, was he **posthumously rehabilitated** by Switzerland, that is, officially recognised after his death. The memorial Yad Vashem in Israel honoured him as **Righteous Among the Nations**.

gewusst: Carl Lutz's rescue operation is regarded as one of the largest civilian rescue operations for Jewish people in the Second World War.
The Glass House in Budapest is now a memorial.

teile.einleitung: Gottfried Keller was one of the most important Swiss poets. He lived in Zurich from 1819 to 1890. His stories such as “Clothes Make the Man” are still read in school today.
wichtigste: Gottfried Keller was born in Zurich in 1819 and died there in 1890.
He wrote novels, stories and poems.
At first he wanted to become a painter and went to Munich for it.
His great novel is called “Green Henry”.
Many stories are set in the invented little town of Seldwyla.
From 1861 to 1876 he was First State Clerk in Zurich.

abschnitte.titel: First a painter, then a poet
abschnitte.text: Gottfried Keller was born in **Zurich** in 1819. His father died early, and the family had little money. As a young man Keller wanted to become a **painter**. So he went to **Munich** to learn art. But success did not come, and he returned to Zurich. Only after that did he become a famous **poet**.

Keller's great novel is called **“Green Henry”** (“Der grüne Heinrich”). The hero Henry wears green clothes that are sewn from the clothes of his father. In the novel Henry, like Keller himself, wants to become a painter. Many experiences in the book recall Keller's own life. Keller later wrote the novel again from scratch.

Keller invented the Swiss little town of **Seldwyla**. In the collection **“The People of Seldwyla”** funny and sad stories take place. The people there are often a little reckless. Keller describes them with a lot of humour. In this way he shows how people deceive themselves and others.

The best-known story is **“Clothes Make the Man”** (“Kleider machen Leute”). It is about **Wenzel**, a poor **tailor** in a fine coat. Because of his fine clothes, everyone believes he is a distinguished **count**. So begins a great case of mistaken identity. The story shows how much people judge by outward appearance.

From 1861 to 1876 Keller was **First State Clerk** of the canton of Zurich. A state clerk heads the chancellery of the government and writes important documents. So Keller wrote a lot in his job, too. After that he devoted himself entirely to writing again. He died in Zurich in 1890.

gewusst: Keller also wrote the poem “To the Fatherland”, which begins with “O my homeland”.
Gottfried Keller was shown on an earlier Swiss banknote, the 10 franc note.

teile.einleitung: In 1415 the Confederates conquered Aargau, which then belonged to the Habsburgs. The trigger was a dispute at the Council of Constance.
wichtigste: The background was the Council of Constance, which was meant to end the schism in the Church.
Duke Frederick IV of Austria helped Pope John XXIII to flee from Constance.
King Sigismund then imposed the imperial ban on Frederick.
Bern conquered most of Aargau.
Zurich conquered the Freiamt Affoltern, today's Knonauer Amt.
The Confederates destroyed the Habsburg castle of Stein above Baden.
Uri at first did not take part because of a peace with Austria.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of the 15th century there were several **popes** at the same time. To end this division, churchmen met in **Constance** for a **council**, a great assembly of the Church. Pope **John XXIII** wanted to escape the council. Duke **Frederick IV of Austria** helped him to flee in 1415. This turned King Sigismund against the duke.

King **Sigismund** punished Frederick with the **imperial ban**. With that the duke was outlawed, that is, without rights in the Empire. The king called on everyone to occupy his territories. The Confederates followed this call. Frederick later bore the nickname “of the empty pockets”, because he lost many territories and a lot of money.

**Bern** secured most of Aargau, including Aarau, Zofingen, Lenzburg and Brugg. This Lower Aargau stayed Bernese until 1798. **Zurich** conquered the **Freiamt Affoltern** west of the Albis, today's **Knonauer Amt**. Lucerne also gained territories. Above the town of Baden the Confederates conquered the Habsburg **Stein Castle** and burned it down.

Some territories were ruled by the places **jointly**. They included the **County of Baden** and the Free Bailiwicks. Such territories are called **common lordships**. The places took turns sending a bailiff. **Uri** at first did not take part in 1415, because it was keeping to a peace with Austria of 1412. Only in 1443 did it join in the joint rule over Baden.

With the conquest the Habsburgs lost their ancestral land. The **Habsburg**, their ancestral castle, lies in Aargau. The Confederates were bound more closely together by the shared territories, because they had to administer them together. Only in 1803 did the present-day **canton of Aargau** come into being.

gewusst: The Habsburg, the ancestral castle of the Habsburgs, stands in the canton of Aargau.
Duke Frederick IV bore the nickname “Frederick of the Empty Pockets”.

teile.einleitung: The Old Swiss Confederacy was the alliance of places in the Alps and on the Central Plateau out of which much later present-day Switzerland grew. It came into being in the late Middle Ages and lasted until 1798. Its members had promised each other help with an oath, which is why they called themselves Confederates.
wichtigste: A Confederate was a member of the alliance, which was made with an oath, a solemn promise.
The alliance began with Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, and the Federal Charter is dated 1291.
Lucerne joined as the fourth place, and Zurich followed soon after.
By 1513 the alliance had grown to 13 places.
The earlier places are today called cantons, and Switzerland now has 26 of them.
The Old Confederacy ended in 1798 with the invasion of French troops.
Switzerland is still officially called the Swiss Confederation.

abschnitte.text: An **oath** is a solemn promise, and a **Confederate** was a member of the alliance. In the **Federal Charter**, which is dated early August 1291, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden promised each other mutual help against attackers. That is why Switzerland celebrates its national holiday on 1 August. In the evening people often light a bonfire on a hill, and there are fireworks and lanterns.

The **Habsburgs** were a powerful noble family who held many rights in the region. Their ancestral castle, the Habsburg, stands in the present-day canton of Aargau. The Confederates resisted their influence and won in 1315 at Morgarten and in 1386 at Sempach. Later, legends arose such as that of William Tell, who stood up against an evil bailiff.

As the fourth place, the city of **Lucerne** on Lake Lucerne joined in 1332. Soon afterwards Zurich, Glarus, Zug and Bern joined, and so the Eight Old Places came into being. In 1481 Fribourg and Solothurn followed, in 1501 Basel and Schaffhausen, and in 1513 Appenzell. Besides these there were **Associated Places** such as St Gallen or the Valais, which were allied with the Confederacy but did not fully belong to it.

Each place governed itself, and there was no common government. Envoys of the places met at the **Diet** to discuss shared matters. In the rural places the free men gathered at the **Landsgemeinde** and voted outdoors by raising their hands. In Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden the Landsgemeinde still exists today. In the cities, by contrast, a council of rich families made the decisions.

The fighters of the places carried the **banner** of their place as a sign of recognition. In the Burgundian Wars the Confederates defeated Duke Charles the Bold in 1476 and 1477.
