Later many young men went abroad as **mercenaries** in foreign military service to earn money. After the heavy defeat at Marignano in 1515 the Confederates stopped waging war as a great power.

From 1520 the **Reformation** split the places into Reformed and Catholic, which led to several wars. Even so, the alliance held together. In 1648 the Peace of Westphalia recognised the separation from the Holy Roman Empire. In 1798 French troops marched in, and the Old Confederacy ended. After years of upheaval the present-day **federal state** with its Federal Constitution came into being in 1848.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solemn promise that you may not break.
A member of the alliance that was made with an oath.
The earlier name for a member of the Confederation; today we say canton.
An open-air assembly at which all eligible voters vote by raising their hands.
A soldier who fights in a foreign army for money.

gewusst: The Federal Charter of 1291 is on display in the Museum of the Federal Charters in Schwyz.
The Papal Swiss Guard in the Vatican still recalls the time of the Swiss mercenaries today; it was founded in 1506.
Only since 1994 has 1 August been an official public holiday throughout Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: ETH Zurich is one of the best-known technical universities in the world. It was founded by the federal government and began operating in 1855 as the Federal Polytechnic School.
wichtigste: ETH began in 1855 as the Federal Polytechnic School, called the “Poly” for short.
It was the first university of the federal government.
The model was the École polytechnique in Paris.
The main building was designed by the architect Gottfried Semper and was finished in 1864.
Since 1908 the university has been allowed to award doctorates.
It has carried the name Federal Institute of Technology since 1911.
Albert Einstein studied at the Polytechnic in Zurich from 1896 to 1900.

abschnitte.titel: A school for the federal government
abschnitte.text: After the founding of the federal state in 1848 people wanted a federal university. Many hoped for a whole **university**. But the Catholic rural cantons resisted, because they feared Reformed and urban dominance. As a **compromise** only a technical school came about. The law for it dates from 7 February 1854.

In 1855 teaching began at the **Federal Polytechnic School**. People usually called it the Polytechnic or **“Poly”** for short. The model was the **École polytechnique** in Paris, a French engineering school. The aim was practical training in technology and natural sciences. In this way Switzerland got its own engineers for railways, bridges and factories.

The main building was designed by the architect **Gottfried Semper**. He won the competition and himself taught at the Polytechnic. The building was completed in 1864 and stands high above the Zurich old town. At first the **University of Zurich** was also housed in it. To this day it is the landmark of the university.

For a long time the Polytechnic could award only **diplomas**. Since 1908 it has also been allowed to award **doctorates**, which strengthened research. In 1911 the school received the name **Federal Institute of Technology**, ETH for short. By this time it had long been internationally respected. Today the federal government also owns ETH in Lausanne, the EPFL.

The best-known student is probably **Albert Einstein**. He studied from 1896 to 1900 in the department for teachers of mathematics and physics. Later, from 1912 to 1914, he was also a **professor** there. Many researchers at ETH have received a **Nobel Prize**. The university is still a centre of technology and science.

gewusst: In the main building of ETH, the University of Zurich was also at home at first.
At ETH Albert Einstein was first a student and later a professor.

teile.einleitung: Each of the 26 Swiss cantons has a coat of arms of its own. The coats of arms show colours, animals, saints or objects connected with the history of the canton. You see them on flags, buildings and number plates.
wichtigste: Switzerland has 26 cantons with coats of arms of their own.
Basel-Stadt shows a black Baselstab, a form of bishop's crozier.
Schaffhausen has a black ram in its coat of arms.
Graubünden shows an ibex in one field.
The coat of arms of Valais has 13 stars.
Glarus shows Saint Fridolin.
The coat of arms of Geneva shows half an eagle and a key.

abschnitte.titel: What is a coat of arms?
abschnitte.text: A **coat of arms** is a sign of recognition, usually in the form of a shield. In the Middle Ages knights wore coats of arms so that they could be recognised. Towns and countries also received coats of arms. The Swiss **cantons** have borne their coats of arms for many centuries. You see them on **flags**, town halls and on **number plates**.

Some coats of arms show only colours. The **Zurich** coat of arms is divided diagonally, **white** above and **blue** below. The **Ticino** coat of arms is divided vertically: **red** on the left, **blue** on the right. The coat of arms of **Lucerne** is divided vertically into blue and white. **Solothurn** shows red above and white below. Such simple coats of arms can be recognised even from afar.

abschnitte.titel: Animals in the coat of arms
abschnitte.text: Many coats of arms show **animals**. **Schaffhausen** has a black **ram** on a yellow ground. In the **Graubünden** coat of arms with three fields, one shows a black **ibex**. **Thurgau** has two yellow **lions** on a green and white ground. **Bern** and Appenzell show a **bear**, Uri a black **bull's head**.

The coat of arms of **Valais** has **13 stars**. They stand for the districts of the canton, which used to be called **Zenden**. **Basel-Stadt** shows a black **Baselstab**, a form of **bishop's crozier**. It recalls that Basel was once subject to a bishop. The coat of arms of **Geneva** shows half an **eagle** on the left and a golden **key** on the right.

abschnitte.titel: A saint in the coat of arms
abschnitte.text: The coat of arms of **Glarus** is special: it shows a person. What can be seen is **Saint Fridolin** as a wanderer with a staff. He is the **patron saint** of Glarus. Glarus is the only canton whose coat of arms shows a person.

gewusst: The coat of arms of Basel and that of Basel-Landschaft both show a Baselstab, but in different colours and shapes.
The canton of Jura came into being only in 1979 and is therefore the youngest canton of Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: In the Second World War Switzerland could bring in little food from abroad. With the Anbauschlacht, the “battle of cultivation”, it was meant to grow as much as possible itself. Almost everyone joined in, including children and people in the cities.
wichtigste: The idea came from Friedrich Traugott Wahlen, which is why it is also called Plan Wahlen.
Wahlen presented his plan in November 1940.
Every free piece of land was used, even parks and sports grounds.
The area of arable land rose from about 183,000 to about 352,000 hectares.
The potato harvest roughly tripled.
Potatoes, vegetables and fruit never had to be rationed.
Wahlen was elected to the Federal Council in 1958.

abschnitte.text: In the **Second World War** almost all the countries around Switzerland were at war. As a result, far fewer goods came across the border. Before the war Switzerland had imported a large part of its food. Around 1940 it produced only about half itself. Many foods were **rationed**: you got only a certain amount, which was written on food coupons.

The agricultural expert **Friedrich Traugott Wahlen** presented his plan in **November 1940**. Switzerland was to farm much more **arable land** and so produce more of its own food. Instead of meadows for cows there were to be more fields for potatoes, grain and vegetables. The plan got the name **Anbauschlacht**, although nobody fought in it.

Every free piece of land was used. **City parks**, **sports grounds** and gardens also became fields. The area of arable land rose from about 183,000 to about 352,000 hectares, so it nearly doubled. The potato harvest became about **three times** as big, and the vegetable harvest even four times as big. By the end of the war Switzerland could produce about **70 per cent** of its food itself.

Almost everyone joined in: farmers, city dwellers, school classes and children. Thanks to the Anbauschlacht there were enough **potatoes, vegetables and fruit**. These foods never had to be rationed. The Anbauschlacht became a **symbol** of the will to get through the hard times together. Wahlen became very well known as a result and was elected to the **Federal Council** in 1958.

gewusst: Even in the middle of big Swiss cities, potatoes grew on public squares during the war.
Friedrich Traugott Wahlen was a member of the Federal Council from 1959 to 1965.

teile.einleitung: Aegidius Tschudi was a politician and historian from Glarus. He lived from 1505 to 1572 and with his chronicle shaped the picture of the old Confederation right up to today.
wichtigste: Tschudi was born in Glarus in 1505 and came from a family of Landammänner, the heads of the canton.
His main work is called “Chronicon Helveticum” and covers the period from 1001 to 1470.
He dated the Rütli Oath to 8 November 1307.
Friedrich Schiller relied heavily on Tschudi for his drama “William Tell” of 1804.
Tschudi was bailiff in Sargans and twice in the County of Baden.
In the second half of his life he was a leading voice of the Catholic Counter-Reformation.

abschnitte.text: Tschudi came from a respected family of Glarus. He took on political offices early. In the **common lordships**, which were ruled jointly by several Confederate places, he was a **bailiff**: first in Sargans, then twice in Baden. In Baden he found many old documents. He later used these papers for his historical works.

The **Chronicon Helveticum** tells the history of the Confederation from 1001 to 1470. In it Tschudi placed the Rütli Oath on **8 November 1307**. The chronicle was printed only in 1734 to 1736 in Basel. In the 19th century, because of the Federal Charter, the year 1291 became accepted as the founding year. Experts today know that Tschudi filled some gaps with assumptions of his own.

The German poet **Friedrich Schiller** wrote the drama “William Tell” in 1804. From Tschudi's chronicle he took many characters and the course of the story of liberation. Through Schiller this story became known throughout the world. In this way Tschudi indirectly helped shape how many people still imagine the origins of Switzerland today.

In 1538 “Uralt warhafftig **Alpisch Rhetia**” appeared, an old title meaning “Ancient, truthful Alpine Rhaetia”. It was the only book printed in Tschudi's lifetime. It contained one of the first accurate maps of Switzerland. He completed his work **Gallia comata** on the early history of Helvetia in 1572, the year of his death. It appeared in print only in 1758.

In Tschudi's time the Reformation split the Confederation. Tschudi joined the Catholic side firmly. In Glarus, where both faiths lived, he became the spokesman of the **Counter-Reformation**. The **Tschudi War** named after him, from 1560, shows how fierce the dispute was. An open war did not break out, however.

gewusst: Tschudi's great chronicle existed only as a manuscript for about 160 years before it was printed.
Without Tschudi, Schiller's “William Tell” would probably have looked quite different.

teile.einleitung: Hornussen is a traditional Swiss sport played mainly in the canton of Bern. In it, a small disc, the Hornuss, is struck far across a field. The other team tries to stop it with wooden boards.
wichtigste: The small object that is struck far is called the Hornuss.
It is struck with a long, flexible rod.
The fielders catch the Hornuss with wooden boards.
The Hornuss hums in flight like a hornet.
Two teams play against each other.
Hornussen is especially popular in the Emmental and the Bernese countryside.

abschnitte.text: The **Hornuss** is a small, flat disc. It flies very fast and very far through the air. As it does so it makes a **humming sound**. This sounds like a **hornet**, and that is where its name comes from. It used to be made of wood, today it is made of plastic.

The Hornuss lies on a sloping launch ramp, the **Bock**. The striker has a long, **flexible rod** with a block of wood at the end. He swings it in a large arc over his head and hits the Hornuss. The farther the Hornuss flies, the more points there are. This takes a lot of practice and strength.

The other team stands in the field, the **Ries**. The players hold **boards** (Schindeln), which are wooden panels on a handle. When the Hornuss comes flying, they throw their board into the air to stop it. If the Hornuss lands in the field anyway, there is a **Nummer**, a minus point. Then the two teams swap.

Hornussen needs a lot of space, so it is played on **large meadows**. It is especially popular in the **canton of Bern**, for example in the **Emmental**. It is also called a **farmers' sport**. There are many Hornussen clubs in villages. Among the big events is the **Federal Hornussen Festival**.

gewusst: A good strike sends the Hornuss more than 200 metres.
Hornussen is one of the living traditions of Switzerland, together with Swiss wrestling and stone putting.

teile.einleitung: Charles the Bold was in the 15th century Duke of Burgundy and one of the most powerful princes of Europe. In the Burgundian Wars he fought against the Confederates and their allies. With his death in 1477 his realm fell apart.
wichtigste: Charles the Bold was born in Dijon in 1433.
He was Duke of Burgundy.
He wanted a royal crown, but never received it.
The Burgundian Wars lasted from 1474 to 1477.
The first battle took place in 1474 at Héricourt.
In 1477 Charles fell in the Battle of Nancy.
His duchy was divided between France and the Habsburgs.

abschnitte.text: Charles was born in **1433** in **Dijon**, the capital of the **Duchy of Burgundy**. From 1467 he ruled as **duke**. His realm stretched from the **Netherlands** to today's **French-speaking Switzerland**. It was very rich and had a large army. Because of his impetuous nature he was called **the Bold**.

Charles wanted to turn his duchy into a **kingdom**. To do so he wanted to link his territories in the north and in the south with each other. He negotiated with the emperor about a **royal crown**. The emperor, however, did not give it to him. When Charles occupied Lorraine and pushed south, he got in the way of the Confederates.

The **Burgundian Wars** lasted from **1474 to 1477**. In November 1474 the Confederates and their allies won at **Héricourt** in the Free County of Burgundy. In 1476 they defeated Charles at **Grandson** and shortly afterwards at **Murten**. In doing so they captured great treasures, which are called the **Burgundian booty**. The victories made the Confederates known as warriors all over Europe.

Charles had occupied the duchy of **Lorraine**. **Duke René II of Lorraine** called in Confederate **mercenaries** to help. In January **1477** they defeated Charles before **Nancy**. Charles the Bold fell in this battle. With this the Burgundian Wars ended.

Charles's daughter **Mary** married the Habsburg **Maximilian**. The Duchy of Burgundy itself was taken by **France**. The rich **Netherlands** went to the **Habsburgs**. So Charles's realm was divided between France and the Habsburgs. This division later led to long disputes between the two powers.

gewusst: Parts of the Burgundian booty can be seen today in the Bernisches Historisches Museum.
The Battle of Murten is still celebrated every year in Murten.

teile.einleitung: Jeremias Gotthelf was a Swiss writer and pastor in the Emmental. He wrote many books about the life of farmers. His real name was Albert Bitzius.
wichtigste: Jeremias Gotthelf was actually called Albert Bitzius.
He was born in Murten in 1797.
He was a pastor in Lützelflüh in the Emmental, canton of Bern.
He wrote mainly about farmers.
His first novel was “Der Bauernspiegel” (“The Farmers' Mirror”) of 1837.
Well known are “The Black Spider” and “Uli the Farmhand”.

abschnitte.text: Albert Bitzius was born in **1797** in **Murten**, where his father was a pastor. He, too, became a **pastor**. From the 1830s he preached in **Lützelflüh** in the **Emmental**. Lützelflüh lies in the **canton of Bern**. Besides his work in the church he wrote many books. He died in Lützelflüh in 1854.

**Jeremias Gotthelf** is a **pen name**, that is, a name he made up himself. It comes from his first novel **“Der Bauernspiegel”** of **1837**. In it the main character is called Jeremias Gotthelf. Later Bitzius used this name for all his books.

Gotthelf wrote mainly about **farmers** in his area. The Emmental is known for its hills and large farms. He told of their work, their worries and their **faith**. Often he also wanted to show his readers how to live well and honestly. In his books many words from **Bernese German** appear.

One of the best-known stories is **“The Black Spider”** of 1842. In it a giant spider brings great misfortune on a village because the people do not keep a promise. The story is a famous **horror story** and is still read in schools today. It has also been performed in the theatre and the opera.

In the novel **“Uli the Farmhand”**, Uli works as a **farmhand** on a farm. At first he is reckless, but he learns to be **hard-working and thrifty**. Later Gotthelf wrote a sequel with the title “Uli the Tenant”. The stories were also filmed. In Lützelflüh there is today a **Gotthelf Centre**.

gewusst: The Uli books were successfully filmed in the 1950s.
As a pastor, Gotthelf also campaigned strongly for better schools.

teile.einleitung: Bern is today the federal city of Switzerland. The city was founded in the Middle Ages in a loop of the Aare, and its heraldic animal, the bear, is still to be seen everywhere.
wichtigste: Duke Berchtold V of Zähringen founded Bern.
The city was founded in 1191.
According to legend Bern got its name from a bear.
In the coat of arms a black bear walks on a yellow stripe.
Bears live today in the Bear Park on the Aare.
The Bern old town has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.

abschnitte.text: Bern was founded in **1191**. Its founder was **Duke Berchtold V of Zähringen**. The Zähringens were a powerful noble family who founded several cities, for example Fribourg too. Berchtold V was the last duke of his family. The city lies on a hill that the **Aare** flows around on three sides. So it was well protected.

A legend tells how Bern got its name. The founder wanted to name the city after the first animal killed in the hunt. The first animal was a **bear**. Whether that really happened is not known. But the bear became the heraldic animal. In the **Bern coat of arms** a black bear walks on a yellow stripe across a red field.

For centuries Bern has kept live bears. In the past they lived in the cramped **Bear Pit**. Today they have more room in the **Bear Park** on the slope by the Aare. There visitors can watch the animals. The Bear Park is among the best-known sights of the city.

abschnitte.titel: An old town as World Heritage
abschnitte.text: The **Bern old town** was added to the list of **UNESCO World Heritage** in 1983. It has many old lanes with **arcades**, covered pavements in front of the houses. There are also fountains with colourful figures and the famous clock tower, the **Zytglogge**. About a hundred years after the founding, the Confederation came into being, which Bern later joined. Since 1848 Bern has been the seat of the Federal Council and Parliament.

gewusst: The arcades in the Bern old town are together several kilometres long.
The bear is so popular in Bern that you find it on fountains, flags and even on chocolate.

teile.einleitung: Johanna Spyri was a Swiss writer. Her book “Heidi”, about a girl in the mountains of Graubünden, is one of the best-known children's books in the world. It has been translated into very many languages and often filmed.
wichtigste: Johanna Spyri was born in Hirzel in the canton of Zurich in 1827.
Her most famous book is “Heidi”.
Heidi lives with her grandfather, the Alm-Öhi.
Her friend is the goatherd Peter.
In Frankfurt Heidi is to keep the sick Clara company.
The story is set above Maienfeld in Graubünden.

abschnitte.text: Johanna Spyri was born in **Hirzel** in the canton of Zurich in **1827**. Later she lived in the city of **Zurich**. She wrote many stories, especially for children. Her best-known book is **“Heidi”**, which appeared around **1880**. Johanna Spyri died in Zurich in 1901.

The orphan **Heidi** comes to her grandfather on the **alp** above **Maienfeld** in the canton of **Graubünden**. The grandfather lives alone in a hut, and the people call him the **Alm-Öhi**, the “Alp Uncle”. At first he is grumpy, but Heidi wins his heart. He has two goats named **Schwänli and Bärli**. With the goatherd **Peter**, Heidi often goes up to the alp.

One day Heidi is taken to **Frankfurt** in Germany. There she is to keep the sick **Clara** company. Clara cannot walk and sits in a **wheelchair**. The strict housekeeper **Fräulein Rottenmeier** runs the household and is very strict with Heidi. Heidi and Clara become friends, but Heidi becomes terribly **homesick** for the mountains.

abschnitte.titel: The grandmother and the bread rolls
abschnitte.text: Peter's **grandmother** is blind and finds it hard to eat the hard bread. So in Frankfurt Heidi collects **soft bread rolls** for her. When Heidi is finally allowed to go home, she brings her the rolls. The story shows how helpful Heidi is.

Later Clara visits Heidi on the alp. In the fresh mountain air and with Heidi's help she becomes stronger. In the end Clara learns to **walk** again. Today there is a **Heidi village** near Maienfeld, which many tourists from all over the world visit. The book has often been **filmed** and also made into a cartoon series.

gewusst: “Heidi” is among the most translated books of Swiss literature.
A Japanese cartoon series of 1974 made Heidi very well known in Asia, too.

teile.einleitung: The Fronts movement was a group of far-right parties in Switzerland in the 1930s. It took its lead from the dictatorships in Germany and Italy, but remained on the political fringe.
wichtigste: After Hitler's appointment as Reich Chancellor in 1933, the Fronts experienced the “Fronts spring”.
The most influential group was the National Front.
In 1933 it won 10 of 125 seats in the Zurich city council.
In 1935 the Fronts won only 2 seats in the National Council.
The Fonjallaz initiative for a ban on Freemasonry was clearly rejected in 1937.
In November 1940 the Federal Council dissolved the National Movement of Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: In January 1933 **Adolf Hitler** became Reich Chancellor in Germany. After that, far-right groups in Switzerland enjoyed a brief upswing. This period is called the **Fronts spring**. The groups called themselves **Fronts**. They rejected democracy and wanted an authoritarian state.

The most influential group was the **National Front**. It came into being in 1933 from a merger with the New Front. It published the newspaper **“Die Front”**. In 1933 it won **10 of 125 seats** in the Zurich city council. That was one of its greatest election successes.

In the **National Council elections of 1935** the Fronts won only **2 of 187 seats**. **Robert Tobler** won one for the National Front in Zurich, and the Union nationale won another in Geneva. In several cantons they came away empty-handed. The **Fonjallaz initiative**, which demanded a ban on Freemasonry, also failed clearly in 1937 with the people and the cantons. Most Swiss people rejected the Fronts.

**Spiritual National Defence** arose against the Fronts. It stressed Swiss values such as democracy, federalism and multilingualism. In 1940 Front groups joined together to form the **National Movement of Switzerland**. It was steered from Germany. In **November 1940** the Federal Council dissolved it.

gewusst: In the National Council elections of 1935 the Fronts won only 2 of 187 seats.
The popular initiative for a ban on Freemasonry was clearly rejected in 1937.

teile.einleitung: The Diocese of Chur is one of the oldest dioceses north of the Alps. Its history goes back to late antiquity and is closely tied to Raetia, present-day Graubünden.
wichtigste: With Asinio, a bishop of Chur is attested for the first time in 451/452.
Until 843 Chur belonged to the ecclesiastical province of Milan, afterwards to Mainz.
Since 1803 the diocese has been directly subject to the pope.
In the 7th and 8th centuries the Victorid family united secular and spiritual power.
Around 806 Charlemagne separated diocese and county.
Saint Lucius is the patron of the diocese.

abschnitte.text: The Diocese of Chur probably came into being as early as the 4th century. The first securely attested bishop is called **Asinio**. He is mentioned in connection with the **Synod of Milan** in 451/452, an assembly of bishops. A **diocese** is the area that a bishop leads in church matters. Chur lay on important routes across the Alps.

At first Chur belonged to the **ecclesiastical province of Milan**. It was a **suffragan diocese**, that is, subordinate to an archbishop in Milan, and looked south. After the division of the Frankish empire in 843 Chur came to the ecclesiastical province of **Mainz**. Since 1803 the diocese has been **exempt**: it belongs to no ecclesiastical province and is directly subject to the pope, like the other Swiss dioceses.

In the 7th and 8th centuries the local family of the **Victorids** ruled in Raetia. They provided the secular heads, the **praesides**, and also the bishops. So secular and church power lay in one hand. The last Victorid was **Bishop Tello**. In his will of 765 he left great property to the monastery of **Disentis**. The will is an important source on the early Middle Ages in Raetia.

Around 806 **Charlemagne** had the diocese and the county separated. This reform is called the **Divisio**. Secular administration was now taken over by a Frankish count. The bishop lost much property and power as a result. Later, however, the bishops of Chur again gained great influence and ruled as prince-bishops over a territory of their own.

The patron of the diocese is **Saint Lucius**. According to legend he was the first messenger of the faith to bring Christianity to Raetia. The legend even made him a British king. How much of this is historical is uncertain. In Chur the church of St Luzi, among other things, recalls him.

gewusst: The bishop of Chur still resides in the Bishop's Court above the old town of Chur.
From the bishop's subjects the League of God's House, one of the Three Leagues, came into being in 1367.

teile.einleitung: Bern is the seat of the Federal Council and Parliament. Because the Federal Constitution names no capital, people usually say federal city instead of capital.
wichtigste: On 28 November 1848 Parliament chose Bern as the seat of the federal authorities.
Zurich and Lucerne also wanted to be the federal city.
The Federal Constitution names no capital.
The Bern old town has arcades kilometres long.
Bern Minster has the tallest church tower in Switzerland.
Zurich has more inhabitants than Bern.
In Bern people speak mainly German, in everyday life Bernese German.

abschnitte.text: In 1848 Switzerland became a **federal state**. Now it needed a place for Parliament and government. **Zurich** and **Lucerne** also wanted this seat. On **28 November 1848** Parliament finally chose **Bern**. Bern lay between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland and was a large, well-known city.

According to the constitution, Switzerland has **no official capital**. Bern is the seat of the **federal authorities**, that is, the Federal Council, Parliament and the federal administration. That is why Bern is called the **federal city**. This suits Switzerland, where the cantons have a lot of power. Other important institutions are deliberately located in other cities, the Federal Supreme Court for example in Lausanne.

The **Bern old town** has **arcades** kilometres long. These are covered pavements in front of the houses. There you can shop dry even in the rain. Above the old town rises **Bern Minster**. Its tower is about 100 metres high, and no other church tower in Switzerland is taller.

In Bern people speak mainly **German**, in everyday life **Bernese German**. The canton of Bern is **bilingual**, however, and in the Bernese Jura and in Biel French is spoken too. Although Bern is the federal city, it is not the biggest city. **Zurich** has clearly more inhabitants. Geneva and Basel are also bigger than Bern.

gewusst: At the very top of the Minster tower there is a viewing platform that you reach up many steps.
The Bern old town with its arcades is also a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: In the Burgundian Wars the Confederates defeated Duke Charles the Bold. In doing so they captured many treasures from his camp. These treasures are called the Burgundian booty.
wichtigste: The Burgundian booty is the captured treasure of Charles the Bold.
It included tapestries, tents, jewellery and tableware.
At Grandson Charles left behind many cannons.
These cannons are called the Burgundian cannons.
The Bernese Historical Museum shows famous tapestries from the booty.

abschnitte.text: **Charles the Bold** was Duke of Burgundy and one of the richest princes in Europe. From 1474 to 1477 the Confederates fought against him. In 1476 they defeated him at **Grandson** and at **Murten**. Each time Charles fled and left his camp behind. In 1477 he died in the Battle of Nancy.

Charles travelled in great splendour. Precious things lay in his camp. The Confederates took away magnificent **tapestries**, tents, **jewellery** and tableware. Banners, weapons and clothes were also part of the **booty**. Most of the Confederates had never seen so much wealth.

At **Grandson** Charles left behind very many **cannons** as he fled. The Confederates took them home. They are called the **Burgundian cannons** today. Some of them are still preserved and can be seen in museums.

The **Bernese Historical Museum** owns precious **tapestries** from the Burgundian booty. They are skilfully woven and show figures, plants and coats of arms. Such tapestries used to be hung on the walls of castles and tents. They kept people warm and showed their owner's wealth. Today they are among the museum's most valuable treasures.

gewusst: The places of the Confederation argued fiercely over the distribution of the booty.
Parts of the Burgundian booty can now be seen in museums in various Swiss cities.

teile.einleitung: Bertha of Swabia was queen of Burgundy over 1,000 years ago. Many legends surround her, and in the canton of Vaud she is still regarded as a good and hard-working queen.
wichtigste: Bertha lived in the 10th century and was queen of Burgundy.
At that time Burgundy also included present-day western Switzerland.
Her first husband was King Rudolf II of Burgundy.
Her daughter Adelaide married Emperor Otto I and became empress.
According to legend Bertha spun wool while riding.
She is buried in Payerne and is a symbol of Vaud.

abschnitte.text: Bertha came from **Swabia**, a region in present-day southern Germany. She married **King Rudolf II** of Burgundy. The kingdom of **Burgundy** also included present-day western Switzerland. Rudolf died in the year 937. After that Bertha married a second time, a king from Italy.

The best-known legend tells that Bertha rode through the land on her horse and **spun wool** as she went. Spinning means twisting wool into a thread. The picture shows her as a **hard-working** queen who was never idle. In the stories she also helped poor people. Whether it was really all like that is not known for certain.

Bertha's daughter was called **Adelaide**. She married **Emperor Otto I**, one of the most powerful rulers of his time. So Adelaide became an **empress**. She is among the most famous women of the Middle Ages. Bertha herself died after the year 966.

Bertha was buried in **Payerne**. In this town stands a large old **abbey church**, a church that belonged to a monastery. In the 19th century Bertha became a **symbol of the canton of Vaud**, to which Payerne belongs. People liked to remember her as a good queen from olden times.

gewusst: In French people say of a long-vanished good old time: “Du temps où Berthe filait”, meaning “in the days when Bertha was spinning”.
The abbey church of Payerne is regarded as one of the most important Romanesque churches in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi was a famous Swiss educator. He wanted all children to be able to learn, including poor ones. His principle of learning with head, heart and hand is still well known today.
wichtigste: Pestalozzi was born in Zurich on 12 January 1746.
He was an educator, that is, an expert in upbringing and teaching.
Children should learn with head, heart and hand.
At the Neuhof near Birr he took in poor children.
In 1799 he looked after orphans in Stans.
He ran schools in Burgdorf and Yverdon.
He died in Brugg in 1827.

abschnitte.text: Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi was born on **12 January 1746** in **Zurich**. His father died early, and the family had little money. Pestalozzi saw how poorly many people in the countryside lived. He wanted to help them, above all through **education**. He became an **educator**, that is, someone who is concerned with upbringing and learning.

In Aargau Pestalozzi bought a farm, the **Neuhof** near **Birr**. There he took in **poor children**. They worked together on the farm and at the same time learned to read, write and calculate. The project, however, earned him no money and had to be given up. After that he wrote the novel **“Lienhard und Gertrud”** about the life of a simple family in the countryside.

Pestalozzi said that children should learn with **head, heart and hand**. The head stands for **thinking**, the heart for **feeling** and the hand for **doing**. All three belong together. Children should not only learn by heart, but look at things and try them out for themselves. This idea shapes many schools to this day.

After the fighting of 1798 there were many orphans in **Stans**. Pestalozzi looked after these **orphans** in **1799**. From **1800** he taught in **Burgdorf** in the canton of Bern and opened a school in the **castle**. From **1805** he led an **institute** in **Yverdon** on Lake Neuchâtel for about 20 years. Visitors from all over Europe came to see his school.

Pestalozzi died on **17 February 1827** in **Brugg**. He was buried in **Birr**, by the Neuhof. Many schools, streets and foundations bear his name today. The **Pestalozzi Children's Village** in Trogen was founded after the Second World War for war orphans. Pestalozzi is regarded as one of the most important educators in history.

gewusst: In 1792 Pestalozzi was named an honorary citizen of the French Republic.
On his gravestone it says, among other things, “Saviour of the poor at the Neuhof”.

teile.einleitung: The Helvetic Society was an association of enlightened Swiss people in the 18th century. Its members wanted people from different places and denominations to see themselves as fellow Confederates. It is regarded as an important forerunner of modern Swiss cohesion.
wichtigste: The Helvetic Society was founded in 1761.
The first meetings took place in Schinznach-Bad.
It wanted to strengthen cohesion across local and denominational boundaries.
Isaak Iselin of Basel was one of the founders.
Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi was also a member.
Since 1914 the New Helvetic Society has continued its ideals.

abschnitte.text: In the 18th century the **Enlightenment** spread in Europe. It relied on reason, education and tolerance. The Confederacy was then a loose alliance of many places, divided by faith. In 1758 **Franz Urs Balthasar** of Lucerne published the pamphlet **“Patriotic Dreams of a Confederate”**. In it he set out ideas for a renewal of the Confederacy, which prompted the founding.

In 1761 enlightened men from different places met for the first time for a friendly exchange. A year later the society gave itself a name and a programme. The meetings took place in the spa town of **Schinznach-Bad** in Aargau. It lay conveniently between Zurich, Basel, Bern and Lucerne. So members from different places could easily travel there.

The main aim was to strengthen **cohesion** across local and **denominational boundaries**. Reformed and Catholics were to see themselves as fellow **Confederates**. Tolerance, education and the common good were in the foreground. Among the founders was the Basel town clerk **Isaak Iselin**. Members also included the educator **Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi** as well as Philipp Albert Stapfer and Albrecht Rengger.

Many members later shaped the **Helvetic Republic**. During the French occupation from **1798 to 1807** the meetings were suspended. After that the society took up its activity again and joined the liberal movement. With the **federal state of 1848** many saw their aims as achieved. In 1858 the society dissolved.

In 1914 the **New Helvetic Society** was founded. It continues the ideals of the old society. Shortly before the First World War it wanted to strengthen cohesion between **German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland**. At that time a trench threatened between the parts of the country. Today, too, it works for exchange within Switzerland.

gewusst: Reformed and Catholics met here at a time when this was anything but a matter of course.
Schinznach-Bad is still a spa resort today.

teile.einleitung: The Freischaren expeditions were two armed attacks by liberals on the canton of Lucerne in 1844 and 1845. They failed, but they sharpened the dispute that led to the Sonderbund War in 1847.
wichtigste: The Freischaren wanted to overthrow the conservative Lucerne government.
They also wanted to drive the Jesuits out of Lucerne.
The first expedition took place on 8 December 1844 and failed quickly.
About 3,500 armed men took part in the second expedition of 1845.
At Malters the fleeing irregulars were caught in an ambush, and about 2,000 were taken prisoner.
The young poet Gottfried Keller went along too.
The conservative cantons then founded a defensive alliance, the Sonderbund.

abschnitte.text: In the 1840s Switzerland was deeply divided. The **liberals** wanted a strong federal state and less influence of the Church. The **Catholic Conservatives** wanted to preserve the old order and the rights of the cantons. In 1844 the canton of **Lucerne** called the **Jesuits** to its higher schools. Many liberals saw this as a provocation.

Volunteer armed groups were called **Freischaren**, or irregulars. On **8 December 1844** about 1,000 irregulars from Aargau, Solothurn and Basel-Landschaft marched against Lucerne. They wanted to overthrow the conservative government. The uprising in Lucerne, however, did not happen. The irregulars quickly withdrew again.

At the end of March 1845 the Freischaren tried again. About **3,500 armed men** marched from Huttwil and Zofingen against Lucerne. They were led by **Ulrich Ochsenbein** and the deposed Lucerne liberal **Jakob Robert Steiger**. Despite their numbers they failed. On the retreat a shot at night set off panic, and at **Malters** they were caught in an ambush.

The people of Lucerne took about **2,000 irregulars** prisoner. The prisoners from other cantons were released only against high **ransoms**. Among the participants was the young Zurich man **Gottfried Keller**, who later became a famous poet. He went along as a convinced liberal, but did not fight.

The Catholic Conservative cantons felt threatened. They joined together in a **defensive alliance** of their own, the **Sonderbund**. This sharpened the conflict further. In 1847 came the **Sonderbund War**, which the liberals won. After that the modern **federal state** came into being in 1848.

gewusst: The poet Gottfried Keller took part in the second Freischaren expedition as a young man.
Ulrich Ochsenbein, a leader of the Freischaren, became one of the first federal councillors in 1848.

t1lsdflf.t: The Founding of the Federal State

teile.einleitung: In 1848 the loose confederation of the cantons became the modern Swiss federal state. It received a common constitution, a government and a parliament. The founding is regarded as the birth of today's Switzerland.
wichtigste: Switzerland became a federal state in 1848.
Unlike a confederation of states, a federal state has a common government and a common parliament.
The Sonderbund War of 1847 had come before.
At the founding, Switzerland consisted of 22 cantons.
On 28 November 1848 Bern was chosen as the seat of the federal authorities.
In 1850 the franc was introduced on the model of the French franc.
1 August was celebrated for the first time as a federal celebration in 1891.

abschnitte.text: Until 1848 Switzerland was a **confederation of states**: the cantons were almost independent states that worked together on only a few questions. There was no common government and no real parliament, only the Diet of the envoys. With the Federal Constitution of 1848 Switzerland became a **federal state** with Federal Council, National Council and Council of States. The cantons, however, kept many rights of their own.

Before the founding, liberal and Catholic Conservative cantons quarrelled fiercely. Seven conservative cantons joined together in the **Sonderbund**, which the Diet declared forbidden. In November 1847 the federal troops under General **Guillaume-Henri Dufour** defeated the Sonderbund in a short war. Dufour took care to spare the opponents, so that the country could come together again afterwards.

On 28 November 1848 the Federal Assembly chose **Bern** as the seat of the federal authorities. The strongest rival was Zurich, and Lucerne was also under discussion. Zurich received, as a kind of compensation, the **ETH**, the Federal Institute of Technology. Because no capital is laid down in law, Bern is still called the “federal city” today.

Before 1848 almost every canton had its own coins, measures and weights. The new federal state standardised these and abolished the customs duties between the cantons. In 1850 the **Swiss franc** was introduced as a single currency, on the model of the French franc. The **post** also became a task of the federal state.

At the founding, Switzerland consisted of **22 cantons**, and the youngest canton, Jura, was added in 1979. The young federal state was shaped by the **Radical Liberals**, who provided all the federal councillors until 1891. In 1891, 1 August was celebrated for the first time as a federal celebration, in memory of the Federal Charter of 1291. The basic order of 1848 forms the foundation of Switzerland to this day.

begriffe.erklaerung: A loose union of independent states without a common government.
A state made up of member states with a common government and a common parliament.
An alliance of seven Catholic Conservative cantons in the 1840s.
The seat of the federal authorities, in Switzerland Bern.
The money used to pay in a country.

gewusst: The Sonderbund War lasted barely four weeks and is regarded as the last war on Swiss soil.
Guillaume-Henri Dufour later also directed the work on the first accurate map of Switzerland, the Dufour Map.
The highest mountain in Switzerland, the Dufourspitze, was named after General Dufour.

teile.einleitung: Since 1848 Switzerland has been a federal state. That means that the cantons have a shared government, a shared parliament and a shared constitution, but still decide many things themselves. In the first decades of the young federal state many things were created that still shape Switzerland today.
wichtigste: The Swiss federal state came into being in 1848 with the first Federal Constitution.
On 16 November 1848 the Federal Assembly elected the first Federal Council.
On 28 November 1848 Bern was chosen as the seat of the federal authorities.
Zurich received the Federal Institute of Technology as compensation.
From 1848 to 1891 the Radical Liberals provided all the federal councillors.
Alfred Escher shaped railway building and the Gotthard tunnel.
The present Federal Palace in Bern was opened in 1902.

abschnitte.text: A **federal state** is a state made up of several member states, in Switzerland the cantons. The federal government takes care of tasks that affect everyone, such as the army, foreign policy or money. The cantons have their own governments, parliaments and laws, for example for schools and police. This division is called **federalism**.

After the first Federal Council, the Federal Assembly had to decide where the authorities would have their seat. On 28 November 1848 **Bern** prevailed over Zurich and Lucerne. Zurich later received the **ETH** instead, which began teaching in 1855. The construction of the present Federal Palace with its great dome was completed in 1902.

After the first Railway Act of 1852, it was mainly **private railway companies** that built the railway lines. The Zurich entrepreneur and politician **Alfred Escher** founded the Northeastern Railway and the Credit Institution and pushed forward the building of the Gotthard tunnel. The tunnel opened in 1882 and connected German-speaking Switzerland with Ticino and Italy. In 1902 the Swiss Federal Railways SBB came into being from several private railways.

In the young federal state the **Radical Liberals**, also called Liberal-Radicals, dominated. From 1848 to 1891 they provided all the members of the Federal Council. Only in 1891 was the first Catholic-Conservative federal councillor elected, **Josef Zemp** of Lucerne. With this the inclusion of further parties in the government began, which is still typical of Switzerland today.

Neuchâtel had been a Swiss canton since 1848, but the king of **Prussia** still claimed rights as prince of Neuchâtel. In 1856 royalists attempted an uprising that failed. Prussia threatened war, and Switzerland mobilised troops. In 1857 the king gave up his rights, and the **Neuchâtel affair** was settled peacefully.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state of several member states with a shared government and shared parliament.
The division of power between the federal government, the cantons and the municipalities.
The seat of government and parliament, in Switzerland Bern.
A liberal political current that strongly shaped the young federal state.

gewusst: Switzerland has no capital in law, and Bern is officially called the federal city.
Thousands of workers, mainly from Italy, worked on the Gotthard tunnel, and many lost their lives in its construction.
Alfred Escher got a large monument in Zurich in front of the main station.

teile.einleitung: The Benedictine convent of St John lies in Müstair, in the far east of Switzerland on the border with Italy. It was founded around 775 and is world famous for its wall paintings from the time around 800. Since 1983 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: The monastery lies in the Val Müstair on the border with Italy.
It was founded around 775.
The date was determined from the tree rings in the building timber.
According to tradition, Charlemagne is said to have founded the monastery.
The church is famous for wall paintings from the Carolingian period.
Benedictine nuns have lived there since the 12th century.
The Planta Tower now houses the monastery museum.

abschnitte.titel: In the far east of Switzerland
abschnitte.text: The **Val Müstair** lies in the far east of Switzerland in the canton of **Graubünden**. Right after the village of Müstair begins **South Tyrol**, which belongs to **Italy**. The monastery is called **St John's**, after John the Baptist. The name Müstair comes from the Latin word for **monastery**. So the village is named after the monastery.

Experts date the founding to about **775**. This falls in the time when the **Franks** were conquering large territories. The **legend** tells that **Charlemagne** founded the monastery. In the church stands a life-size **statue** of him. Experts determined the founding date with **dendrochronology**: they compared the **tree rings** in the building timber with known patterns and so knew when the trees were felled.

The monastery church is world famous for its **wall paintings** from the time around **800**. These pictures on wet plaster are called **frescoes**. They show numerous scenes from the life of Jesus and from the Bible. There are hardly so many early wall paintings from the **Carolingian period** anywhere else. For this reason the monastery was added to the **UNESCO World Heritage** list in **1983**.

The monastery was at first a **monastery for men**. Since the **12th century** **Benedictine nuns** have lived there, that is, nuns following the rule of Saint Benedict. Around **960** a mighty residential and defensive tower was built. The abbess **Angelina von Planta** later extended it, which is why it is called the **Planta Tower**. Today the **monastery museum** is housed in it.

gewusst: Müstair Monastery has been inhabited without interruption for over 1,200 years.
The frescoes were hidden for a long time under later paintings and were uncovered only in the 20th century.

teile.einleitung: Helvetia is a female figure who represents Switzerland. You see her on coins, stamps and statues. She is also called the mother of the nation.
wichtigste: Helvetia is a female figure for Switzerland.
Her name comes from the Celtic people of the Helvetii.
She holds a spear and a shield with the Swiss cross.
The standing Helvetia is on the half franc, the one franc coin and the two franc coin.
In Basel the statue “Helvetia on a Journey” sits by the Rhine.

abschnitte.text: **Helvetia** is not a real person, but a **symbolic figure**. A symbolic figure stands for something greater, here for the whole of Switzerland. She is also called the **mother of the nation**. Many countries have such female figures, for example Marianne in France. Helvetia became especially popular in the 19th century.

The name Helvetia comes from the **Helvetii**. They were a **Celtic people** in the area of today's Switzerland. For this reason the Romans called the land Helvetia. The abbreviation **CH** also recalls this. It stands for Confoederatio Helvetica, Latin for the Swiss Confederation.

Helvetia appears on the **half franc**, the **one franc coin** and the **two franc coin**. In one hand she holds a **spear**. With the other hand she holds a **shield** with the **Swiss cross**. The cross shows that she stands for Switzerland. On the five franc coin, by contrast, a herdsman's head can be seen.

In **Basel** Helvetia sits on the **Kleinbasel bank of the Rhine** by the Mittlere Brücke. The statue is called **“Helvetia on a Journey”**. She has laid shield and spear down beside her and looks at the Rhine. It looks as if she is taking a break. Many people in Basel know her well.

gewusst: The abbreviation CH on cars comes from the Latin name Confoederatio Helvetica.
Swiss stamps say “Helvetia” because this Latin name is the same for all the national languages.

teile.einleitung: Einsiedeln Abbey in the canton of Schwyz is one of the best-known monasteries in Switzerland. Benedictine monks live here, and for centuries people have made pilgrimages to the Black Madonna. The history of the place begins with the hermit Meinrad.
wichtigste: Einsiedeln Abbey lies in the canton of Schwyz.
In the 9th century the hermit Meinrad lived here.
Meinrad was killed by robbers on 21 January 861.
The monastery was founded in the year 934.
Benedictine monks live in the monastery.
In the Chapel of Grace stands the Black Madonna.
The monastery has bred horses for a long time.

abschnitte.text: In the **9th century** the area around Einsiedeln was still a dense, dark forest, the **Dark Forest** (Finsterer Wald). The monk **Meinrad** withdrew there from the monastery of Reichenau. He lived alone as a **hermit** and prayed. On **21 January 861** he was killed by robbers. Since then he has been venerated as a **martyr** and is regarded as the spiritual founder of Einsiedeln.

A **legend** tells that Meinrad had two **ravens**. After his death the ravens are said to have pursued the culprits until they were caught. That is why **two ravens** can be seen in the **coat of arms** of Einsiedeln. The story is a legend, but it is very well known in Einsiedeln.

On the site of Meinrad's cell a **monastery** was founded in the year **934**, that is, in the **10th century**. **Benedictine monks** live here. They follow the rule of Saint Benedict: **pray and work**. The present large **monastery church** was built in the 18th century in the **Baroque** style. The monastery also runs a school.

In the **Chapel of Grace** in the monastery church stands the **Black Madonna**. It is a figure of Mary with the infant Jesus. Einsiedeln is an important **place of pilgrimage**. For many centuries people have **made pilgrimages** there to pray. Many even come on foot along the **Way of St James**, which leads through Einsiedeln.

The monks have **bred horses** for a long time. The monastery has one of the **oldest horse studs in Europe**. The horses are called **Einsiedler**. In earlier times they were in demand as strong riding and draught horses. Today you can visit the Marstall, that is, the horse stable.

gewusst: The monastery's horse stud has been documented since the Middle Ages.
The large square in front of the monastery church is one of the most impressive Baroque squares in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Without Daniel Peter there might be no milk chocolate. The Swiss from Vaud was the first to mix milk into chocolate and so made Switzerland the land of chocolate.
wichtigste: Daniel Peter invented milk chocolate.
After many attempts he succeeded in 1875.
He lived and worked in Vevey on Lake Geneva.
He used thickened condensed milk.
Before that he worked in candle making.
The condensed milk came from his neighbour Henri Nestlé.

abschnitte.text: Daniel Peter came from the canton of **Vaud**. At first he worked in **candle making** in **Vevey** on Lake Geneva. When paraffin lamps came in, fewer candles were needed. Peter therefore looked for new work. He married into the family of the chocolate maker **Cailler** and began making chocolate himself.

Peter wanted to make chocolate with **milk**. That was difficult. Fresh milk contains a lot of **water**. Water and cocoa butter mix badly, and the chocolate went off quickly. For many years Peter tried out ever new mixtures.

The solution was **condensed milk**. This is milk from which a large part of the water has been removed, so it is **thickened**. This milk was supplied to him by his neighbour **Henri Nestlé**, who made milk products in Vevey. In 1875 Peter succeeded in this way with the first **milk chocolate**. Later he improved the recipe further.

Milk chocolate was milder and sweeter than dark chocolate. It soon became popular in many countries. Daniel Peter's firm grew and later merged with other chocolate firms. Today these brands belong to the **Nestlé** group in Vevey. Switzerland is still world-famous for its chocolate.

gewusst: Vevey is still the headquarters of Nestlé, one of the largest food companies in the world.
It took several years full of experiments before milk chocolate really worked well.

teile.einleitung: In 1798 French troops marched into Switzerland. This is called the French invasion. It meant the end of the Old Confederacy.
wichtigste: In January 1798 Vaud, with French support, proclaimed the Lemanic Republic.
Frédéric-César de La Harpe from Vaud urged France to intervene.
On 5 March 1798 the Bernese won at Neuenegg, but lost at Grauholz.
After that the French marched into Bern and took the state treasury with them.
The Old Confederacy collapsed, and a new state came into being.
In September 1798 Nidwalden fiercely resisted the French.

abschnitte.text: Since the **French Revolution** of 1789, France had been spreading the ideas of **freedom and equality**. In the Old Confederacy there were still masters and **subjects**. Many subjects wanted more rights. France also wanted Switzerland as an ally and for the sake of the Alpine passes.

**Vaud** was a subject territory of Bern. **Frédéric-César de La Harpe** from Vaud fought for its liberation and urged France to intervene. He was the private tutor of the later Russian tsar Alexander I. On **24 January 1798** Vaud proclaimed the **“Lemanic Republic”**. Shortly afterwards French troops moved in.

At the beginning of March 1798 the French attacked Bern. On **5 March** the Bernese won at **Neuenegg** and drove the French back. On the same day, however, they lost at **Grauholz** near Bern. Bern then surrendered. The French marched into the city.

Bern was very rich. The French took the **Bernese state treasury** with them. With the money they paid for their wars, among other things. Other cities also had to hand over money and goods. Many people suffered from the levies and the foreign soldiers.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the Old Confederacy
abschnitte.text: With the French invasion the **Old Confederacy** collapsed. In April 1798 the **Helvetic Republic** came into being, a unitary state on the French model. Not everyone agreed. **Nidwalden** did not want to accept the new order. In September 1798 there was heavy fighting there with many dead.

gewusst: On the same day the Bernese won at Neuenegg and lost at Grauholz.
Frédéric-César de La Harpe was the tutor of the later Tsar Alexander I of Russia.

t1q92gr3.t: The Internment of the Bourbaki Army

teile.einleitung: In February 1871 an entire French army crossed the border into Switzerland. The roughly 87,000 soldiers of the so-called Bourbaki Army were disarmed and cared for in Switzerland. It was one of the greatest humanitarian tasks in the history of the young federal state.
wichtigste: The Bourbaki Army came to Switzerland in the Franco-Prussian War.
About 87,000 soldiers were interned at the beginning of February 1871.
The Treaty of Les Verrières regulated the crossing and the disarmament.
General Hans Herzog led the Swiss troops.
The soldiers were distributed among almost all the cantons.
France paid back the costs of over 12 million francs.
In Lucerne the Bourbaki Panorama recalls the event.

abschnitte.text: In the **Franco-Prussian War** of 1870 and 1871, France fought against Prussia and its allies. The French **Army of the East** was under General Charles Denis Bourbaki, which is why it is called the **Bourbaki Army**. In the harsh winter it was pushed back into the **Jura**. The soldiers were exhausted, hungry and poorly clothed. The only way out left to them was into neutral Switzerland.

On **1 February 1871** a treaty was signed in **Les Verrières** in the canton of Neuchâtel. On the Swiss side **General Hans Herzog** of Aargau, the commander in chief of the Swiss troops, signed. He demanded that the French **hand over all their weapons**. As a neutral country, Switzerland could not take in soldiers ready for combat. After that about **87,000 men** crossed the border, together with about **12,000 horses**.

The **Federal Council** distributed the interned soldiers among all the cantons except **Ticino**. Many **municipalities** helped with accommodation in churches, schoolhouses and gymnasiums. The population brought food, clothes and blankets. The young **Swiss Red Cross** also helped with the care. Many soldiers and horses were ill and completely starved, and some did not survive despite the help.

In **March 1871** the war ended, and the soldiers returned to France. The internment had cost over **12 million francs**. **France** paid this amount back to Switzerland. The taking in of the Bourbaki Army is regarded to this day as an example of Switzerland's **humanitarian tradition**.

The painter **Edouard Castres** had himself experienced the internment as a helper. He created a huge **circular painting** showing the crossing of the army at Les Verrières. The picture is over **100 metres long** and hangs in a round building. Since 1889 it has been on display in **Lucerne**. Anyone standing in the middle has the feeling of being right in the middle of the events.

gewusst: The Bourbaki Panorama in Lucerne is one of the few large circular paintings in the world to survive.
Besides the soldiers, thousands of horses also had to be fed and cared for.
During the internment the painter Castres worked as a volunteer for the Red Cross.

teile.einleitung: The year 1816 went down in history as the “year without a summer”. In Switzerland and large parts of Europe it was cold and wet, and the harvests spoiled. The cause lay far away, in a volcano in Indonesia.
wichtigste: 1816 is called the “year without a summer”.
The main cause was the eruption of the volcano Tambora in April 1815.
Tambora lies on the island of Sumbawa in Indonesia.
In Switzerland it snowed almost every month down to about 800 metres.
In 1816 and 1817 many people went hungry, especially in eastern Switzerland.
Tsar Alexander I of Russia sent money and grain.
On Lake Geneva Mary Shelley began her novel “Frankenstein”.

abschnitte.text: In **April 1815** the volcano **Tambora** on the island of **Sumbawa** in Indonesia erupted violently. It was one of the strongest volcanic eruptions of recent centuries. Huge amounts of ash and gases reached high into the **atmosphere**. They spread around the whole Earth and blocked part of the sunlight. As a result the **climate cooled** worldwide.

The year **1816** was unusually cold and rainy in Europe. In Switzerland it snowed at least once in every month down to about **800 metres**. In July snow fell even in the lowlands. Because of the cold and **continuous rain** the grain grew badly, and potatoes rotted in the fields. There was also a lack of hay for the cattle.

Because the harvests failed, **grain prices** rose sharply. By June 1817 grain in German-speaking Switzerland cost about **two to three times as much** as in 1815. Many people could no longer afford bread. Out of need they ate **grass and leaves**, snails and unripe fruit. Many people emigrated afterwards, for example to America.

**Eastern Switzerland** was hit especially hard. Many families there lived from **cottage industry** in the textile trade, for example from spinning and weaving. They had no land of their own and had to buy their food. When prices rose, their wages were no longer enough. **Tsar Alexander I** of Russia felt connected to Switzerland and donated **100,000 roubles** and grain.

In the rainy summer of 1816 the writer **Mary Shelley**, the poet **Lord Byron** and friends were stuck in the **Villa Diodati** on **Lake Geneva**. Because they could hardly go out, they told each other ghost stories. In the course of this Mary Shelley began to write her novel **“Frankenstein”**. So out of bad weather arose one of the best-known books in the world.

gewusst: As a teenager Tsar Alexander I had Frédéric-César de La Harpe from Vaud as his teacher.
In North America, too, snow fell in the summer of 1816.
The hunger years of 1816 and 1817 are regarded as the last great famine in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Gotthard Tunnel of 1882 is a railway tunnel under the Gotthard. It connects Göschenen in the canton of Uri with Airolo in Ticino. When it opened, it was the longest tunnel in the world.
wichtigste: The tunnel was opened in 1882 after about ten years of construction.
It is about 15 kilometres long.
It connects Göschenen and Airolo.
Most of the workers came from Italy.
The rock was blasted with dynamite and drilled with compressed air.
Officially 199 workers died in accidents.

abschnitte.text: The **Gotthard Tunnel** runs under the **Gotthard**. It begins in **Göschenen** in the canton of Uri and ends in **Airolo** in Ticino. The tunnel is about **15 kilometres** long. At that time it was the longest tunnel in the world. It is part of the **Gotthard Railway**, which connects the north with Ticino.

It was built from 1872 to 1882. With the then new **dynamite** the hard rock could be blasted. The drilling machines ran on **compressed air**. At the entrances, the **portals**, water-driven plants compressed air. The compressed air drove the drills and brought some fresh air into the tunnel.

Most of the workers came from **Italy**. They worked under very hard conditions: it was hot, dusty and dangerous. Officially **199 workers** died in accidents. Many more fell ill or died later from the effects of the work. The building contractor **Louis Favre** also died in the tunnel in 1879, before the end of the work.

The construction was very expensive. Besides Switzerland, **Italy** and **Germany** also paid high contributions. Both countries wanted a fast rail link through the Alps. An important promoter in Switzerland was **Alfred Escher**. Without the help of the neighbouring countries, the project would hardly have been possible.

The tunnel connected **German-speaking Switzerland** and **Ticino** much better. By train you could quickly reach the south and go on to Italy. The mail coaches over the pass lost their importance. In 2016 the much longer **Gotthard Base Tunnel** was opened. The old tunnel, however, is still in use.

gewusst: When it opened in 1882, the Gotthard Tunnel was the longest tunnel in the world.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel of 2016, at about 57 kilometres, is almost four times as long.

teile.einleitung: Ferdinand Hodler was one of the best-known Swiss painters. He lived from 1853 to 1918 and painted mountains, lakes, people and heroes of Swiss history.
wichtigste: Ferdinand Hodler was born in Bern in 1853, and his family was poor.
As a boy he learned painting in Thun.
He lived most of the time in Geneva, where he died in 1918.
He often painted mountains and lakes, especially Lake Thun.
One well-known picture shows Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau above a sea of fog.
“The Woodcutter” and his picture of William Tell are also famous.

abschnitte.text: Ferdinand Hodler was born in **Bern** in 1853. His family was **poor**, and he lost his parents early. As a boy he came to **Thun**. There he learned the craft from a painter. He painted pictures for tourists to earn money.

Already as a young man Hodler moved to **Geneva**. He lived there for most of his life. He kept educating himself and painted a great deal. For a long time he had little success. Later he became famous in Switzerland and abroad. He died in Geneva in 1918.

Hodler liked to paint **landscapes** with mountains and lakes. He painted **Lake Thun** with its mountains again and again. One well-known picture shows **Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau** in the Bernese Oberland above a **sea of fog**. He painted with **clear colours and shapes**. Often he arranged things so that they repeat and form a pattern.

Hodler also painted people who look strong and determined. In the picture **“The Woodcutter”** a man swings an axe at a tree. The picture is very well known. Hodler also painted **William Tell** as a strong man stepping out of the clouds, carrying his **crossbow**. With such pictures he shaped how people imagined Swiss history.

Today Hodler is regarded as one of the most important Swiss **artists**. His pictures hang in many museums, for example in Bern, Geneva and Zurich. He also painted large **murals** on Swiss history. His pictures are sold for very high prices. Many people know his mountains and the woodcutter.

gewusst: Hodler painted Lake Thun so often that these pictures are among his best known.
Hodler painted William Tell as if he were coming straight out of the clouds towards the viewers.

teile.einleitung: The files scandal came to light in 1989. It then became known that the Swiss state security service had for decades monitored hundreds of thousands of people and organisations and recorded them on index cards.
wichtigste: A “Fiche” is an index card with notes about a person or organisation.
Until 1990 the federal government and cantons created about 900,000 files.
The central card index was kept by the Federal Police of the Federal Prosecutor's Office.
Most people were put on file during the Cold War, out of fear of communists.
A Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry (PUK) uncovered the scandal in 1989.
The president of the PUK was Moritz Leuenberger.
On 3 March 1990 about 30,000 people demonstrated in Bern against the “snooper state”.

abschnitte.text: **Fiche** is the French word for **index card**. On such cards the police noted observations about people and organisations. They recorded, for example, who went to which meeting or whom someone met. Between 1900 and 1990 the federal government and cantons created about **900,000 files**. More than 700,000 people and organisations were recorded.

The central card index was kept by the **Federal Police** of the Federal Prosecutor's Office. Cantonal police offices supplied it with many reports. Most people were put on file during the **Cold War** because **communists** were feared. A lot of things that looked like left-wing politics were suspicious. Those monitored included trade unionists, peace activists and foreigners.

It all began with the resignation of Federal Councillor **Elisabeth Kopp** in early 1989. After that a **Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry**, **PUK** for short, investigated her Department of Justice and Police. The president of the PUK was the Social Democrat **Moritz Leuenberger**, who later became a federal councillor himself. In November 1989 the PUK presented its report. It had come across the huge card index.

Many people were outraged. On **3 March 1990** about 30,000 people demonstrated in Bern against the **“snooper state”**. Many demanded **access** to their own file, and hundreds of thousands made an application. They often received their files with blacked-out passages. After that state security was reorganised and more strictly controlled.

gewusst: Many files contained quite harmless things, for example who read a particular newspaper or was at a festival.
The PUK president Moritz Leuenberger later became a federal councillor himself.

teile.einleitung: Albert Anker was one of the best-loved painters in Switzerland. He lived from 1831 to 1910 and liked best to paint children and simple village life.
wichtigste: Albert Anker was a Swiss painter and lived from 1831 to 1910.
He was born in Ins in the Bernese Seeland and lived there.
At first he studied theology, because he was meant to become a pastor.
He learned painting in Paris with the Swiss painter Charles Gleyre.
He particularly liked to paint children playing, learning or sleeping.
As well as paintings, he also designed pictures for ceramic plates.

abschnitte.text: Albert Anker was born in 1831 in **Ins** in the Bernese Seeland. The village lies between Lake Biel and Lake Neuchâtel. Anker stayed faithful to Ins all his life. For many years he spent the winters in Paris and the summers in Ins. You can visit his house with the studio today.

At first Anker was supposed to become a pastor. So he studied **theology**, that is, the study of God and of faith. But he would rather paint. He went to **Paris** and learned there with the Swiss painter **Charles Gleyre**. At that time Paris was the most important city for art in Europe.

Anker liked best to paint **children**: playing, learning, knitting or sleeping. He also showed schoolrooms, farm parlours and old people in the village. In the picture **“The School Walk”** a school class goes on an outing with the teacher. His pictures seem calm, precise and friendly. That is why they are still very popular today.

Anker also earned money with other work. He designed many pictures for **ceramics**, for example for painted plates. He also drew pictures for books, such as stories by the Bernese writer Jeremias Gotthelf. Incidentally, his surname Anker is also the German word for the device that holds a ship in place.

gewusst: Albert Anker's paintings are among the best-known paintings in Switzerland and hang in many museums.
Anker was not only a painter, he also sat for a time in the Grand Council of the canton of Bern.

teile.einleitung: Banking secrecy obliges banks to keep silent about their customers. In Switzerland it was anchored in the Banking Act in 1934. Since 2008 it has lost much of its importance in relation to other countries.
wichtigste: Article 47 of the Banking Act of 1934 makes breaching banking secrecy a punishable offence.
In 2008 and 2009 UBS came under pressure in the USA for aiding tax evasion.
In 2009 UBS paid 780 million dollars and handed over customer data.
On 13 March 2009 the Federal Council adopted the OECD standard on administrative assistance in tax matters.
Since 2014 the US law FATCA has obliged Swiss banks to report accounts of US taxpayers.
With the automatic exchange of information (AEOI), account data flowed to partner states for the first time in 2018.

abschnitte.text: A bank knows a lot about its customers: how much money they have and what they spend it on. **Banking secrecy** obliges the bank not to pass on this information. In Switzerland it is set out in the **Banking Act** of **1934**. Anyone who breaches it can be punished under Article 47. This penal provision still applies within Switzerland today.

In 2008 and 2009 US authorities accused the major bank **UBS** of helping American customers hide assets from the tax office. This is called **aiding tax evasion**. Important information was supplied by the former employee **Bradley Birkenfeld**, a so-called whistleblower. In February 2009 UBS paid **780 million dollars** and handed over customer data. The case became a turning point.

On **13 March 2009** the Federal Council announced that it would in future apply the **OECD standard** on administrative assistance in tax matters. This meant Switzerland could also help other states in cases of tax evasion. In 2013 Switzerland concluded an agreement with the USA on the law **FATCA**. Since 2014 Swiss banks have had to report accounts of US taxpayers.

In the **automatic exchange of information (AEOI)**, banks automatically report the account data of foreign customers to their home states. The legal basis has applied in Switzerland since 1 January 2017. In autumn **2018** the first data were exchanged, at first mainly with EU states. In relation to other countries, banking secrecy has thereby been largely lifted.

People argued about banking secrecy for a long time. Supporters see in it a protection of **privacy**: how much money someone has is nobody else's business. Critics said it helped people to evade taxes that are then missing elsewhere. For customers resident in Switzerland, banking secrecy still applies.

gewusst: The whistleblower Bradley Birkenfeld later received a reward of 104 million dollars from the US authorities.
FATCA stands for Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act, an American law about accounts abroad.

teile.einleitung: In 1874 Switzerland got a completely reworked Federal Constitution. It made the federal government stronger and gave the people more say. With many amendments it applied until the end of 1999.
wichtigste: A first draft was narrowly rejected in 1872.
In April 1874 the people and the cantons accepted the new constitution.
Military matters were strongly centralised in the federal government.
Freedom of trade and industry now applied to the whole of Switzerland.
Civil marriage became compulsory throughout Switzerland in 1874.
The founding of new monasteries was banned, until 1973.
The revision was pushed through mainly by the Radical Liberals.

abschnitte.text: A **total revision** means that a constitution is drawn up completely anew. The first draft of 1872 wanted to make the federal government very strong. It failed **narrowly** with the people and the cantons. Two years later a weakened draft came. In **April 1874** it was accepted, and it came into force at the end of May 1874.

abschnitte.titel: More power for the federal government
abschnitte.text: Before, the cantons had equipped their troops very differently. Now the **training and armament of the army** lay largely with the federal government. In addition the constitution guaranteed **freedom of trade and industry**. Anyone who wanted to run a business could now in principle do so anywhere in Switzerland. Cantonal barriers were removed.

The constitution placed **marriage** under the protection of the federal government. A federal law of 1874 prescribed **civil marriage**. That means: marriage is concluded before an official of the civil registry office. A church wedding was afterwards voluntary. In this way the state, and no longer the Church, decided who is married.

At that time there was a fierce dispute between the state and the Catholic Church, the **Kulturkampf**. The constitution of 1874 banned the **founding of new monasteries** and orders. This ban applied until 1973. The Catholic-Conservative cantons were mostly against the new constitution.

The revision was pushed through mainly by the **Radical Liberals**, supported by the Democrats. Under it the people could now vote on federal laws with the **optional referendum** if enough signatures were collected. In addition the **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne became a permanent court. The constitution of 1874 stayed valid until the end of 1999.

gewusst: The popular initiative for partial amendments to the constitution was added only in 1891.
The constitution of 1874 was amended very often in over 120 years before a new one came into force in 2000.

teile.einleitung: Columbanus was an Irish travelling monk who founded several monasteries on the European mainland around 600. His path also led him to Lake Constance, to the area of today's Switzerland. He is regarded as an important figure of the Irish mission.
wichtigste: Columbanus came from the Irish monastery of Bangor.
Around 590 he founded the monasteries of Annegray, Luxeuil and Fontaine in the Frankish realm.
Around 610 he had to leave because of a conflict with the royal court.
After that he worked for a time at Lake Constance near Bregenz.
Finally he founded the monastery of Bobbio in northern Italy and died there in 615.

abschnitte.text: **Columbanus** lived in the Irish monastery of **Bangor**. Around 590 he set out for the European mainland with some companions. The Irish monks wanted to spread the Christian faith and lead a strict life. This is called the **Irish mission**. In the **Vosges** in the Frankish realm he founded the monasteries of **Annegray**, **Luxeuil** and **Fontaine**. Luxeuil became especially famous, which is why he is also called **Columbanus of Luxeuil**.

Columbanus came into **conflict with the royal court**. Around 610 he had to leave the Frankish realm. His path led him with his companions to **Lake Constance**. For a time he lived near **Bregenz**. Among his companions was **Gallus**, after whom the town of **St Gallen** was later named. Gallus stayed in the area when Columbanus moved on.

Columbanus crossed the **Alps** to the **Lombards** in northern Italy. There around 612 to 614 he founded his last monastery, **Bobbio**. In the year **615** he died in Bobbio. His monasteries and his strict monastic rule had great influence for a long time.

gewusst: From the hermitage of his companion Gallus, the famous monastery of St Gallen later developed.

teile.einleitung: Jean Tinguely was a Swiss artist who built artworks that move. His machines turn, rattle and squeak. Many of them can be seen in Basel and Zurich.
wichtigste: Jean Tinguely was born in Fribourg in 1925.
He built moving artworks, often from scrap metal.
