The Fasnacht Fountain of 1977 stands in Basel in front of the theatre.
In the fountain, figures of metal spray water.
The Museum Tinguely stands on the Rhine in Basel.
He was married to the artist Niki de Saint Phalle.
The machine “Heureka” stands at the Zürichhorn.

abschnitte.text: Jean Tinguely was born in **1925** in **Fribourg**, but already as a child grew up in **Basel**. He became an artist and built **machines** that do nothing useful at all. They turn, wobble, clatter and make noise. This is exactly what makes them funny and exciting. Such works are called **kinetic art**, that is, art in motion.

Tinguely liked to collect **scrap metal**: old wheels, cogwheels, pipes and other parts from the scrapyard. From these he built his machines and often drove them with **electric motors**. Some works are small, others as big as a house. Some machines he even built so that they destroyed themselves during a demonstration.

Since **1977** the **Fasnacht Fountain**, also called the Tinguely Fountain, has stood in **Basel** in front of the theatre. In the water basin many **figures of metal** move. They turn, nod and **spray water** in all directions. That is why many people stop and watch. In winter funny ice figures sometimes form.

On the **Rhine** in Basel stands the **Museum Tinguely**, which opened in 1996. There you can see many of his machines in motion. In **Zurich**, at the **Zürichhorn**, stands the large machine **“Heureka”**. Tinguely built it for the **national exhibition of 1964** in Lausanne. At certain times it is switched on and moves.

Tinguely was married to the artist **Niki de Saint Phalle**. She made large, colourful and cheerful figures. Together the two also created **joint artworks**, for example a fountain in Paris next to the Centre Pompidou. Tinguely died in Bern in 1991.

gewusst: In the Fasnacht Fountain in Basel there are ten moving figures.
One of Tinguely's machines destroyed itself in front of an audience in New York in 1960.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Constitution of 1874 was the first major revision of the Swiss constitution of 1848. It gave the people more say and the federal government more tasks. With many amendments it stayed in force for 125 years.
wichtigste: The people and the cantons accepted the totally revised constitution on 19 April 1874.
A first draft had failed with the people and cantons in 1872.
There was now the optional referendum on laws.
The permanent Federal Supreme Court received its seat in Lausanne.
Primary school teaching became compulsory, free and religiously neutral.
Civil marriage under state supervision was introduced.
The constitution applied until the end of 1999.

abschnitte.text: The Federal Constitution of 1874 is a **total revision** of the constitution of 1848. Many Swiss felt that the federal government should take on more tasks and the people should have more say. A first draft of 1872 went too far for many and was narrowly rejected. A second, more moderate draft was accepted on **19 April 1874**.

The most important innovation was the **optional referendum**. With it, eligible voters with enough signatures could demand a popular vote on a new federal law. A well-known example is the **Factory Act** for the protection of workers, which was narrowly accepted in 1877. In 1891 the popular initiative for partial revisions of the constitution was added.

Before, the Federal Supreme Court met only when needed. From 1875 there was a permanent **Federal Supreme Court** with its seat in Lausanne. The constitution abolished the **death penalty** in civil criminal law. It also introduced civil marriage, which means that marriages were now concluded by the state and no longer only by the Church.

The constitution came about in the middle of the **Kulturkampf**, a dispute between the state and the Catholic Church over power and influence. It therefore contained several articles on church policy, for example a ban on new monasteries. Primary school teaching had to be **compulsory**, free and religiously neutral. In this way all children were to be able to attend school, whatever religion they belonged to.

The constitution of 1874 anchored **freedom of trade and industry**. This means that in principle everyone may open a business and practise a profession. In military matters the federal government received more powers, especially over training and armament. Before, the cantons had largely organised their troops themselves.

The constitution of 1874 stayed in force until the end of 1999. In that time it was changed very often by **partial revisions**, for example in 1971 by women's suffrage. As a result it became hard to follow over time. Since 1 January 2000 a new, more clearly ordered Federal Constitution has therefore applied.

begriffe.erklaerung: The right to demand, with signatures, a popular vote on a law.
A dispute in the 19th century between the state and the Catholic Church.
A marriage that is concluded before a state authority.
The right to practise a profession or run a business freely.

gewusst: The Factory Act of 1877 limited work in factories to eleven hours a day.
In its 125 years the constitution of 1874 was amended well over a hundred times.
Because of the new constitution, the Federal Supreme Court did not move to Bern but to French-speaking Switzerland, to Lausanne.

teile.einleitung: In the Old Confederacy a bailiff (Landvogt) was an official who administered a subject territory in the name of a city or a place. Bailiffs existed until 1798. Many of their castles can still be visited today.
wichtigste: A bailiff administered a subject territory for his place.
He usually lived and worked in a bailiff's castle.
From 1424 to 1798 the bailiffs of Zurich sat in Kyburg Castle.
In Vaud the Bernese bailiffs were called “baillis”.
A local under-bailiff helped the bailiff.
The bailiffs of the Common Lordships rendered accounts at the Diet.

abschnitte.text: In the Old Confederacy there were free places and **subject territories**. The people in the subject territories were not allowed to decide for themselves. A **bailiff** governed there in the name of a city or a place. He administered justice, collected dues and kept order. His territory was called a **bailiwick**.

The bailiff usually lived in a **bailiff's castle**. There he also had his offices. A well-known example is **Kyburg Castle** in the canton of Zurich. From 1424 to 1798, a total of 59 bailiffs of Zurich resided there. In **Baden** there is also a bailiff's castle. Today many of these castles are museums.

The bailiff came from outside and usually stayed only a few years. For this reason he often did not know the territory well. In the individual offices an **under-bailiff** helped him. He usually came from the area itself. In this way the authorities knew better what was happening in the land.

In 1536 Bern conquered **Vaud** and governed it with bailiffs. In French they were called **baillis**. Their administrative district was called a **bailliage**. The Bernese bailiffs lived in castles such as those in Lausanne, Morges or Yverdon. This rule lasted until 1798.

Some territories belonged to several places together. They are called **Common Lordships**. Their bailiffs had to render accounts every year at the **Diet** (Tagsatzung). The Diet was the assembly of the envoys of the Confederate places. With the French invasion and the Helvetic Republic in **1798**, the time of the bailiffs ended.

gewusst: A bailiff also appears in the legend of William Tell: Gessler.
At Kyburg Castle, 59 bailiffs of Zurich lived over the course of almost 400 years.

teile.einleitung: The Escalade is the great festival of the city of Geneva. It recalls the night of 11 to 12 December 1602, when Geneva repelled an attack by the Savoyards.
wichtigste: In 1602 the Duke of Savoy wanted to conquer Geneva.
His soldiers attacked at night and climbed the city wall with ladders.
The attack failed, and Geneva stayed free.
According to legend, Mère Royaume poured hot soup on an attacker.
Today at the Escalade people smash a soup pot made of chocolate, the Marmite.
Many children go through the streets in costume.

abschnitte.text: Duke **Charles Emmanuel of Savoy** wanted to conquer the city of **Geneva**. In the night of **11 to 12 December 1602** his soldiers crept up to the city wall. They wanted to surprise the people of Geneva in their sleep. With **ladders** they climbed up the wall. The word Escalade comes from the Latin word for ladder.

The people of Geneva noticed the attackers in time. The citizens took up arms and defended their city. The attack **failed**, and the Savoyards had to retreat. Geneva remained a free **republic**. A year later peace was made with Savoy.

The best-known story of the Escalade is about **Mère Royaume**. According to legend she poured her pot of hot **vegetable soup** on an attacker. Then she threw the pot after it. In this way she became the heroine of the city. Her soup pot is still the symbol of the festival.

For the Escalade there is a soup pot made of **chocolate**, the **Marmite**. Inside are small vegetables made of **marzipan**. Traditionally the **youngest and the oldest person** at the table smash the pot together. As they do so they say a saying about the enemies of the republic. Then everyone shares the pieces.

Every year in **December** Geneva celebrates the Escalade. Many **children** dress up and go through the streets. There are **processions** with people in old costumes, with torches and music. A popular part is also a big **run** through the old town. For the people of Geneva the Escalade is a festival of the freedom of their city.

gewusst: The word Escalade originally means climbing a wall with ladders.
In the chocolate Marmite hide small vegetables made of marzipan, which recall the soup.

teile.einleitung: On 1 March in many villages of Graubünden, schoolchildren go through the lanes with bells and songs. The custom is called Chalandamarz and is meant to drive away the winter.
wichtigste: Chalandamarz is celebrated on 1 March.
The name comes from the Latin word for the first day of March.
Schoolchildren go through the village with bells and cowbells.
The noise is meant to drive away the winter.
In the Engadine the children often sing in Romansh.
The book “Schellen-Ursli” tells of this custom.

abschnitte.text: **Chalandamarz** is celebrated on **1 March**. The name comes from the Latin word **Calendae**, which was what the Romans called the first day of a month. In Roman times the new year used to begin with March. The custom is widespread in Graubünden, especially in the **Engadine**.

On Chalandamarz it is mainly the **schoolchildren** who are out and about. They go through the village with loud **bells** and **cowbells**. With the noise the **winter** is to be **driven away** and the spring awakened. The children often wear traditional costumes or blue herdsmen's shirts. In front of the houses they sing songs and get small presents or a little money for it.

In the Engadine people speak **Romansh**, the fourth national language of Switzerland. That is why on Chalandamarz the children sing many songs in this language. They practise the songs in school weeks beforehand. In this way the custom also helps to keep the language alive.

The famous children's book **“Schellen-Ursli”**, meaning Little Ursli with the Bell, appeared in 1945. The text was written by **Selina Chönz** and the pictures painted by **Alois Carigiet**. For the parade Ursli gets only a small bell. But he wants the **biggest bell**. So he bravely fetches it from the **Maiensäss**, his family's summer hut in the mountains. The book is still one of the best-known picture books in Switzerland.

gewusst: “Schellen-Ursli” was translated into many languages and also made into a film.
Chalandamarz is one of the best-known customs of Graubünden.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland, the long period of economic growth after the Second World War, roughly from 1950 to 1973, is called the economic boom. In these years many families became better off, and motorways, housing estates and factories were built. The oil crisis of 1973 ended this upswing abruptly.
wichtigste: The economic boom in Switzerland lasted roughly from 1950 to 1973.
The economy grew almost every year, and there was hardly any unemployment.
Hundreds of thousands of foreign workers, above all from Italy, came to Switzerland.
In 1958 the people and the cantons accepted the constitutional article on the national roads.
In 1964 the national exhibition Expo 64 took place in Lausanne.
The oil crisis of 1973 ended the economic boom.
In 1975 Swiss economic output shrank in real terms by about 7 per cent.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland had come through the Second World War without destroyed factories and could at once supply goods for a devastated Europe. This began a long **growth phase**, which is called the **economic boom**. It lasted roughly from 1950 to 1973. Wages rose, and many people could afford a car, a refrigerator or a television for the first time. For this reason people also speak of the emergence of the **consumer society**.

Because there was more work than workers, Switzerland brought in people from abroad. An agreement with **Italy** of 1948 regulated recruitment, and later people also came from Spain, Portugal and Yugoslavia. Many worked as **seasonal workers** on building sites, in factories and in hotels. They built roads, dams and tunnels, often under hard conditions.

In 1958 the people and the cantons accepted the constitutional article on the **national roads**. In 1962 the **Grauholz motorway** near Bern was opened as the first section of the N1. At the same time the cities and urban areas grew, and new blocks of flats, schools and hospitals arose everywhere. Many hydroelectric power stations in the Alps were also built in this period.

The **Peace Agreement** of 1937 in the machine and metal industry shaped the cooperation of employers and trade unions. Instead of striking, the social partners negotiated with each other. In 1959 the **magic formula** came into being in the Federal Council, with 2 seats each for the FDP, the Catholic Conservatives and the SP, and 1 seat for the BGB. This distribution lasted until 2003 and provided political stability.

Oil and petrol were very cheap in this period, and so consumption rose sharply. The environmental historian **Christian Pfister** calls the sudden rise in the use of cheap fossil energy from the 1950s the **1950s syndrome**. More cars, oil heating systems and factories burdened air, rivers and lakes. Only later did awareness of **environmental protection** grow.

The **oil crisis** of 1973 made the oil price rise sharply and ended the economic boom. In 1975 the Swiss economy shrank in real terms by about 7 per cent. Many foreign workers had to leave the country when jobs disappeared, and so people spoke of the **“export of unemployment”**. The **watch industry** lost particularly many jobs because of the new electronic watches from Japan and the USA, while the service sector grew strongly.

begriffe.erklaerung: The general state of the economy, that is, whether it is currently growing or shrinking.
A foreign worker who was allowed to work in Switzerland for only a few months a year.
The cooperation of employers and trade unions, who resolve conflicts through negotiation.
The period from 1973 when oil suddenly became very expensive and scarce.
The part of the economy in which people offer services, for example banks, insurance, trade or tourism.

gewusst: During the oil crisis there were three car-free Sundays in Switzerland in November and December 1973, on which you could walk or cycle on the motorway.
At Expo 64, visitors could dive into Lake Geneva in the Mesoscaph, a tourist submarine.

teile.einleitung: In the Old Zurich War from 1440 to 1450, Confederates fought against Confederates. Zurich quarrelled with Schwyz and the other places over the inheritance of the Counts of Toggenburg and even allied with Habsburg.
wichtigste: The trigger was the inheritance of Count Frederick VII of Toggenburg, who died without a will in 1436.
The war lasted, with interruptions, from 1440 to 1450.
Zurich's opponent was the Schwyz Landammann Ital Reding.
In 1443 the Zurich mayor Rudolf Stüssi fell at St Jakob an der Sihl.
An arbitration ruling under Heinrich von Bubenberg ended the war in 1450.
Zurich had to dissolve the alliance with Habsburg, and the Höfe went to Schwyz.

abschnitte.text: Count **Frederick VII of Toggenburg** owned large territories in eastern Switzerland. He died in **1436** without descendants and without a will. **Zurich** and **Schwyz** both wanted parts of his inheritance. Zurich was led by the mayor **Rudolf Stüssi**, Schwyz by the Landammann **Ital Reding** the Elder. The dispute grew ever fiercer.

The other Confederate places took the side of Schwyz. In the **Peace of Kilchberg** of 1440 Zurich had to give up the Höfe and rights in Sargans. But the dispute soon broke out again. Zurich made an alliance with **Habsburg**, the old opponent of the Confederates. That is why people speak of a **civil war** within the alliance.

In 1443 the Confederates won the Battle of **St Jakob an der Sihl** outside Zurich. Rudolf Stüssi was killed there while defending the Sihl bridge. In 1444 the Confederates besieged the castle of **Greifensee**. Afterwards they had about 60 defenders executed. This deed was seen as cruel even at the time and is called the **Murder of Greifensee**.

After years of war all sides wanted peace. The Bernese Schultheiss **Heinrich von Bubenberg** led a court of arbitration in **Einsiedeln**. His ruling of 1450 forced Zurich to dissolve the **alliance with Habsburg**. Zurich remained part of the Confederation. The **Höfe** on the upper Lake Zurich, with Pfäffikon, Wollerau and Hurden, went to Schwyz and still belong to that canton today.

gewusst: Because the Höfe went to Schwyz at that time, Pfäffikon on Lake Zurich still belongs to the canton of Schwyz and not to Zurich.
The Old Zurich War showed that the Confederation could survive even a war among its own members.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is not a member of the European Union. It regulates its relations with the EU through many individual treaties, the so-called bilateral agreements.
wichtigste: In 1992 the people and the cantons narrowly rejected joining the EEA.
After that Switzerland took the bilateral path.
Bilaterals I comprise seven agreements and were accepted by the people in 2000.
Because of the guillotine clause, all seven lapse if one lapses.
Bilaterals II were signed in Luxembourg in 2004.
Accompanying measures are meant to protect Swiss wages from wage dumping.
In May 2021 the Federal Council broke off the negotiations on the framework agreement.

abschnitte.text: On **6 December 1992** the people and the cantons voted on joining the **European Economic Area** (EEA). They narrowly rejected it. After that Switzerland looked for another way. It negotiated individual treaties with the EU. These are called **bilateral**, which means between two sides.

**Bilaterals I** consist of seven agreements, for example on the **free movement of persons**, on land transport and on research. They were signed in 1999. On **21 May 2000** about 67 per cent said yes, and they came into force in 2002. The agreements are linked by the **guillotine clause**: if one lapses, the others become invalid too. Free movement of persons allows people from Switzerland and the EU to live and work in the other area.

Many feared that free movement of persons would lead to lower wages being paid. That is why since 2004 there have been **accompanying measures**. They allow checks on wages and working conditions, including for workers sent by foreign firms. This is meant to prevent **wage dumping**, that is, undercutting the usual wages.

On 26 October 2004 **Bilaterals II** were signed in **Luxembourg**. They include, for example, agreements on statistics, the environment and taxation of savings. After the EU's eastward enlargement, the people agreed on 25 September 2005, with about 56 per cent, to extend free movement of persons to ten new EU states. Later too, the treaties were put to a vote again and again.

On 9 February 2014 the people narrowly accepted the **Mass Immigration Initiative**. It demanded that Switzerland control immigration itself, and so called free movement of persons into question. The EU also wanted a **framework agreement** that would regulate the treaties jointly. In May 2021 the Federal Council broke off these negotiations. After that new talks began on a package of treaties. Some see close relations with the EU as bringing advantages for business and research, while others want more independence.

gewusst: The EU is Switzerland's most important trading partner.
Bilaterals II also include Switzerland's participation in the Schengen area, which is why there are no longer fixed checks at many borders.

teile.einleitung: The Alamanni were an alliance of Germanic groups that from the 3rd century fought again and again with the Roman Empire. Later they came under Frankish rule. Their language lives on in the Alemannic dialects, which include Swiss German.
wichtigste: The name is usually interpreted as “all men”, that is, an alliance of many groups.
Around 259/260 the Alamanni pushed as far as Italy and were beaten near Milan by Emperor Gallienus.
In 357 the Caesar Julian defeated a large army under King Chnodomar near Strasbourg.
Around 500 the Alamanni came under pressure after Frankish victories, and Theodoric the Great took parts of them under his protection.
In the early 8th century the law code “Lex Alamannorum” was written.
The Blood Court of Cannstatt in 746 ended the independent Alamannic duchy.

abschnitte.text: The **Alamanni** were not a single people with one king. They were a union of different Germanic groups with several leaders. Their name is usually interpreted as **“all men”** or “people altogether”. They first lived east of the Rhine in the area of present-day southern Germany. From there they made raids into the Roman Empire again and again.

In the 3rd century the Roman Empire was in a serious crisis. Around 259/260 Alamanni pushed across the Alps as far as northern Italy. Emperor **Gallienus** defeated them near Milan, which was then called Mediolanum. In the year 357 a great battle took place at **Argentoratum**, the present-day Strasbourg. The later Emperor **Julian** defeated the army of the Alamannic king **Chnodomar**, who was taken prisoner.

Around 500 the Frankish king **Clovis** defeated the Alamanni. The Ostrogothic king **Theodoric the Great** asked for mercy for them and took parts of the Alamanni under his protection, for example in Raetia. In 536/537 they came completely under Frankish rule. They kept their own dukes, however. Under Duke **Lantfrid** the **Lex Alamannorum** was written down in the early 8th century, a law code with rules on fines and church rights.

The Alamannic dukes wanted to stay as independent as possible. In the year 746 the Frankish mayor of the palace **Carloman** had numerous Alamannic nobles executed at Cannstatt. This event is called the **Blood Court of Cannstatt**. After that Frankish counts administered the territory directly. The independent duchy was thereby at an end.

After the end of Roman rule, Alamanni also settled in the north and east of present-day Switzerland. Their language developed into the **Alemannic dialects**. These include Swiss German, Alsatian and the dialects of south-western Germany. Many place names ending in “-ingen” also go back to Alamannic settlements.

gewusst: In French, Germany is still called “Allemagne” to this day, after the Alamanni.
We know a lot about the battle near Strasbourg because the Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus described it in detail.

teile.einleitung: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice stands in the Lower Valais on the Rhone. It was founded in the year 515 and is regarded as the oldest monastery in the West where a religious community has lived without a break since its foundation.
wichtigste: The abbey was founded on 22 September 515.
Its founder was Sigismund, the son of the Burgundian king.
It is named after Saint Maurice, the leader of the Theban Legion.
In Roman times the place was called Agaunum.
With the “Laus perennis” people sang and prayed there day and night without a break.
Today Augustinian canons live there, and they also run a secondary school.

abschnitte.text: At Saint-Maurice the Rhone valley becomes very narrow. Here the Romans had a customs and military post called **Agaunum**. Anyone who wanted to go from Lake Geneva into the Valais and on to the Alpine passes had to pass through here. Later the graves of martyrs were venerated at Agaunum. So the place became a destination for pilgrims, that is, a **place of pilgrimage**.

According to a legend, **Maurice** led a Roman unit from Thebes in Egypt, the **Theban Legion**. The soldiers were Christians. Towards the end of the 3rd century they are said to have been killed because they refused to obey orders that went against their faith. The oldest source for this was written by Bishop **Eucherius of Lyon** in the 5th century. The French name Maurice comes from Mauritius.

In the year 515 the Burgundian king's son **Sigismund** founded a monastery over the graves. He later became king of the Burgundians himself and was venerated as a saint. In the abbey the monks introduced the **Laus perennis**, the perpetual praise. They took turns in groups, so that the singing never fell silent. This custom came from the East and spread from here in the West.

Since its foundation a religious community has lived in Saint-Maurice without a break. Today they are **Augustinian canons**, that is, priests who live by a common rule. They run the **Collège de l'Abbaye**, one of the best-known secondary schools in the Valais. The abbey also owns a famous church treasure with very old, precious vessels. In 2015 it celebrated its 1,500th anniversary.

gewusst: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice is older than the Swiss Confederation and even older than the monastery of St Gallen.
Maurice is the patron saint of many churches, and in German-speaking Switzerland too some churches are called St Mauritius.

t3r5suu.t: The Border Occupation in the First World War

teile.einleitung: In the First World War from 1914 to 1918, Switzerland stayed neutral. Even so, soldiers guarded the borders for years, which is called the border occupation. This period brought a lot of hardship and conflict in the country.
wichtigste: At the beginning of August 1914 the Federal Council decided on general mobilisation.
A “trench” separated German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland.
Soldiers received no compensation for loss of earnings, and many families fell into hardship.
In 1916 the Colonels' Affair sharpened the trench.
Federal Councillor Arthur Hoffmann had to resign in 1917.
Theophil Sprecher von Bernegg was Chief of the General Staff.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of **August 1914** the First World War broke out. The Federal Council decided on general **mobilisation**, which means that the soldiers were called up. After that they guarded the national borders for years. The commander in chief was General **Ulrich Wille**. The General Staff was headed by **Theophil Sprecher von Bernegg** from Graubünden.

Switzerland was divided in this period. Many **German-speaking Swiss** sided with Germany, many **French-speaking Swiss** with France. This opposition was called the **“trench”** (“Graben”). In 1916 the **Colonels' Affair** sharpened it. Two colonels of the General Staff had passed secret reports on to Germany and Austria, which caused great outrage in French-speaking Switzerland.

In 1917 Federal Councillor **Arthur Hoffmann**, together with the socialist **Robert Grimm**, wanted to broker a peace between Germany and Russia. Such a **separate peace** would have benefited Germany above all. When a telegram became known, **neutrality** was seen as violated. Hoffmann resigned. His successor was Gustave Ador of Geneva.

Anyone in military service received no wages from the employer and no **compensation for loss of earnings**. Often the breadwinner of the family was missing for months. At the same time prices rose, and food became scarce. Many families became poor. This hardship also led to the **General Strike** of 1918.

In the Jura, **Gilberte Montavon** served the soldiers in the inn at **Courgenay**. She was friendly and knew many by name. The soldiers sang a song about her that became very popular. In 1941 a film was even made about her. In this way she became a well-known figure of the border occupation.

gewusst: Only in the Second World War, in 1940, did Switzerland introduce compensation for loss of earnings for soldiers.
Some people still know the song “La petite Gilberte” today.

teile.einleitung: The Thirteen-Place Confederation was the alliance of thirteen places from 1513 to 1798. It grew out of the eight old places and for a long time formed the shape of the Old Confederacy.
wichtigste: To the eight old places Fribourg and Solothurn were added in 1481, so ten places came about.
In 1501 Basel and Schaffhausen joined, and now there were twelve places.
With Appenzell the thirteenth place was added in 1513.
From the old places the present-day cantons later came.
Allies without full rights were called Associated Places, for example Geneva.
Some territories such as Thurgau were subject territories and were ruled jointly by several places.
The alliance of thirteen places ended in 1798 with the French invasion.

abschnitte.titel: From an alliance of eight to thirteen
abschnitte.text: The eight old places were Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Lucerne, Zurich, Glarus, Zug and Bern. In 1481 the cities of **Fribourg** and **Solothurn** were admitted. So the alliance had ten places. In 1501 the Rhine cities **Basel** and **Schaffhausen** joined, which made twelve. The last place, **Appenzell**, followed in 1513.

A **place** was a full member of the alliance. Each place governed itself and had its own laws. Shared matters were discussed by the envoys at the **Diet**, an assembly of the places. There was no shared government or capital. From the places the present-day **cantons** later came.

Besides the thirteen places there were allies with fewer rights. They were called **Associated Places**. They included, for example, **Geneva**, the Valais, the Three Leagues in present-day Graubünden and the city of St Gallen. They were friends and partners of the alliance. Geneva became a full canton only in 1815.

Some territories had no say at all. They were called **subject territories** or common lordships. **Thurgau**, for example, was ruled jointly by several places from 1460. The places took turns sending a **bailiff** who administered the territory. The territories in present-day Ticino were also ruled in this way.

In almost all thirteen places people spoke **German**. Only in Fribourg did a large part of the people speak French. The alliance lasted almost 300 years. In 1798 French troops marched in. With that the **Old Confederacy** came to an end.

gewusst: From 1513 to 1798 Appenzell was the youngest of the thirteen places.
The thirteen places had no shared capital, and the Diet met in changing places.

teile.einleitung: St John's Monastery in Müstair lies in the canton of Graubünden, very close to the border with Italy. It is about 1,250 years old and famous for its very old wall pictures. Since 1983 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: Müstair Monastery lies in the canton of Graubünden.
It lies in the Val Müstair beyond the Ofen Pass.
It was founded around the year 775.
The legend says that Charlemagne founded it.
Famous are the wall pictures from the time of Charlemagne.
Today Benedictine nuns live in the monastery.
Since 1983 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.titel: A monastery beyond the Ofen Pass
abschnitte.text: Müstair Monastery lies in the **Val Müstair** in the canton of **Graubünden**. To get there you drive from the Engadine over the **Ofen Pass**. The village of Müstair is very close to the border with **Italy**. The name **“Müstair”** comes from the Latin word for **monastery**. So the village is named after its monastery.

The monastery was founded around the year **775**. So it is about **1,250 years old**. The **legend** says that **Charlemagne** founded the monastery. Charlemagne was a powerful king of the Franks and later emperor. In the church stands a **statue** of him.

The monastery church is famous for its **wall pictures**. They date from the time of Charlemagne and are over **1,200 years old**. The pictures show stories from the **Bible**. Because such old wall pictures are very rare, the monastery is important for the whole world. Since **1983** it has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

Today **Benedictine nuns** live in the monastery. These are **nuns** who live by the rules of Saint Benedict. They pray several times a day and work in the monastery. Visitors can see the church and a **museum** in the old tower of the monastery.

gewusst: Müstair is one of only a few World Heritage monasteries in Switzerland, and the other well-known one is the monastery of St Gallen.
With the help of the tree rings in the old timber, it was possible to find out when the monastery was built.

teile.einleitung: The Grütli Association was a Swiss association for craftsmen and workers. It was founded in 1838 and wanted to strengthen its members through education. Later it also became politically important.
wichtigste: The Grütli Association was founded in Geneva in 1838.
Its motto was “Through education to freedom”.
Its members were mainly journeymen and workers.
From 1851 the association newspaper “Der Grütlianer” appeared.
In 1901 it joined with the Social Democratic Party.
In 1916 it left again and dissolved in 1925.

abschnitte.text: On 20 May 1838 **German-speaking craftsmen** founded the Grütli Association in **Geneva**. The founding was inspired by **Albert Galeer**. The name recalls the **Rütli**, which used to be called “Grütli” too. Soon **sections**, that is, local groups, arose in many towns. Members were mainly travelling **journeymen** and later workers.

The motto of the association was **“Through education to freedom”**. Through further education, journeymen were to become independent **master craftsmen** and responsible **citizens**. With his writing of 1846, Albert Galeer gave the association its self-image as an association for education and citizenship. The association combined education, sociability and **love of country**. Later it also became politically active.

From 1851 the association newspaper **“Der Grütlianer”** appeared. From 1906 to 1923 it even came out daily. For a time it bore the subtitle “Social Democratic Daily”. In this way the association reached many readers. The newspaper was an important mouthpiece of the working class.

In 1901 the Grütli Association and the **Social Democratic Party** united in the so-called **“Solothurn Wedding”**. The association, however, remained independent in its organisation. The link did not last. The patriotic Grütli Association resisted full incorporation and the SP's course to the left in the First World War. In 1916 it left, then lost many members and dissolved in 1925.

gewusst: The association was founded not in German-speaking Switzerland but in Geneva.
The name “Grütli” is an older form of “Rütli”.

teile.einleitung: The Thirteen Old Places were the full members of the Old Swiss Confederacy from the early 16th century to 1798. From the three founding places Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden the alliance grew step by step to thirteen places. They formed the core of present-day Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Confederation began with Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden.
By 1353 it had grown to eight places, which included Lucerne, Zurich, Glarus, Zug and Bern.
In 1481 Fribourg and Solothurn were admitted after the Convention of Stans.
In 1501 Basel and Schaffhausen joined, and in 1513 Appenzell came as the thirteenth place.
After the Swabian War of 1499 the Confederation was practically independent of the Empire.
In the Peace of Westphalia of 1648 independence was also recognised in law.
The French invasion of 1798 ended the Old Confederacy.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning stood the three **forest cantons** of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden. In the 14th century Lucerne (1332), Zurich (1351), Glarus and Zug (1352) and Bern (1353) joined them. This group is called the **Eight Old Places**. They were connected with one another by various alliance treaties, not by a single shared treaty.

After the Burgundian Wars the **city places** and the **rural places** argued fiercely, among other things over the admission of Fribourg and Solothurn. In 1481 the Confederation threatened to break apart. In Stans they finally agreed on the **Convention of Stans**, with the hermit Niklaus von Flüe said to have helped with his advice. In the same year Fribourg and Solothurn were admitted as the ninth and tenth places.

abschnitte.titel: The Swabian War and new places
abschnitte.text: In 1499 the Confederates fought in the **Swabian War** against King Maximilian I and the Swabian League. After their victories the Confederation was practically independent of the Empire through the Peace of Basel. In 1501 **Basel** and **Schaffhausen** joined. In 1513 **Appenzell** was admitted as the thirteenth and last place.

The thirteen places were independent small states that helped one another. Their envoys discussed shared matters at the **Diet**. Besides these there were **Associated Places** such as the Valais, the Three Leagues or the city of St Gallen, which were allied but did not take part in decisions on equal terms. Territories such as Thurgau were ruled jointly by several places as common lordships.

In the **Peace of Westphalia** of 1648, which ended the Thirty Years' War, the Confederation also became independent of the Empire in law. The Basel mayor Johann Rudolf Wettstein had worked for this. The places often remained disunited, however, and since the **Reformation** there had been Reformed and Catholic places. In 1798 French troops marched in, and with the **Helvetic Republic** the Old Confederacy ended.

begriffe.erklaerung: This is what a full member of the alliance was called in the Old Confederacy.
An ally that was not allowed to take part in decisions on equal terms.
The assembly of the envoys of the Confederate places.
The period from 1798 to 1803, when Switzerland was a unitary state on the French model.

gewusst: The thirteen places correspond roughly to today's cantons of Uri, Schwyz, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Lucerne, Zurich, Glarus, Zug, Bern, Fribourg, Solothurn, Basel, Schaffhausen and Appenzell.
Until 1798 no further full places were added, and for almost 300 years it stayed at thirteen.
Niklaus von Flüe, called Brother Klaus, was canonised in 1947 and is regarded as the patron saint of Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: In 1353 the city of Bern made a perpetual alliance with Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden. In this way Bern became the eighth place of the Confederation and later its most powerful member.
wichtigste: On 6 March 1353 Bern made a perpetual alliance.
The partners were the three forest cantons of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden.
With this Bern became the eighth place of the Confederation.
Since 1323 there had already been a time-limited alliance with the forest cantons.
Bern was connected with Zurich and Lucerne only indirectly.
In 1384 Bern bought the towns of Burgdorf and Thun.

abschnitte.text: On **6 March 1353** Bern allied itself with the three **forest cantons** of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden. The alliance was valid for ever, which is why it is called a **perpetual alliance**. Since 1323 Bern and the forest cantons had already had an alliance for a limited time. Now it became a firm bond. The partners promised to help one another in danger.

Before Bern, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Lucerne, Zurich, Glarus and Zug belonged to the Confederation. So Bern became the **eighth place**. After that no new place joined for a long time. These eight are called the **Eight Old Places**. Only in 1481 did Fribourg and Solothurn join.

The old Confederation was not a state with a shared constitution. It was a **web of individual treaties**. Bern had a federal charter only with the forest cantons. With Zurich and Lucerne it was therefore connected only **indirectly**, through the forest cantons. Even so, the places stuck together in many wars.

Bern was a rich and powerful city and wanted to enlarge its territory. After the **Burgdorf War** the counts of Neu-Kyburg were deeply in debt. In 1384 Bern bought the towns of **Burgdorf** and **Thun** from them. Many more territories were added later. So Bern became the largest city state north of the Alps.

gewusst: As early as 1339 troops from the forest cantons helped Bern at the Battle of Laupen, before the perpetual alliance.
The canton of Bern is still one of the largest cantons of Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: In the Old Confederacy, a Common Lordship was a territory that belonged to several places together. These places governed it jointly through a bailiff. The people there were subjects with no say.
wichtigste: “Common” here means “shared”.
A bailiff governed on the spot, usually for two years.
In 1415, after the conquest of Aargau, the County of Baden came into being.
In 1460 the Confederates conquered Thurgau.
In Ticino lay the Bailiwicks beyond the Mountains.
The inhabitants had no right of say in the Diet.
The Common Lordships ended in 1798 with the Helvetic Republic.

abschnitte.text: The word **“common”** in this term means **“shared”**. A Common Lordship belonged jointly to several Confederate **places**. Places was the name then given to the members of the Confederacy, such as Zurich, Bern or Uri. They had mostly conquered these territories in war. Instead of dividing them up, they administered them together.

On the spot a **bailiff** governed. The places involved appointed him in turn, usually for two years. He administered justice, collected dues and kept order. The inhabitants were **subjects** of the ruling places. In the **Diet** (Tagsatzung), the assembly of the places, they could not have a say.

After the conquest of Aargau in 1415, the **County of Baden** and the bailiwick around Muri came into being, which from the 16th century was called the **Free Bailiwicks**. In 1460 the Confederates conquered the Habsburg **Thurgau**. In today's canton of St Gallen lay the **Rhine Valley** and the **Sarganserland**. South of the Alps, in today's Ticino, lay the **Bailiwicks beyond the Mountains** such as Lugano and Locarno. The old German word for “beyond the mountains” was “ennetbirgisch”.

Not every place took part in every Common Lordship. **Bern** had not taken part in the conquest of Thurgau in 1460. Only the peace after the **Second War of Villmergen** in 1712 gave Bern a right of say there. In this war between Reformed and Catholic places, Zurich and Bern had won. After that, Catholic places lost influence in some Common Lordships.

In 1798 **France** marched into Switzerland. The **Helvetic Republic** came into being. The subject territories were freed and made equal. From many former Common Lordships, **cantons** of their own later arose, for example Thurgau, Aargau and Ticino.

gewusst: The Diet of the Confederates often met in Baden, so in a Common Lordship.
Thurgau was a Common Lordship for over 330 years, from 1460 to 1798.

teile.einleitung: Arnold Winkelried is a hero from an old Swiss legend. In the Battle of Sempach in 1386 he is said to have sacrificed himself so that the Confederates could win against the Habsburg army of knights.
wichtigste: Winkelried is said to have come from Unterwalden, more precisely from Nidwalden.
In the Battle of Sempach the Confederates fought against the Habsburgs.
He is said to have grasped many enemy lances and so opened a gap.
According to the legend he died in doing so, and his sacrifice helped the others to victory.
Whether Winkelried really lived is not known for certain.
In Stans there has been a large Winkelried monument since 1865.

abschnitte.text: In **1386** the Confederates fought at **Sempach** in the present-day canton of Lucerne against a **Habsburg army of knights**. The knights stood close together. They held long **lances** in front of them, like a wall of points. For the Confederates it seemed almost impossible to get at them.

According to the legend, **Arnold Winkelried** stepped forward. He called out that he wanted to make a **gap** for the Confederates. They should look after his wife and children. Then he is said to have grasped many enemy lances with his arms and pressed them to his chest. Through the opening the Confederates could attack. Winkelried died in doing so, but the Confederates won the battle.

Winkelried is said to have come from **Unterwalden**, more precisely from **Nidwalden**. Whether he really lived is not known for certain, however. The story appears in chronicles only many decades after the battle. An old hero story that perhaps did not happen exactly like this is called a **legend**. Even so, Winkelried became one of the best-known Swiss heroes.

On the battlefield at Sempach stands the **battle chapel**. Every year the battle is commemorated there. On the village square of **Stans**, the main town of Nidwalden, a large **Winkelried monument** has stood since **1865**. It shows the hero with the lances in his arms.

gewusst: In the Battle of Sempach the leader of the Habsburgs, Duke Leopold III of Austria, also fell.
Since the 19th century Winkelried has appeared in many pictures, monuments and school books.

teile.einleitung: Expo.02 was the sixth national exhibition of Switzerland. It took place in 2002 in the Three Lakes region, around Lake Biel, Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Murten.
wichtigste: Expo.02 was the sixth Swiss national exhibition.
It took place in 2002 in the Three Lakes region.
The exhibition sites were called Arteplages and lay in Biel, Neuchâtel, Murten and Yverdon-les-Bains.
In addition there was a floating Arteplage of the canton of Jura.
In Lake Murten floated the Monolith by Jean Nouvel.
Originally the exhibition was planned as Expo.01 for 2001.
It counted about 10.3 million admissions.

abschnitte.text: Expo.02 did not take place in a single location. It was spread across the **Three Lakes region**, around Lake Biel, Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Murten. This area lies on the border between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland. So the exhibition linked two language regions. It lasted from May to **20 October 2002**.

The exhibition sites were called **Arteplages**. The word combines “art” and the French “plage”, beach. There were four Arteplages on the lakeshores: **Biel**, **Neuchâtel**, **Murten** and **Yverdon-les-Bains**. In addition there was a **floating Arteplage** of the canton of Jura, which travelled from place to place. Bern was not an exhibition site.

A well-known structure was the **Monolith** in **Lake Murten**. This was a large, rusty **steel cube** that floated on the water. It was designed by the French architect **Jean Nouvel**. Inside there was a large panoramic painting of the Battle of Murten. Many people still remember this cube today.

The exhibition was first planned for the year 2001 and was called **Expo.01**. During planning, however, there were big problems, including with money. So it was **postponed** by a year. In the end it took place in 2002. It counted about **10.3 million admissions**, and the record day was the last day.

gewusst: One of the Arteplages floated and travelled from place to place on the lakes.
The last day of the exhibition, 20 October 2002, was the day with the most admissions.

teile.einleitung: Anna Göldi was sentenced to death and executed in Glarus in 1782. She is regarded as one of the last women in Europe to be killed for alleged witchcraft. In 2008 she was officially rehabilitated by the canton of Glarus.
wichtigste: Anna Göldi worked as a servant for the doctor Johann Jakob Tschudi in Glarus.
She was accused of having bewitched the doctor's daughter.
In June 1782 she was executed with the sword in Glarus.
Officially the verdict was for poisoning, not for witchcraft.
She is often called “the last witch of Europe”.
In 2008 the canton of Glarus declared the verdict a judicial murder.

abschnitte.titel: A maid in the Tschudi house
abschnitte.text: Anna Göldi worked as a **servant**. A maid helped in the household, cooked, cleaned and looked after the children. Last of all she worked for the doctor **Johann Jakob Tschudi** in Glarus. Tschudi was also a councillor and judge, so a powerful man. After an argument Anna Göldi was dismissed and later accused.

The doctor's daughter was said to have spat out **pins**. It was claimed that Anna Göldi had conjured the pins into her food and bewitched the child. The court in Glarus conducted the trial. Under torture Anna Göldi made a confession. Today experts suspect that with the accusation Tschudi wanted to prevent a scandal about himself.

In **June 1782** Anna Göldi was sentenced to death and executed with the **sword**. This was in the time of the **Enlightenment**, when many educated people no longer believed in witches. So in the verdict the court called her not a witch but a **poisoner**. In substance, however, it was about sorcery. Even then critics spoke of a **judicial murder**, that is, the execution of an innocent person after a wrongful verdict.

The case became known throughout Europe and caused outrage. Books were later written and films made about Anna Göldi. In **2008** the cantonal parliament and government of the canton of Glarus officially declared the verdict a judicial murder. In this way Anna Göldi was **rehabilitated**, that is, declared innocent after the event. Today a museum in the canton of Glarus recalls her.

gewusst: Anna Göldi was not burned, as people often imagine for witch trials.
More than 225 years lay between her execution and her rehabilitation.

teile.einleitung: Henri Nestlé was a pharmacist and entrepreneur. He came from Germany and lived in Vevey on Lake Geneva. With his infant cereal he laid the foundation for one of the largest food companies in the world.
wichtigste: Henri Nestlé was actually called Heinrich Nestle and came from Frankfurt am Main.
He was a trained pharmacist.
He lived and worked in Vevey on Lake Geneva.
Around 1867 his infant cereal for babies came onto the market.
The company logo shows a bird's nest.
Today Nestlé is a large food company.

abschnitte.text: Henri Nestlé was born in **Frankfurt am Main** in Germany in 1814. Actually he was called **Heinrich Nestle**. He trained as a **pharmacist** and therefore knew a lot about mixtures. Later he moved to Switzerland, to **Vevey** on Lake Geneva. There he adapted his name to the French language.

At that time many **babies** died because they did not get enough good food. Henri Nestlé wanted to help. In 1866 and 1867 he developed a powder of **milk** and **grain** for babies, the **infant cereal**. Around 1867 it came onto the market. It was quickly sold in many countries.

In his dialect the name Nestle means **“little nest”**. That is why Henri Nestlé chose a **bird's nest** as the company logo. It shows a mother bird feeding her young. The picture suited a product for babies well. To this day the logo recalls the founder.

Henri Nestlé sold his company a few years later. After his death it merged with another milk company. From the small firm grew one of the **largest food companies in the world**. The headquarters is still in **Vevey** today. There is also a museum about nutrition there, the **Alimentarium**.

gewusst: Henri Nestlé died in 1890 in Glion above Montreux.
The fork that stands in Lake Geneva at Vevey belongs to the Alimentarium.

teile.einleitung: “The Gotthard Mail Coach” is one of the best-known paintings in Switzerland. The painter Rudolf Koller created it in 1873. It shows a mail coach racing at full speed over the Gotthard Pass.
wichtigste: Rudolf Koller painted “The Gotthard Mail Coach” in 1873.
Five horses pull the coach, which is why it is called a five-in-hand.
In front of the coach a frightened calf runs away.
The coach is travelling on the Tremola on the south side of the Gotthard.
The picture was a farewell present for Alfred Escher.
Today it hangs in the Kunsthaus Zurich.

abschnitte.text: **Rudolf Koller** was a painter from **Zurich**. He was known above all for his **animal pictures**, for example cows and horses. In 1873 he painted “The Gotthard Mail Coach”. The picture became very famous. It is regarded as a symbol of the old era of the mail coach.

abschnitte.titel: What can be seen in the picture
abschnitte.text: A yellow mail coach is driving downhill at full speed. It is pulled by **five horses**, which is why it is called a **five-in-hand**. In front run three greys, behind two bays. In front of the coach a **calf** runs away in panic. Beside it a **herd of cows** is on the road, and everything looks very lively.

Koller painted the south side of the Gotthard. There the **Tremola**, with many tight bends, leads down towards **Airolo**. The landscape in the picture, however, was freely put together by Koller. He wanted no exact depiction, but an impressive picture. So you see mountains, road and animals in an exciting scene.

The **Gotthard Mail Coach** was a mail coach that travelled regularly over the pass. It carried **passengers** as well as **letters and parcels**. In this way it linked the north side with **Ticino**. In 1882 the **Gotthard railway tunnel** was opened. After that people travelled by train, and the regular coach journeys ended.

The **Northeastern Railway** gave the picture to **Alfred Escher** as a farewell present. Escher was an important promoter of the **Gotthard Railway**. So the picture shows precisely the coach that was soon to disappear because of the railway. In 1898 the painting came as a gift to the **Kunsthaus Zurich**. There you can still look at it today.

gewusst: Of all people, the railway promoter Alfred Escher received a picture of the mail coach that the railway replaced.
Even today, in summer, a historic Gotthard mail coach again travels over the pass for tourists.

teile.einleitung: The Burgundian Wars were wars of the Confederates against Duke Charles the Bold of Burgundy in the years 1474 to 1477. The Confederates won the great battles at Grandson, Murten and Nancy. After that they were regarded all over Europe as feared warriors.
wichtigste: The Burgundian Wars lasted from 1474 to 1477.
The Confederates' opponent was Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy.
At Grandson in 1476 the Confederates captured over 400 cannons and rich treasures.
The Battle of Murten took place on 22 June 1476.
In the Battle of Nancy in 1477 Charles the Bold died.
Bern drove the war forward especially, and King Louis XI of France paid money.
After the war, Confederate mercenaries were in great demand all over Europe.

abschnitte.text: **Charles the Bold** was Duke of Burgundy from 1467 and one of the richest princes in Europe. His realm stretched from the present-day Netherlands and Belgium to Burgundy in France. He wanted to close the gap between these territories and found a kingdom of his own. In doing so he came dangerously close to the Confederates and their allies on the Upper Rhine.

**Bern** above all wanted to extend its power westwards into Vaud and saw Burgundy as a danger. The French king **Louis XI** was an enemy of Charles and supported the Confederates with money. In 1474 the Confederates concluded the Perpetual Settlement with the Habsburg Duke Sigmund and so got rid of their old enemy. After that they declared war on Burgundy.

On 2 March 1476 the Confederates defeated Charles's army at **Grandson** on Lake Neuchâtel. They captured over 400 cannons, tents, carpets and valuables, the **Burgundian booty**. On 22 June 1476 followed the Battle of **Murten**, in which thousands of Burgundians died. On 5 January 1477 Charles the Bold fell in the Battle of Nancy in Lorraine.

After Charles's death his daughter and heiress **Mary of Burgundy** married Maximilian of Habsburg in 1477. As a result a large part of the Burgundian inheritance went to the Habsburgs, who became even more powerful. The Duchy of Burgundy itself went to France. In this way the wars changed the map of Europe.

The victories made the Confederate foot soldiers famous, and many went off as **mercenaries** into foreign wars. Bern and Fribourg received Murten, Grandson, Orbe and Echallens as **common lordships**. The dispute over the distribution of the booty almost tore the Confederation apart. Only the Convention of Stans in 1481 settled the quarrel.

Parts of the Burgundian booty, such as magnificent tapestries, are on display in the **Bernese Historical Museum**. In Murten a monument recalls the battle. A huge **panorama painting** of the Battle of Murten from 1893 was shown at Expo.02. The battles are still among the best-known events in Swiss history.

begriffe.erklaerung: A high noble title for a prince who rules over a large territory.
A soldier who fights for a foreign lord in return for payment.
Valuable things that the victors take from their opponent after a fight.
A territory that several Confederate places administered together.

gewusst: A legend tells that after the Battle of Murten a messenger ran all the way to Fribourg and there collapsed dead with a lime branch.
In memory of this legend there is a Murten to Fribourg run every year.
At Grandson, Charles the Bold had to leave behind his entire camp with tents, silver tableware and gemstones.

teile.einleitung: In 58 BC the Helvetii left their homeland on the Swiss Central Plateau to emigrate to Gaul. Julius Caesar opposed them, defeated them and sent them back. Almost everything we know about it comes from Caesar himself.
wichtigste: The Helvetii set out in the spring of 58 BC.
According to Caesar, the exodus was planned by the rich nobleman Orgetorix.
Before setting out they burned their 12 towns and about 400 villages.
Their goal was the territory of the Santones in south-western Gaul.
Caesar had the Rhone bridge at Geneva destroyed.
After their defeat the Helvetii had to return to their homeland.

abschnitte.text: The **Helvetii** were a Celtic people on the Swiss Central Plateau. According to Caesar, the rich nobleman **Orgetorix** persuaded them to emigrate. But he died as early as **60 BC**, before the march began. The Helvetii held to the plan anyway. In the spring of **58 BC** they set out with allied tribes.

Before they set out, according to Caesar, the Helvetii set fire to their **12 towns** and about **400 villages**. That way nobody would get the idea of turning back. Their goal was the territory of the **Santones** in the south-west of present-day France, near the Atlantic. There they hoped for more land and security. Caesar gives the figure of 368,000 people, about 92,000 of them warriors. Experts today consider this figure exaggerated.

The easiest route led across the Rhone at **Geneva**. Geneva belonged to the people of the Allobroges and already lay within the Roman sphere of power. **Julius Caesar** had the **Rhone bridge** broken down and the bank fortified. The Helvetii had to take another route. Caesar followed them with his legions and finally defeated them at **Bibracte** in Gaul.

After the defeat Caesar forced the Helvetii to return to their old homeland. They were to rebuild their settlements. Caesar wanted to prevent **Germanic tribes** from beyond the Rhine from occupying the empty land. So the Helvetii were to serve as a **buffer**. In this way the Central Plateau gradually came under Roman influence.

Almost everything we know about the exodus comes from Caesar's work **“De bello Gallico”**, in English “The Gallic War”. But Caesar was himself a **party to the war**. He wanted to show in Rome how successful he was. That is why his account is not neutral. Experts therefore examine his statements critically.

gewusst: Switzerland is called “Helvetia” in Latin, after the Helvetii. That is why CH stands for Confoederatio Helvetica.
Caesar's account of the Gallic War is still read in Latin lessons today.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland's refugee policy during the time of National Socialism is a difficult chapter of history. Switzerland took in many people, but also turned away many persecuted people at the border, especially Jewish people.
wichtigste: In 1938 Switzerland and Germany agreed on the “J stamp” in the passports of Jewish people.
Heinrich Rothmund headed the federal aliens police.
On 13 August 1942 Switzerland closed the border to Jewish refugees.
Federal Councillor Eduard von Steiger said in 1942: “The boat is full.”
Almost 300,000 people found protection in Switzerland, for shorter or longer, during the war.
In 1995 Federal President Kaspar Villiger apologised for the J stamp.
The Bergier Commission investigated Switzerland's role and presented a refugee report in 1999.

abschnitte.text: From 1933 Jewish people were persecuted in Germany. Many wanted to flee, including to Switzerland. On **29 September 1938** Switzerland and Germany agreed on a marking: Germany stamped a red **“J”** in the passports of Jewish people. In this way Swiss border officials could recognise them at once and turn them away. **Heinrich Rothmund**, the head of the aliens police, helped to shape this policy.

On **13 August 1942** Switzerland closed the border to Jewish refugees. Anyone who fled only for “racial reasons” did not count as a **political refugee**. Justice minister **Eduard von Steiger** compared Switzerland in August 1942 to a full lifeboat. His saying **“The boat is full”** became very well known. Many people in Switzerland protested against this harsh policy.

At the same time almost **300,000 people** found protection in Switzerland, for shorter or longer. They included **civilian refugees**, interned **soldiers** and children sent to recover. Some individuals also helped the persecuted against the rules. A well-known example is the St Gallen police commander **Paul Grüninger**. He lost his job because of it and was rehabilitated only in 1995.

abschnitte.titel: Coming to terms with the past
abschnitte.text: For a long time little was said in Switzerland about this period. On the 50th anniversary of the end of the war, Federal President **Kaspar Villiger** **apologised** in 1995 on behalf of the Federal Council for the J stamp. In the 1990s the **Bergier Commission**, under the historian Jean-François Bergier, investigated Switzerland's role in the Second World War. Its refugee report of 1999 criticised the rejection of many persecuted people.

gewusst: The saying “The boat is full” is quoted to this day in discussions about refugees.
Paul Grüninger helped refugees and was dismissed for it, and only in 1995 was he rehabilitated.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Charter is a treaty from the year 1291 in which Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden promised each other mutual help. It is regarded as one of the most important documents of Swiss history. Many see in it the beginning of the Confederation, even if the real history is more complicated.
wichtigste: The Federal Charter is dated early August 1291.
It was made by the valley communities of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden.
The text is written in Latin on parchment.
The places promised each other help in danger, and to last for ever.
They did not want foreign judges who had bought their office or did not come from the valley.
The Federal Charter renewed an older alliance that already existed.
Today the original lies in the Museum of the Federal Charters in Schwyz.
Because of the date, Switzerland celebrates its national holiday on 1 August.

abschnitte.text: The Federal Charter is an **alliance treaty**, that is, an agreement for a league between several partners. The men of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden committed themselves in it to stand by one another against attacks from outside. The treaty was meant to apply not just for a few years but expressly **for ever**. The text also says that an older alliance is being renewed by it.

The letter is dated early August 1291, and it does not name an exact day. At that time the area belonged to the Holy Roman Empire, and powerful noble families such as the **Habsburgs** wanted to extend their influence. In July 1291 King Rudolf I of Habsburg had died, and the situation was uncertain. The valley communities therefore wanted to secure their order and peace themselves.

Besides mutual help, the Federal Charter also regulates life together. The places did not want to accept **foreign judges** who had bought their office or were not locals. If there was a dispute between Confederates, the wisest people were to settle it. The letter also contains rules against murder, arson and theft.

The Federal Charter is written in **Latin**, the language of scholars and documents in the Middle Ages. **Parchment**, that is, specially treated animal skin, served as the writing material. The sheet is about the size of a school exercise book. The treaty was confirmed with wax **seals**, which hang on cords at the bottom of the parchment.

abschnitte.titel: Museum of the Federal Charters in Schwyz
abschnitte.text: The original is kept today in the **Museum of the Federal Charters** in Schwyz, which opened in 1936. Other old alliance charters and banners of the Confederates can also be seen there. School classes from all over Switzerland visit the museum. Because parchment is delicate, the letter lies well protected in a display case.

For a long time the Federal Charter was hardly known, and other alliances were considered more important. Only in the 19th century was it declared the **founding document** of Switzerland. In 1891 people celebrated 600 years since 1291 with the first federal celebration on 1 August. Today experts see the Federal Charter as one of many steps on the way to the Confederation.

begriffe.erklaerung: An agreement by which several partners join together and help one another.
Thinly treated animal skin on which important texts were written in the Middle Ages.
An impression in wax that shows that someone agrees to a text, a little like a signature.
People who have bound themselves with an oath, that is, a solemn promise.
The community of people who live in a valley and administer it together.

gewusst: Neither William Tell nor the Rütli Oath appears in the Federal Charter.
Examinations of the parchment have confirmed that it may date from around 1291.
Only since 1994 has 1 August been an official public holiday throughout Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Great St Bernard is an Alpine pass between Valais and the Italian Aosta Valley. Celts and Romans already crossed it. It is also known for its hospice and the St Bernard dogs.
wichtigste: The pass connects Valais with the Aosta Valley.
The summit of the pass lies at 2,469 metres above sea level.
Emperor Claudius had the mule track extended into a road for vehicles.
On the summit of the pass stood a temple to Jupiter Poeninus.
The road connected Octodurus (Martigny) and Augusta Praetoria (Aosta).
On Roman roads, milestones gave the distances.

abschnitte.text: The pass road leads from the **Rhone Valley** through the **Val d'Entremont** over into the Italian **Aosta Valley**. The summit of the pass lies at **2,469 metres above sea level**. In winter the road is closed because of snow. Since 1964 there has been a road tunnel under the pass. The Romans already used this route, which was the shortest link from Italy to Lake Geneva and to **Gaul**.

The **Celts** worshipped the god **Poeninus** on the pass. The Romans linked him with their chief god **Jupiter** and built a temple to **Jupiter Poeninus**. In 57 BC Caesar sent the legate **Servius Sulpicius Galba** to Valais to open the way for merchants. Galba spent the winter in Octodurus, but withdrew after fierce attacks by the Valais tribes. In 25 BC Rome subdued the people of the **Salassi** in the Aosta Valley.

After the victory over the Salassi, Rome founded the colony **Augusta Praetoria**. The name **Aosta** comes from it. On the Valais side lay **Octodurus**, later called **Forum Claudii Vallensium**, today's **Martigny**. It was the most important Roman place in Valais. An **amphitheatre** and remains of a temple are still preserved there.

Earlier the pass could be crossed only with **pack animals**. In the 1st century AD Emperor **Claudius** had the road extended for wagons. **Milestones** stood along the way. These stone pillars gave the distance to the next important place and often the name of the emperor. Some of them now stand in museums.

In the Middle Ages Saint **Bernard of Aosta** founded a **hospice** on the summit of the pass. The pass is named after him. The monks took in travellers there and helped in times of need. Famous are the **St Bernard dogs**, which helped to search for people buried in the snow. In 1800 **Napoleon** also crossed the pass with his army.

gewusst: The dog “Barry” is said to have saved the lives of many people in the snow, and today he stands stuffed in the Natural History Museum in Bern.
The Valais Alps are called “Alpes Poeninae” in Latin, after the god Poeninus.

teile.einleitung: The Kappel Milk Soup is a famous story from the year 1529. Instead of fighting each other, soldiers from Zurich and Central Switzerland ate a milk soup together. It is regarded as a sign of the cohesion of the Confederates.
wichtigste: The Kappel Milk Soup took place in 1529 in the First War of Kappel.
Zurich was Reformed, and the Central Swiss places remained Catholic.
The Central Swiss brought the milk, the people of Zurich the bread.
The pot stood on the border between Zurich and Zug.
There was no battle, but a peace.
Albert Anker painted the scene in 1869.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of the 16th century came the **Reformation**. **Zurich** became **Reformed** under the reformer Huldrych Zwingli. The **Central Swiss places** such as Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug stayed **Catholic**. They fell into a fierce quarrel over the right faith. In **1529** both sides marched against each other with troops.

abschnitte.titel: A soup instead of a battle
abschnitte.text: At **Kappel am Albis** the armies faced each other. But the soldiers did not want to fight. According to tradition, the **Central Swiss** put a large pot of **milk** exactly on the **border** between Zurich and Zug. The people of **Zurich** brought **bread** to go with it. Together this made a **milk soup**, and each side ate from its own side of the border.

In the **First War of Kappel** there was **no battle**. The leaders concluded a peace, the **First Peace of Kappel**. The dispute, however, was not yet over. Two years later, in 1531, fighting did break out in the Second War of Kappel. The milk soup of 1529 nevertheless remains in memory as a peaceful moment.

The Bernese painter **Albert Anker** painted the scene in **1869**. In the picture the soldiers sit peacefully around the pot. The painting is very well known and is often shown in schoolbooks. The story shows: **a quarrel can end peacefully** if people talk and share.

gewusst: In Kappel am Albis a monument recalls the milk soup.
The Kappel Milk Soup is often named as an example of the Swiss way of resolving conflicts through compromise.

teile.einleitung: At the Alpaufzug, farmers bring their cows up to the alp in early summer. There the animals eat fresh mountain grass all summer long. The Alpaufzug is an old custom that is still celebrated today.
wichtigste: At the Alpaufzug the cows move up to the alp.
It usually takes place in early summer, often in June.
The cows wear large bells or “Treicheln” while doing so.
On the alp the dairyman, the “Senn”, makes alpine cheese from the milk.
The Senn lives and works in the alp hut.
In autumn the cows return to the valley, decorated, in the Alpabzug.

abschnitte.text: In spring the grass grows first in the valley. Higher up in the mountains it takes longer. When enough grass has grown on the **alps**, usually in **June**, the alpine summer begins. Then the farmers go up with their cows. This procession is called the **Alpaufzug**, which in some regions is also called the Alpauffahrt.

At the Alpaufzug the cows often wear large **bells** or **Treicheln** around their necks. Treicheln are large bells made of sheet metal. The loud ringing can be heard far around and is part of the festival. The dairymen and farmers often wear their **traditional costume**. Many spectators come to see the procession.

On the alp the **Senn**, the dairyman, lives in an **alp hut**. He milks the cows and processes the milk. In a large cauldron he makes **alpine cheese** from it. Because the cows eat mountain grass and herbs, this cheese tastes special. In autumn the cheese is brought down to the valley.

In **September** it gets cold on the alp and the grass becomes scarce. Then the cows return to the valley. This festival is called the **Alpabzug** or Alpabfahrt, in French the **Désalpe**. The cows often wear **flowers and wreaths** on their heads. This shows that the alpine summer went well.

gewusst: Every summer very many cows, cattle, sheep and goats in Switzerland spend a few weeks on an alp.
The cow with the biggest bell often walks right at the front in the Alpaufzug.

teile.einleitung: Jean Daniel Abraham Davel, usually called Major Davel, wanted in 1723 to free Vaud from the rule of Bern. His attempt failed, and he was executed. Today he is regarded in the canton of Vaud as a hero of freedom.
wichtigste: Vaud had been a subject territory of Bern since 1536.
On 31 March 1723 Davel marched to Lausanne with 500 to 600 soldiers.
The city authorities of Lausanne betrayed him to Bern.
Davel was executed at Vidy on 24 April 1723.
He said that God had given him the task.
In 1798 Vaud became independent of Bern, and in 1803 a canton of its own.

abschnitte.text: In **1536** **Bern** conquered Vaud from Savoy. After that it was a **subject territory**. That means the people of Vaud were not allowed to decide about their own land. Bern governed the territory with its own **bailiffs**, who sat in the castle. Many people of Vaud felt this rule to be unjust.

Davel was born in 1670 and was an experienced **officer**. He had fought in foreign service and was highly respected in Vaud. As a **major** he commanded militia soldiers. He was very devout and convinced that God had given him a task.

On **31 March 1723** Davel marched to **Lausanne** with **500 to 600 soldiers**. The men had actually been called together for an **inspection** and at first did not know what their commander had in mind. In Lausanne Davel presented to the council his plan to free Vaud from Bern. The city authorities at first acted friendly, but **betrayed him to Bern**. Davel was arrested.

In the **interrogations** Davel insisted that **God** had given him the task. Even under torture he named no fellow conspirators. He was convicted and beheaded on **24 April 1723** at **Vidy** in Lausanne. To the end he remained calm and composed. It was precisely this attitude that later made him a **symbolic figure**.

Only in **1798** did Vaud, with the support of France, declare itself independent of Bern. In **1803** it became a **canton** of Switzerland in its own right. The people of Vaud see in Davel an early fighter for their **freedom**. In front of **Saint-Maire Castle** in Lausanne, the seat of the Vaud government, stands a **statue** of him. From this castle the Bernese bailiffs had earlier governed.

gewusst: The statue stands, of all places, in front of the castle where the Bernese rulers used to sit.
The painter Charles Gleyre from Vaud painted a well-known picture of Major Davel.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Council is the government of Switzerland. It consists of seven members who lead the country together. Unlike in many other countries, there is no single boss but a team that makes all important decisions together.
wichtigste: The Federal Council has seven members and is the national government of Switzerland.
It is elected by the United Federal Assembly, that is, the National Council and Council of States together.
The term of office is four years, and re-election is possible.
Each member heads a department, for example for finance or defence.
The President of the Confederation is elected for only one year at a time.
Under the principle of collegiality the Federal Council decides together and defends its decisions together.
The first Federal Council was elected on 16 November 1848.

abschnitte.text: The Federal Council is the **executive** of Switzerland, that is, the authority that carries out laws and governs the country. It sits in the **Federal Palace** in Bern. The seven members are called federal councillors. They are supported by the Federal Chancellery, which is headed by the Federal Chancellor.

The people do not elect the Federal Council directly. The **United Federal Assembly**, that is, all 246 members of the National Council and Council of States together, elects each member individually. The election takes place every four years, in December after the National Council elections. If someone resigns, the seat is filled anew in a by-election.

The Federal Council works by the **principle of collegiality**: it deliberates and decides together, and everyone defends the decision outwardly, even those who were against it internally. The **President of the Confederation** chairs the meetings and represents Switzerland at important occasions. This office changes every year. The person is not a boss over the others, however, but “first among equals”.

Each member of the Federal Council heads a **department**, which is a kind of large ministry. There is, for example, the Department of Foreign Affairs, the Finance Department and the Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport. Other departments take care of home affairs, justice and police, economic affairs and education, and the environment, transport and energy. Thousands of federal employees work in each department.

The Federal Council has existed since the founding of the federal state in 1848. The first president was **Jonas Furrer** of Zurich, and even then, with Stefano Franscini, a Ticinese sat in the government. For a long time only the Radical Liberals provided federal councillors, and in 1943 Ernst Nobs became the first Social Democrat to join. In 1984 **Elisabeth Kopp** was elected as the first woman to the Federal Council.

From 1959 the so-called **magic formula** applied: the FDP, the Catholic Conservatives (today Die Mitte) and the SP had two seats each, and the BGB (today the SVP) one. In this way the big parties were represented in government together. In 2003 the distribution changed when the SVP got a second seat. Today the SVP, SP and FDP have two seats each and Die Mitte one.

begriffe.erklaerung: The executing power in the state, that is, the government that carries out laws.
A large area of the federal administration that a member of the Federal Council heads.
The rule that the Federal Council decides together and appears together.
The idea that all the big parties sit in government together.
The National Council and Council of States when they meet together, for example for elections.

gewusst: Federal councillors can often move around Bern without bodyguards and sometimes even travel by train.
