Switzerland has no single head of government but a team of seven people with equal rights.
Federal councillors are very rarely voted out, and since 1848 it has happened only a few times.

teile.einleitung: Cottage industry (Heimarbeit) means that people work at home for a trader. Before there were factories, many families in Switzerland spun and wove in their living rooms. In the Zurich Oberland in particular, this work was very important.
wichtigste: In the putting-out system a merchant supplied the raw material and bought the finished goods.
In the 18th century many families in the Zurich Oberland spun cotton.
Around 1800, cheap machine-spun yarn from England plunged hand spinning into crisis.
Many then turned to hand weaving.
The first factories arose on streams because of the water power.
Research calls this phase proto-industrialisation.

abschnitte.text: Cottage industry was often organised in the **putting-out system**. The **merchant-manufacturer** was a trader who advanced the raw material. The home workers processed it at home and gave the goods back. The merchant then sold the products in distant markets. In this way the home workers remained **dependent** on him and his prices.

In the 18th century the **spinning of cotton** was the most important home work in the **Zurich Oberland**. In many farmhouse parlours the **spinning wheel** turned, and cotton became yarn. Women and children also earned an extra wage with it. Particularly dependent on it were **smallholders with little land** and **cottagers** (Tauner), that is, day labourers with little or no land. Cottage industry allowed them to make a living and encouraged population growth.

In **England** **spinning machines** were invented. They produced yarn much more cheaply and evenly. Around 1800 this cheap **machine-spun yarn** also came to Switzerland. The hand spinners could no longer keep up on price. Many families turned to **hand weaving** and wove cloth from the machine-spun yarn.

Soon **textile factories** arose in Switzerland too. Because the country had hardly any **coal**, **water power** was used. Water wheels and later turbines drove the machines. On the **Aabach** in the Zurich Oberland, numerous spinning mills were therefore lined up one after another. Later **power looms** made hand weaving unprofitable too.

Research calls the phase of rural cottage industry before the factories **proto-industrialisation**. “Proto” means “before” or “first”. Rural households then produced on a large scale for markets beyond their region. The transition to the factories was hard for many. In 1832 desperate home weavers set fire to a weaving mill with power looms in the **Uster Fire**.

gewusst: The factories on the Aabach can be visited today on an industrial heritage trail in the Zurich Oberland.
Embroidery in eastern Switzerland and watchmaking in the Jura were also done as home work for a long time.

teile.einleitung: Huguenots was the name given to the Reformed Christians in France. Because they were persecuted for their faith, many of them fled abroad. Geneva in particular, and other Reformed Swiss towns, took in many refugees.
wichtigste: The Huguenots were Reformed people from France and followed the teaching of Calvin.
In 1572 thousands of Huguenots were murdered in Paris in the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre.
In 1685 King Louis XIV banned the Reformed faith in France.
Particularly many refugees came to Geneva.
The Huguenots brought watchmaking and other crafts with them.
Many moved on to Germany, for example to Brandenburg and Hesse.

abschnitte.text: In the 16th century the **Reformation** also spread in France. The Reformed Christians there were called **Huguenots**. They followed the teaching of **John Calvin**, who worked in Geneva. They spoke **French** and were therefore well understood in French-speaking Switzerland. In France, however, they were a minority.

Between Catholics and Huguenots there were bloody **wars of religion**. In the **St Bartholomew's Day Massacre** of 24 August 1572, thousands of Huguenots were murdered in Paris. Many survivors fled to Geneva. In 1598 the **Edict of Nantes** allowed the Huguenots their faith. In 1685, however, King **Louis XIV**, the “Sun King”, revoked this edict again, and tens of thousands fled.

**Geneva** lies right on the border with France and was Reformed. For that reason very many refugees arrived there. Towns such as Bern, Zurich, Basel and Lausanne also took in Huguenots. Among the refugees were skilled **watchmakers** and **goldsmiths**. They helped to make the **watchmaking trade** in Geneva great.

Switzerland could not keep all the refugees. After a stop, many moved on to **Germany**. **Brandenburg** and **Hesse** in particular took them in. There they founded congregations of their own and brought new crafts with them. In some German towns, Huguenot churches recall them.

abschnitte.titel: On the trail of the flight
abschnitte.text: Today a hiking trail recalls the flight: the **Huguenot and Waldensian Trail**. It leads from southern France through Switzerland as far as Hesse in Germany. The path follows the old **escape routes**. The **Waldensians** were another persecuted religious group. Those who walk the trail learn a lot about the history of the refugees.

gewusst: The Geneva watch industry owes an important part of its success to the Huguenots.
The Huguenot and Waldensian Trail is a cultural route of the Council of Europe.

teile.einleitung: The Chapel Bridge (Kapellbrücke) is the best-known landmark of the city of Lucerne. It is a covered wooden bridge over the Reuss and is among the oldest of its kind in Europe. Beside it stands the octagonal Water Tower.
wichtigste: The Chapel Bridge stands in Lucerne.
It crosses the Reuss where the river flows out of Lake Lucerne.
It was built around 1365 as a covered wooden bridge.
It takes its name from St Peter's Chapel.
Under the roof hang painted panels from the 17th century.
In August 1993 a large part of the bridge burned down.
The octagonal Water Tower stands in the river beside the bridge.

abschnitte.text: The **Chapel Bridge** stands in **Lucerne**. It crosses the **Reuss** at an angle, exactly where the river flows out of **Lake Lucerne**. It was built around **1365**. So it is over 650 years old. It is a **covered wooden bridge** with a tiled roof and is among the oldest of its kind in Europe.

The bridge is named after **St Peter's Chapel**, which stands nearby. In earlier times the bridge was part of the **city fortifications**. It protected the city from attack from the lake side. Today it is a popular route for locals and tourists.

Beside the bridge, in the river, stands the octagonal **Water Tower**. It is older than the bridge. In earlier times it served, among other things, as a **prison**, a **treasury** and an archive. Together with the bridge it is one of the most photographed subjects in Switzerland.

In the roof gable of the bridge hang **triangular painted panels** from the **17th century**. They show stories from Lucerne and Switzerland, for example about patron saints of the city. Anyone walking across the bridge can look at the pictures as in a picture book. Many of the panels were later destroyed in the fire.

In **August 1993** a fire broke out on the bridge. A large part of the Chapel Bridge **burned down**, and many panels were destroyed. The people of Lucerne were deeply affected. The bridge was afterwards **rebuilt** as faithfully as possible and reopened the following year. The fire had spared the Water Tower.

gewusst: The Chapel Bridge is about 200 metres long.
Some charred panels deliberately hang in the bridge today as a reminder of the fire.

teile.einleitung: Huldrych Zwingli was a pastor and reformer in Zurich. He wanted to renew the church and base it on the Bible. His Reformation has shaped German-speaking Switzerland to this day.
wichtigste: Zwingli was born in Wildhaus in the Toggenburg in 1484.
From 1519 he preached at the Grossmünster in Zurich.
Reformation means renewal of the church.
In 1524 images and statues were removed from the Zurich churches.
Zwingli fought against mercenary service.
He died in 1531 in the Battle of Kappel am Albis.

abschnitte.text: Huldrych Zwingli was born in **Wildhaus** in the **Toggenburg** in 1484. His birthplace can still be visited today. He studied and became a **pastor** and preacher. At first he worked in Glarus and Einsiedeln. As a **field chaplain** he accompanied Swiss mercenaries on campaigns to Italy.

From 1519 Zwingli preached at the **Grossmünster** in **Zurich**. He wanted to renew the church, which is what the word **Reformation** means. The church was to be based on the **Bible** again. From Zurich his teaching spread to other places. The city council supported him.

Zwingli thought that **images and figures of saints** distracted from prayer. So in 1524 they were removed from the Zurich churches. The churches became plain and simple. In addition, Zwingli and his helpers translated the Bible into **German**. In this way people could read it themselves, and this translation is today called the **Zurich Bible**.

Many young Swiss fought as **mercenaries** for foreign rulers and lost their lives doing so. Zwingli had experienced this himself as a field chaplain. So he fought against **mercenary service**. Zurich finally banned the recruiting of mercenaries. This also made him opponents.

Between Reformed and Catholic places a quarrel broke out. In 1531 Zwingli went along with the Zurich troops in the **Second War of Kappel**. In the **Battle of Kappel am Albis** he was killed. His successor in Zurich was **Heinrich Bullinger**. Since 1885 a monument has stood by the **Wasserkirche** in Zurich showing Zwingli with **Bible and sword**.

gewusst: In 1522 friends of Zwingli publicly ate sausage during Lent, and this “sausage meal” is regarded as the beginning of the Zurich Reformation.
In 1529 Zwingli and Martin Luther met in Marburg, but could not agree about communion.

teile.einleitung: On 14 July 1865 people stood for the first time on the summit of the Matterhorn. The first ascent was a great success but ended with a serious accident.
wichtigste: The Matterhorn is 4,478 metres high.
The first ascent succeeded on 14 July 1865.
The party was led by the Englishman Edward Whymper.
The party started in the Valais village of Zermatt and climbed via the Hörnli ridge.
On the descent a rope broke, and four of the seven climbers fell to their deaths.
Three days later Jean-Antoine Carrel reached the summit from the Italian side.

abschnitte.text: The **Matterhorn** is 4,478 metres high and lies on the border between Switzerland and Italy. With its shape like a pyramid it is one of the best-known mountains in the world. For a long time it was regarded as unclimbable. Many climbers tried in vain. In the middle of the 19th century a real **race** for the summit began.

The Englishman **Edward Whymper** was an illustrator and mountaineer. He had already tried the Matterhorn several times. In July 1865 he set off with six companions in the Valais village of **Zermatt**. They included the Zermatt mountain guides **Peter Taugwalder, father and son**. The party climbed via the **Hörnli ridge**, the north-east ridge.

On **14 July 1865** the seven men reached the summit. They were the first people up there. At the same time another rope team was on its way on the Italian side. The mountain guide **Jean-Antoine Carrel** from Breuil reached the summit three days later, on 17 July, via the **Lion ridge**.

On the **descent** one of the men slipped. The **rope** broke, and four of the seven climbers fell into the depths. Only Whymper and the two Taugwalders survived. The accident made headlines all over Europe. The broken rope can be seen today in the **Matterhorn Museum** in Zermatt.

The **Hörnli ridge** is now the most frequently climbed route on the Matterhorn. On it stands the **Hörnli hut**, where climbers spend the night. Every year many people attempt the ascent, usually with a mountain guide. Through the mountain, Zermatt has become a well-known holiday resort. The Matterhorn is regarded as a landmark of the Swiss Alps.

gewusst: The broken rope from the first ascent is today in the Matterhorn Museum in Zermatt.
Only three days after Whymper, Jean-Antoine Carrel also stood on the summit from Italy.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Palace in Bern is the building where the Swiss Parliament meets and the Federal Council works. With its green dome it is one of the best-known buildings in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Parliament and the Federal Council meet in the Federal Palace.
The parliament building was built from 1894 to 1902 and opened on 1 April 1902.
The architect was Hans Wilhelm Auer.
The dome is green because its copper turned green with time.
At the very top stands a gilded Swiss cross.
In the dome hall stands a statue of the three Confederates.
On the Bundesplatz there are 26 water jets, one for each canton.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland is governed in the **Federal Palace**. Here the **Parliament** meets with its two chambers, the **National Council** and the **Council of States**. The **Federal Council**, the government, also has its rooms here. The Federal Palace consists of three parts: the West Wing, the parliament building in the middle and the East Wing.

The present **parliament building** was built from 1894 to 1902. It was planned by the architect **Hans Wilhelm Auer**. He had already built the East Wing earlier. The building was opened on **1 April 1902**. In construction about 30 kinds of stone from 13 cantons were used. In this way the house shows the **diversity** of Switzerland.

The large **dome** is covered with **copper**. Copper is reddish brown at first. Through air and rain a green layer forms in time. At the very top of the dome stands a gilded **Swiss cross**, about 60 metres above the ground. You can see it from far away.

In the **dome hall** stand three large figures. They show the **three Confederates** at the Rütli Oath. The statue was unveiled in 1914. It recalls the founding legend of Switzerland. In the hall there are also stained glass windows with the coats of arms of the cantons.

In front of the Federal Palace lies the **Bundesplatz**. **26 fountains** spray out of the ground. Each stands for one **canton**. In summer children often play in the water here. Markets and demonstrations also take place on the square.

gewusst: You can visit the Federal Palace on guided tours and listen to the debates from the gallery during the sessions.
The green colour of copper is called patina.

teile.einleitung: The Henzi Conspiracy was a planned coup in Bern in 1749. Discontented burghers wanted to break the power of the few ruling families. The conspiracy was betrayed before it began.
wichtigste: It was directed against the rule of the patrician families in Bern.
It was also called the “burghers' uproar”.
A theology student betrayed the plans at the beginning of July 1749.
Samuel Henzi and two fellow conspirators were executed on 17 July 1749.
Henzi's reform memorandum demanded access to office for all citizens.
Gotthold Ephraim Lessing wrote a drama fragment about Henzi.

abschnitte.text: In the 18th century only a few **patrician families** ruled in Bern. Patricians were distinguished lineages who shared the important offices among themselves. Most **burghers**, that is, citizens of the city, had hardly any access to power. In 1744 citizens criticised the elections to the **Grand Council** in memoranda. The government reacted with fines and banishments, and **Samuel Henzi** also had to leave the city.

Henzi wrote a **reform memorandum**. It demanded **access to office for all citizens**. In addition there were a guild constitution, the **popular election** of officials and a public **state account**. The aim was more say for the burghers. The conspiracy was later also called the **“burghers' uproar”**.

The conspirators met in secret in a **dyeworks in the Sulgenbach**. It belonged to Johann Friedrich Küpfer, and craftsmen, merchants and officers came together there. On the evening of 2 July 1749 the **theology student** Friedrich Ulrich informed a councillor. The next day the Secret Council knew about it and took action. Those involved were arrested.

On 17 July 1749 Samuel Henzi, Samuel Niklaus Wernier and Emanuel Fueter were **executed** in front of the Upper Gate. Others involved received house arrest or were **banished**. The rule of the patricians then lasted for almost 50 more years. Only in 1798 did the old order in Bern collapse.

The German poet **Gotthold Ephraim Lessing** wrote a drama about Henzi. He did not finish it, which is why it is called a **drama fragment**. It was written in 1749 and appeared in 1753 under the title “Samuel Henzi”. It is regarded as an early **bourgeois drama** about a current political case. In this way the Bernese conspiracy also became known abroad.

gewusst: Lessing wrote about the conspiracy in the very same year in which it happened.
Only with the end of the Old Confederacy in 1798 did the Bernese patricians lose their privileges.

teile.einleitung: The Bergier Commission was a group of historians that investigated Switzerland's role in the Second World War. Its official name is the Independent Commission of Experts Switzerland, Second World War. Its report of 2002 showed that Switzerland was not only a victim of the threat but had also made mistakes.
wichtigste: The Federal Council set up the commission in December 1996.
It was led by the historian Jean-François Bergier, after whom it is named.
The trigger was the debate about dormant assets of Holocaust victims in Swiss banks.
The commission was also allowed to inspect the archives of private firms such as banks and insurers.
Its budget finally came to 22 million francs.
The final report appeared on 22 March 2002.
According to the report, during the war Switzerland turned back or deported more than 20,000 refugees.

abschnitte.text: In the 1990s there was fierce international argument about Switzerland in the Second World War. It was mainly about **dormant assets**, that is, bank accounts of Holocaust victims whose owners had been murdered. Many heirs had tried in vain after the war to get at this money. Jewish organisations and politicians in the USA put great pressure on the Swiss banks. As a result Switzerland fell into a serious crisis of trust.

In January 1997 the security guard **Christoph Meili** discovered old files at the Swiss Bank Corporation in Zurich that were to be destroyed in the shredding room. Among them were documents from wartime. He rescued the files and handed them to a Jewish organisation. His action made headlines around the world, but in Switzerland he was also attacked. Meili later moved to the USA.

In December 1996 the **Federal Council** set up the Independent Commission of Experts. Its president was the French-speaking Swiss historian **Jean-François Bergier**. Among the members was also the well-known Holocaust historian Saul Friedländer. The commission was given a special right: it was allowed to inspect the **archives** of private firms such as banks and insurers, and they were not allowed to destroy any files. The budget finally came to 22 million francs.

The commission investigated how Swiss firms and the National Bank did business with Nazi Germany. The National Bank bought large quantities of German gold. Part of it was **looted gold**, which came from the central banks of occupied countries such as Belgium and the Netherlands and from persecuted people. Swiss firms also supplied weapons and other goods to Germany.

An important subject was the treatment of **refugees**. According to the final report, during the war Switzerland turned back or deported more than 20,000 refugees at the border. From August 1942 the border was closed to many Jewish people, although the authorities knew about the murders. At the same time Switzerland also took in tens of thousands of people. The commission concluded that the authorities could have saved many more people.

On 22 March 2002 the commission presented its **final report**, and numerous individual studies appeared as well. As early as 13 August 1998 the major Swiss banks had agreed with plaintiffs in the USA, in a **global settlement**, on 1.25 billion US dollars. The report set off many discussions in Switzerland, with some finding it too critical and others important and overdue. It changed the picture of Switzerland in the Second World War and is now taught in history lessons.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of experts who investigate a particular task.
Money in accounts whose owners have not been in touch for many years.
Gold that the Nazis had stolen from other countries or from persecuted people.
A place where old documents and files are kept.

gewusst: Besides the final report, the commission published about 25 volumes of individual studies.
Jean-François Bergier was a professor at ETH Zurich and died in 2009.
The commission consisted of experts from several countries, including Switzerland, Israel, the USA, Britain and Poland.

teile.einleitung: After the time of Napoleon the cantons concluded a new Federal Treaty in 1815. It held Switzerland together as a loose confederation of states until 1848.
wichtigste: On 7 August 1815 the cantons swore the Federal Treaty in Zurich.
Envoys of the cantons met at the Diet.
Each full canton had one vote, divided cantons half a vote.
The monastery article guaranteed the continued existence of the monasteries.
A shared currency was lacking, which made trade harder.
In 1819 a federal military school was founded in Thun.
The period from 1814 to 1830 is called the Restoration.

abschnitte.text: After the end of **Napoleon's** rule the cantons had to reorder their life together. On **7 August 1815** they swore the **Federal Treaty** in **Zurich**. Geneva, the Valais and Neuchâtel were also new members. In the same year the European great powers recognised the **neutrality** of Switzerland. The Federal Treaty applied until 1848.

The most important shared institution was the **Diet**. Envoys of the cantons met there. They acted according to the instructions of their cantonal governments. Each canton had **one vote**, however big it was. Divided cantons such as Appenzell had half a vote each.

A special article guaranteed the continued existence of the **monasteries**. It is called the **monastery article**. When the canton of Aargau abolished its monasteries in 1841, there was therefore fierce dispute. The Catholic cantons saw this as a breach of the Federal Treaty. This dispute contributed to the tensions before the Sonderbund War.

Under the Federal Treaty each canton had its own **coins**, its own **measures** and its own **customs duties**. Anyone transporting goods through Switzerland often had to pay several times. This made trade much harder. A **shared currency** came only in the federal state: from 1850 the Swiss franc.

The period from 1814 to 1830 is called the **Restoration**, which means re-establishment. The old families in the cities won back much of their former power. Even so, there were also shared innovations. In 1819 the first federal **military school** was founded in **Thun**. There officers from all the cantons were trained together.

gewusst: Under the Federal Treaty Switzerland consisted of 22 cantons for the first time.
In Thun members of the Swiss army are still trained today.

teile.einleitung: The canton of Jura is the youngest canton of Switzerland. It came into being on 1 January 1979, after the French-speaking, Catholic north of the Jura had separated from the canton of Bern following long disputes. Its founding is regarded as an example of how Switzerland resolved a serious conflict by means of votes.
wichtigste: The canton of Jura has officially existed since 1 January 1979.
It consists of the former Bernese districts of Delémont, Franches-Montagnes and Porrentruy.
The capital is Delémont, called Delsberg in German.
The Moeckli Affair of 1947 is regarded as the trigger of the separatist movement.
In the first Jura plebiscite of 23 June 1974, just under 52 per cent voted for a new canton.
On 24 September 1978 the whole of Switzerland approved the founding with about 82.3 per cent Yes.
Since 1 January 2026 the town of Moutier has also belonged to the canton of Jura.

abschnitte.text: The canton of Jura lies in the north-west of Switzerland on the border with France. It covers the Jura mountains with their hills, forests and pastures as well as the high plateau of the **Franches-Montagnes** (Freiberge in German). The river **Doubs** forms a deeply cut gorge. The main language is French, and the population is mostly Catholic.

For centuries the area belonged to the **Prince-Bishopric of Basel**, whose bishop resided in Porrentruy after the Reformation. At the **Congress of Vienna** in 1815 the Jura was assigned to the canton of Bern. The Catholic, French-speaking northern Jura often felt like a stranger in Reformed, German-speaking Bern. From this arose the so-called **Jura question**.

In 1947 the Bernese cantonal parliament refused the French-speaking member of the government Georges Moeckli an important department. This **Moeckli Affair** is regarded as the trigger of the movement for a canton of its own. From 1951 the **Rassemblement jurassien** was the most important organisation of the separatists, and its leading figure was **Roland Béguelin**. The youth group of the Béliers (the “Rams”) drew attention to itself with spectacular actions. In 1984, for example, it toppled the soldiers' monument “Le Fritz” on the Col des Rangiers from its plinth.

In the first **Jura plebiscite** of 23 June 1974, just under 52 per cent in the whole Bernese Jura voted for a new canton. In further votes the southern districts decided to stay with Bern. So only **Delémont**, **Franches-Montagnes** and **Porrentruy** formed the new canton. On 24 September 1978 the people and the cantons of the whole of Switzerland approved with about 82.3 per cent Yes, and on 1 January 1979 the Jura became the 23rd canton by the count of the time.

The Jura question occupied Switzerland even after 1979. The German-speaking **Laufental** moved from the canton of Bern to the canton of Basel-Landschaft in 1994. The town of **Moutier** voted on 18 June 2017 for a move to the Jura, but the vote was declared invalid because of irregularities. After a new vote in 2021, Moutier has belonged to the canton of Jura since 1 January 2026.

In the Jura the **watch industry** and precision engineering are important, as is agriculture. Well known are the horses of the **Freiberger** breed and the distilling of Damassine, a small plum. Worth seeing are the medieval little town of **Saint-Ursanne** on the Doubs, the castle of Porrentruy and the moorland lake Étang de la Gruère. The canton has about 74,000 inhabitants (as of 2023, before Moutier joined).

begriffe.erklaerung: People who want to separate from a state or canton.
A popular vote on an important question of principle.
The long dispute over whether the Jura should belong to the canton of Bern or be independent.
A territory in which a bishop was not only a church leader but also a secular ruler.

gewusst: The canton of Jura is the only canton that came into being after the founding of the federal state in 1848 through a vote of the whole Swiss people.
The Freiberger horses come from the high plateau of the Franches-Montagnes and are still bred and promoted today by the national stud in Avenches.
The Fête du peuple jurassien in Delémont recalls the struggle for the canton's own existence every year in September.

teile.einleitung: Basel is one of the most important centres of the chemical and pharmaceutical industry in the world. It all began in the 19th century with colourful dyes for the city's silk ribbons.
wichtigste: The Basel chemical industry began in the 19th century with synthetic dyes from coal tar.
From 1859 Alexander Clavel made the red dye fuchsine.
Important customers were the Basel silk ribbon weaving mills.
The lack of patent protection for chemical processes made the rise easier.
The Rhine supplied water and served as an outlet for waste water.
Ciba stood for “Gesellschaft für Chemische Industrie in Basel”, the Society for Chemical Industry in Basel.
In 1895 Sandoz entered the medicines business with the fever remedy antipyrine.

abschnitte.text: For centuries Basel was a centre of **silk ribbon weaving**. The dye works constantly needed new, bright colours. In the middle of the 19th century people learned to make dyes artificially from **coal tar**. They are called **tar dyes** or synthetic dyes. From **1859** **Alexander Clavel** made the red dye **fuchsine** in his silk dye works.

For a long time Switzerland had no **patent protection** for chemical processes. A patent protects an invention so that others may not simply copy it. Basel firms were therefore allowed to imitate processes that were protected elsewhere. Only at the beginning of the 20th century did chemical processes become patentable in Switzerland. The closeness to Germany and France also helped.

Chemical production needs large amounts of **water**. In Basel the **Rhine** supplied it right on the doorstep. At the same time the **waste water** was then often led into the river untreated. That did great harm to nature. Today there are strict rules and sewage treatment plants so that the Rhine stays clean.

Out of Clavel's business a large company later grew. In **1884** the firm Bindschedler & Busch became **Ciba**, the “Gesellschaft für Chemische Industrie in Basel”. In **1886** Alfred Kern and Edouard Sandoz founded the firm **Sandoz**. **Geigy** and later **Hoffmann-La Roche** also became important Basel firms.

In time the Basel firms made not only dyes but also **medicines**. In **1895** Sandoz began with the fever-reducing remedy **antipyrine**. Today the **pharmaceutical industry** is much more important than dyes. In 1996 Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz merged to form **Novartis**.

gewusst: The abbreviation Ciba is made up of the first letters of “Chemische Industrie Basel”.
The pharmaceutical industry is now one of Switzerland's most important export sectors.

teile.einleitung: The Grimm-Hoffmann affair was a political scandal in Switzerland in 1917. A federal councillor and a socialist secretly tried to broker a peace in the middle of the First World War. When this became known, Swiss neutrality was seen as endangered.
wichtigste: Robert Grimm had founded the Zimmerwald movement in 1915.
Arthur Hoffmann headed the Political Department.
They wanted a separate peace between Germany and Russia.
Grimm was in Petrograd in 1917 when the affair came to light.
A Swedish newspaper published the telegram.
Gustave Ador became Hoffmann's successor in the Federal Council.

abschnitte.text: **Robert Grimm** was a socialist from Bern and an opponent of the war. In September 1915 he organised the conference of **Zimmerwald** in the canton of Bern. Socialist opponents of the war from different countries met there, and from this the **Zimmerwald movement** arose. **Arthur Hoffmann** was a federal councillor and headed the **Political Department**. So he was responsible for Switzerland's foreign policy.

After the **February Revolution** of 1917, Grimm travelled to **Petrograd**, today's Saint Petersburg. Hoffmann informed him by **telegram** that Germany would not attack in the east as long as a peace was possible. The aim was a **separate peace** between Germany and Russia. A separate peace is a peace only between some of the parties to a war. It would have benefited Germany above all.

The coded telegram was intercepted. The Swedish newspaper **“Socialdemokraten”** published it. So the **Allies**, the opponents of Germany, learned of the peace attempts. Because the telegram came from Hoffmann as foreign minister, it weighed especially heavily. Grimm had to leave Russia, and Hoffmann resigned.

In June 1917 the Federal Assembly elected the Geneva liberal **Gustave Ador**. Ador was at that time president of the **International Committee of the Red Cross**, ICRC for short. He led it from 1910 to 1928. The election of a French-speaking Swiss and friend of the Allies was meant to reassure **Romandy** and foreign countries. It strengthened the image of a humanitarian and impartial Switzerland.

gewusst: Gustave Ador was at the same time a federal councillor and president of the ICRC.
Robert Grimm became one of the leaders of the General Strike in 1918.

teile.einleitung: Heinrich Bullinger was a reformer in Zurich. After the death of Huldrych Zwingli he led the Zurich church for over 40 years. His writings and letters had an effect across Europe.
wichtigste: Bullinger was born in Bremgarten in Aargau in 1504.
In 1531 he became Zwingli's successor at the Grossmünster.
As Antistes he led the Zurich church until his death in 1575.
In 1549 he reached agreement with John Calvin on communion in the Consensus Tigurinus.
His Second Helvetic Confession appeared in 1566.
About 12,000 letters by him survive.

abschnitte.text: Heinrich Bullinger was born in **Bremgarten** in 1504. The small town in today's Aargau lay at that time in a **Common Lordship**. His father was a priest. Bullinger studied in Cologne and got to know the writings of the reformers there. After that he turned to the **Reformation**.

In 1531 **Huldrych Zwingli** died in the Battle of Kappel. At the end of 1531 Bullinger became pastor at the **Grossmünster** in Zurich. He became **Antistes**, the chief pastor of the Reformed church of the city. He held this office for about **44 years**, from December 1531 until his death in September 1575. This long term of office put the Zurich Reformation on a lasting footing.

The Reformed in Zurich and Geneva understood **communion** differently. Communion is a ceremony with bread and wine in memory of Jesus. In 1549 Bullinger and **John Calvin** reached agreement in the **Consensus Tigurinus**, the Zurich Consensus. With it the churches of Zurich and Geneva moved closer together. At the same time they set themselves apart from Lutheran teaching.

Bullinger wrote a **confession of faith**, which was printed in 1566: the **Second Helvetic Confession**, in Latin Confessio Helvetica posterior. A confession of faith sums up what a church believes. It was adopted by Reformed churches in many countries. In this way Bullinger became known far beyond Zurich.

Historians know Bullinger especially for his huge **correspondence**. About **12,000 letters** survive. He was in contact with scholars and princes all over Europe. In 1555 Zurich under Bullinger took in **Reformed people from Locarno**, who had to leave their homeland. Some of them later founded important silk businesses.

gewusst: Bullinger also wrote a chronicle of the history of the Reformation.
His letters are still being edited to this day by researchers in Zurich.

teile.einleitung: Upper Burgundy was a kingdom in the early Middle Ages. It covered large parts of today's French-speaking Switzerland and areas in today's France. From 888 to 1032, kings from the house of the Welfs ruled there.
wichtigste: Rudolf I had himself proclaimed king in Saint-Maurice in 888.
The kings came from the older house of the Welfs.
In 919 Rudolf II lost near Winterthur against Duke Burchard II of Swabia.
Around 930 Rudolf II united Upper Burgundy with Lower Burgundy.
Conrad the Peaceful ruled from 937 to 993.
In 1033 Conrad II was crowned in Payerne, and Burgundy came to the Holy Roman Empire.

abschnitte.text: In the 9th century the great empire of the **Carolingians** fell apart. Several new kingdoms arose from it. In 888 **Rudolf I** had himself proclaimed king of Upper Burgundy in the abbey of **Saint-Maurice** in Valais. He belonged to the older house of the **Welfs**. His descendants ruled Burgundy until 1032.

His son **Rudolf II** wanted to extend the kingdom to the east. In 919, however, he suffered a defeat near **Winterthur** against Duke **Burchard II of Swabia**. With this the expansion to the east was stopped. Around 930 **Hugh of Provence** gave up Lower Burgundy. In return Rudolf II gave up his claims in Italy, and a united **Kingdom of Burgundy** came into being.

**Adelaide** was a daughter of Rudolf II. She first married King **Lothair of Italy**. After his death in 950, **Berengar II** held her prisoner. After that she married the East Frankish king **Otto I** and later became empress. She was one of the most important women of her time.

Adelaide's brother **Conrad** grew up at the Saxon court and was protected by **Otto I**. He ruled Upper Burgundy from 937 to 993. His long reign is regarded as peaceful, which is why he is called **Conrad the Peaceful**. His son **Rudolf III** was the last king from the house of the Welfs. He died in 1032 without a successor.

After the death of Rudolf III, Emperor **Conrad II** had himself crowned on 2 February 1033 in the monastery of **Payerne**. Payerne is called **Peterlingen** in German. With this, Burgundy came to the **Holy Roman Empire**. So now western and eastern Switzerland also belonged to the same empire. The mighty abbey church of Payerne can still be visited today.

gewusst: The Burgundian queen Bertha, wife of Rudolf II, is still known today in French-speaking Switzerland as “Queen Bertha”.
The abbey of Saint-Maurice in Valais has existed for over 1,500 years.

teile.einleitung: The Habsburgs are one of the most famous ruling families of Europe. Their history began in today's canton of Aargau, where their ancestral castle, the Habsburg, stands. Later they ruled from Vienna as kings and emperors over huge territories, and in Swiss history they were for a long time the great opponents of the Confederates.
wichtigste: The ancestral castle of the Habsburgs stands in today's canton of Aargau.
Count Radbot is regarded as the builder of the Habsburg around 1020/1030.
Radbot and his wife Ita of Lorraine founded the monastery of Muri in 1027.
Rudolf I was elected Roman-German king in 1273 as the first Habsburg.
King Albrecht I was murdered near Windisch by his nephew in 1308.
In 1415 the Habsburgs lost Aargau to the Confederates.
Later their centre of power lay in Austria with its capital Vienna.

abschnitte.text: The **Habsburg** stands on a hill near Brugg in the canton of Aargau. Count **Radbot** is said to have built it around 1020/1030, and the family named itself after it. In 1027 Radbot and his wife Ita of Lorraine founded the **monastery of Muri**. Since 1804 the castle has belonged to the canton of Aargau, and today there is a restaurant in it.

The Habsburgs acquired many territories and rights on the Swiss Plateau. In 1273 **Rudolf I** was elected Roman-German king, and with this the family rose into the highest layer of the nobility. He acquired Austria, which later became the centre of their power. His son **Albrecht I** was murdered near Windisch by his nephew Johann in 1308, and at this spot the monastery of Königsfelden arose.

In their territories the Habsburgs appointed **bailiffs**, who administered and dispensed justice. The valley communities of Central Switzerland wanted to preserve their freedoms and came into conflict with the Habsburgs. In the battles of **Morgarten** in 1315 and **Sempach** in 1386 the Confederates defeated Habsburg armies, and at Sempach Duke Leopold III even died. The legend of William Tell and the bailiff Gessler is set in this period.

In 1415 the Confederates conquered **Aargau**, and the Habsburgs lost their ancestral lands. In 1460 Thurgau also came under Confederate rule. With the **Perpetual Settlement** of 1474, Duke Sigismund of Habsburg and the Confederates mutually recognised each other's possessions. With this the long struggles largely ended.

From **Vienna** the Habsburgs ruled for centuries over Austria and many other lands. Through skilful marriages they acquired the Netherlands and Spain, among others. In the 16th century Emperor **Charles V** ruled over an empire in which “the sun never set”. Their rule ended in 1918 with the end of the First World War, when Austria-Hungary fell apart.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ruling family whose power is passed on over many generations.
The castle from which a noble family originally comes and after which it is often named.
An official who administered a territory and dispensed justice on behalf of a lord.
A peace treaty of 1474 between the Habsburgs and the Confederates.

gewusst: The castle after which one of the most powerful families in the world is named is rather small.
The name Habsburg is often interpreted as “hawk castle”.
Empress Maria Theresa and Empress Elisabeth, called Sisi, also belonged to the House of Habsburg.

teile.einleitung: In 15 BC Emperor Augustus had the peoples of the Alps subdued. His stepsons Drusus and Tiberius led the campaign from two sides. After that Rome controlled the Alpine passes and the land as far as the Danube.
wichtigste: The Alpine campaign took place in 15 BC.
Drusus advanced into the Alps from the south, from Italy.
At the same time Tiberius came from the west, from Gaul.
On Lake Constance there was a naval battle against the Vindelici.
The victory monument Tropaeum Alpium near La Turbie names 46 defeated Alpine peoples.

abschnitte.text: Emperor **Augustus** wanted safe routes from Italy over the Alps to the north. So in **15 BC** he sent out two armies. **Drusus** marched north from northern Italy through the Alpine valleys. His brother **Tiberius** came at the same time from the west, from Gaul. Together they defeated the **Raetians** in the mountains and the **Vindelici** in the Alpine foreland.

Tiberius advanced against the Vindelici from the west. According to the Greek geographer **Strabo**, he defeated them, among other things, in a battle on **Lake Constance**. For this the Romans needed ships on the lake. The area around Lake Constance borders present-day eastern Switzerland.

After the campaign Rome controlled the **Alpine passes** and the foreland as far as the **Danube**. The Roman province of **Raetia** later emerged from the area. Around 7/6 BC the **Tropaeum Alpium** was built at La Turbie above Monaco. Its inscription lists 46 defeated Alpine peoples. Parts of it still stand today.

gewusst: Tiberius, one of the two commanders, later became Roman emperor himself.

teile.einleitung: The Gotthard Pass connects the canton of Uri in the north with Ticino in the south. Since the Middle Ages it has been one of the most important Alpine crossings between north and south. Merchants, mule drivers and pilgrims travelled over it to Italy.
wichtigste: Around 1230 a wooden bridge made the Schöllenen Gorge passable.
Already in the Middle Ages a hospice stood on the summit of the pass.
The pass is named after Saint Godehard of Hildesheim.
Mule drivers brought goods over the pass with mules and horses.
In warehouses, the Susten, the goods were reloaded.
In 1410 the Urseren Valley bound itself to Uri through a treaty of citizenship.

abschnitte.text: For a long time the narrow **Schöllenen Gorge** in the canton of Uri was hardly possible to cross. Around 1230 a **wooden bridge** made the gorge passable. Only with this did the Gotthard become an important route. The best-known bridge there is today called the **Devil's Bridge**. From the north the way now led directly through Ticino into Lombardy to **Milan**, the most important trading city of northern Italy.

On the summit of the pass stood a **chapel** for Saint **Godehard**, a bishop of Hildesheim. The name **Gotthard** comes from his name. The Archbishop of Milan consecrated the chapel in 1230. The summit of the pass belonged to the south in church terms. Next to it there was a **hospice**, a simple inn where travellers found shelter from cold and storms.

**Mule drivers** (Säumer) were men who brought goods over the passes with **pack animals** such as mules and horses. A pack animal carries loads on its back. The mule drivers led the animals over the mountain in columns. In warehouses, the **Susten**, the goods were unloaded. There the next mule drivers' association took them over, and fees were charged for this.

Directly below the summit of the pass, on the north side, lies the **Urseren Valley** with **Andermatt**. In the Middle Ages it belonged to the Benedictine monastery of **Disentis** in the Surselva. The way over the Oberalp Pass connected the two valleys. In 1410 Ursern concluded a **treaty of citizenship** with **Uri**. With this, Uri controlled the whole northern ramp of the pass.

In the 19th century a road for vehicles was built over the pass. Stagecoaches now drove over the winding **Tremola** on the south side. In 1882 the **Gotthard railway tunnel** was opened. Later a road tunnel followed, and in 2016 the **Gotthard Base Tunnel**. To this day the Gotthard is one of the most important connections through the Alps.

gewusst: Gotthard is the name of a saint from Germany, Godehard of Hildesheim.
Great rivers such as the Rhine, the Reuss, the Rhone and the Ticino rise around the Gotthard massif.

teile.einleitung: Expo 64 was a Swiss national exhibition in Lausanne. It was open from 30 April to 25 October 1964 and showed how Switzerland lives and where it wants to develop.
wichtigste: Expo 64 took place in 1964 in Lausanne on Lake Geneva.
It lasted just under six months.
The centrepiece was called the “Way of Switzerland”.
With the Mésoscaphe, a submarine by Jacques Piccard, you could dive into Lake Geneva.
A monorail ran on a single rail across the site.
Jean Tinguely built the moving machine “Heureka”.

abschnitte.text: A **national exhibition** shows what makes up Switzerland: work, culture, technology and the future. Expo 64 took place in **Lausanne** on the shore of Lake Geneva. It was open from **30 April to 25 October 1964**, so just under six months. People travelled there from all over Switzerland. For many it was a great experience.

The centrepiece of the exhibition was the **“Way of Switzerland”**. It led visitors through various themes. It showed nature and people, **rights and freedoms** and the tasks of the future. The Expo did not only want to celebrate but also to make people think. It asked how Switzerland wants to live in a modern world.

A main attraction was the **Mésoscaphe**, a **submarine** for visitors. With it you could dive into Lake Geneva. It was built by the deep-sea explorer **Jacques Piccard**. His father **Auguste Piccard** had flown into the stratosphere in a balloon. Today the Mésoscaphe stands in the **Swiss Museum of Transport** in Lucerne.

A **monorail** ran across the site. This is a railway on only **one rail**. “Mono” means “one” and “rail” means rail. From above, passengers had a good view of the exhibition. The monorail was one of the great attractions of the Expo.

The artist **Jean Tinguely** liked to build works of art that **move**. For Expo 64 he created the large machine **“Heureka”**. Wheels turn, and parts rattle and swing. It attracted many visitors. After the Expo, “Heureka” came to the **Zürichhorn** in Zurich, where it still stands on the lakeshore today.

gewusst: At Expo 64, quite ordinary visitors could dive into Lake Geneva in the Mésoscaphe.
Tinguely's machine “Heureka” still stands at the Zürichhorn today.

teile.einleitung: Refugee policy decides how a country treats people who flee from war and persecution. In Swiss history there are moments of great helpfulness, but also dark chapters. Particularly disputed is the policy during the time of National Socialism from 1933 to 1945.
wichtigste: From 1938 the passports of German Jews were marked with a J stamp.
Heinrich Rothmund, as head of the Police Division, was responsible for refugee policy.
On 13 August 1942 the border was closed to refugees who fled only for “racial reasons”.
Federal Councillor Eduard von Steiger compared Switzerland to a small, full lifeboat.
In the Second World War Switzerland took in about 51,000 civilian refugees.
Many people were turned away at the border, and the exact number is disputed.
Police captain Paul Grüninger saved hundreds of refugees and was acquitted only in 1995.

abschnitte.text: After the annexation of Austria in 1938 many Jews fled to Switzerland. Switzerland wanted to limit entry and negotiated with Germany. This led to the **J stamp**, a mark in the passports of German Jews that made them recognisable at the border. According to more recent research, the German authorities proposed it in order to prevent a general **visa requirement** for Germans, but Switzerland agreed.

When the deportations to the extermination camps began in 1942, more and more people fled. With the instruction of **13 August 1942**, refugees who fled only for “racial reasons” were to be turned away. Among those responsible was **Heinrich Rothmund**, head of the Police Division in the Federal Department of Justice and Police. On 30 August 1942 Federal Councillor Eduard von Steiger spoke of a small, heavily occupied **lifeboat**, and later this became the saying “The boat is full”.

After public protests the Federal Council shortly afterwards relaxed the rejections for a time. In total Switzerland sheltered about **300,000** people during the war, military internees included. Among them were about 51,000 civilian refugees, about 20,000 of them Jewish. How many were turned away is disputed because of incomplete records and different ways of counting, and for many the rejection meant death.

The St Gallen police captain **Paul Grüninger** backdated entries in 1938 and 1939 so that refugees could stay legally. He was dismissed and convicted for this, and only in 1995, 23 years after his death, was he acquitted. The diplomat **Carl Lutz** saved tens of thousands of Hungarian Jews in Budapest in 1944 with letters of protection. Many private individuals also hid refugees or helped them across the border.

abschnitte.titel: Coming to terms with the past
abschnitte.text: In 1957 the **Ludwig Report**, commissioned by the Federal Council, examined refugee policy since 1933. In the 1990s Switzerland's role in the Second World War was researched closely again, among others by the **Bergier Commission**. In 1995 Federal President Kaspar Villiger apologised on behalf of the Federal Council for the J stamp. Today this chapter is an important part of history lessons.

In 1951 the **Geneva Refugee Convention** came into being. It sets out who counts as a refugee and receives protection, and Switzerland joined it. In 1956 Switzerland took in many refugees from Hungary, later also from Tibet, Czechoslovakia and Vietnam. Today the Asylum Act regulates who receives protection in Switzerland. Since 2022 refugees from Ukraine have received a special **protection status S**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who has to leave their home because they are persecuted or threatened there.
Protection that a state grants to persecuted people.
Soldiers of foreign armies who came into a neutral country and had to stay there until the end of the war.
The forced removal of people to another place.
An international agreement of 1951 for the protection of refugees.

gewusst: Paul Grüninger is honoured in St Gallen today, and a stadium and a bridge bear his name.
Carl Lutz is regarded as one of the greatest rescuers of Jews in the Second World War.
The expression “The boat is full” later became the title of a well-known Swiss film of 1981.

teile.einleitung: Johann Rudolf Wettstein was mayor of Basel and an important diplomat of the Confederacy. In the Peace of Westphalia of 1648 he achieved the independence of the Confederacy from the Holy Roman Empire. That is why a bridge and a square in Basel recall him.
wichtigste: Wettstein was born in Basel in 1594.
From 1645 he was mayor of Basel.
In 1646 he travelled to Westphalia as an envoy.
In Münster he negotiated with the envoys of the emperor.
In 1648 the Confederacy became independent of the Empire.
After the Peasants' War of 1653 he pushed through harsh punishments.
The Wettstein Bridge in Basel bears his name.

abschnitte.text: Johann Rudolf Wettstein was born in **Basel** in **1594**. He made a political career in the city. In **1645** he became **mayor** of Basel, at that time the highest office in the city. He was regarded as a skilful negotiator. He died in 1666.

From **1618 to 1648** the **Thirty Years' War** raged in central Europe. It devastated large parts of today's Germany. The Confederacy was largely spared. At the end of the war, a peace was negotiated in Westphalia. The talks took place in the cities of **Münster** and **Osnabrück**.

abschnitte.titel: Dispute with the Imperial Chamber Court
abschnitte.text: The occasion for Wettstein's journey was a dispute with the **Imperial Chamber Court** in Speyer. This court of the Empire had summoned citizens of Basel and had goods of Basel **merchants** seized. Basel saw this as an interference in its own judicial sovereignty. The city wanted the court no longer to be allowed to judge people of Basel.

In **1646** Wettstein travelled to Westphalia as an envoy, at first for Basel and the other **Reformed places** such as Zurich and Bern. At the beginning of 1647 he also received a mandate from the whole Confederacy. In **Münster** he negotiated with the envoys of the emperor. In the **Peace of Westphalia** of **1648** the Confederacy was released from the **Holy Roman Empire**. With this it was also legally an **independent state**.

In the **Peasants' War of 1653** peasants rose up in several places, including the Basel countryside. After the uprising Wettstein pushed through the **execution of seven leaders**. This hard side also belongs to his story. Today in Basel the **Wettstein Bridge** recalls him, which connects Greater Basel with Kleinbasel. The **Wettsteinplatz** also bears his name.

gewusst: The independence of the Confederacy was recognised under international law for the first time in 1648.
The peace negotiations in Münster and Osnabrück lasted several years.

teile.einleitung: The Wars of Kappel were two wars of religion in the Confederacy in 1529 and 1531. Reformed Zurich faced the five Catholic inner places. In the second war the reformer Huldrych Zwingli fell.
wichtigste: The Wars of Kappel took place in 1529 and 1531.
They are named after Kappel am Albis in the canton of Zurich.
Zurich's opponents were Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug.
The first war ended without a battle, and the Kappel Milk Soup is well known.
In the second war Huldrych Zwingli fell on 11 October 1531.
The Catholic places won the Second War of Kappel.
The Second Peace let each place decide its own faith for itself.

abschnitte.text: In **Zurich** **Huldrych Zwingli** had introduced the **Reformation**. Bern and other places also became Reformed. The **five inner places** Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug, however, held to the old, **Catholic** faith. The Confederacy was thereby deeply divided. Both sides looked for allies and distrusted each other.

abschnitte.titel: The First War of Kappel in 1529
abschnitte.text: In 1529 the Reformed pastor **Jakob Kaiser** was captured in Schwyz and executed as a **heretic**. Zurich took this as the occasion to march against the Catholic places. At **Kappel am Albis**, near the border with the canton of Zug, the armies faced each other. But there was no battle. According to tradition the soldiers ate the **Kappel Milk Soup** together, and after that the **First Peace** was concluded.

The peace did not last long. In **1531** Zurich and Bern imposed a **food blockade** on the inner places. This was a **ban on supplies**: grain and salt were no longer allowed to be brought to them. The Central Swiss places suffered from it and answered with an **attack**. So began the **Second War of Kappel**.

abschnitte.titel: The Second War of Kappel in 1531
abschnitte.text: On **11 October 1531** the battle took place at **Kappel**. The Catholic places defeated the people of Zurich. **Huldrych Zwingli**, who had gone along as field chaplain, was killed. Shortly afterwards Central Swiss troops attacked a Reformed army at night on the **Gubel** near Menzingen in the canton of Zug. This second defeat ended the war in favour of the **Catholic places**.

In the **Second Peace of Kappel** of 1531 it was laid down that **each place decides its own faith**. After that the Reformation could not spread further in the Confederacy. The Confederacy remained **divided by confession** into Reformed and Catholic places for a long time. Even so, the alliance of the Confederates held together.

gewusst: In Kappel am Albis a monument recalls the spot where Zwingli fell.
After Zwingli's death, Heinrich Bullinger carried on the Zurich Reformation.

teile.einleitung: In Kaiseraugst in the canton of Aargau a nuclear power plant was to be built in the 1970s. In 1975 thousands of people occupied the building site. The plant was never built, and Kaiseraugst became a symbol of the Swiss anti-nuclear movement.
wichtigste: Kaiseraugst lies in the Fricktal in the canton of Aargau.
On 1 April 1975 the occupation of the building site began.
About 15,000 people took part in it.
The occupation lasted eleven weeks.
The occupiers relied on non-violent civil disobedience.
In 1988 the project was given up politically.
The federal government paid 350 million francs in compensation.

abschnitte.text: In the 1960s and 1970s Switzerland built several **nuclear power plants**. One was to be built in **Kaiseraugst**. The place lies in the **Fricktal** in the **canton of Aargau**, near the border with Basel-Landschaft. Many people in the **north-western Switzerland** region were against it. They were afraid of accidents and radioactive waste.

On **1 April 1975** opponents of nuclear power occupied the **building site**. Many at first took the news for an **April Fool's joke**. But it became serious: in total about **15,000 people** took part. They came from very different political camps, including farmers, students and families. The occupiers obstructed the **excavation work** and held out on the site for **eleven weeks**.

The occupiers followed a **non-violent** concept. This is called **civil disobedience**: you deliberately do not follow a rule, but stay peaceful. After eleven weeks the **authorities postponed the start of construction** and negotiated with the opponents. The occupiers then left the site.

The dispute over Kaiseraugst lasted many more years. At the end of the 1980s the project was dropped for **political reasons**, and **1988** is regarded as the year of renunciation. The plant was **never built**. The Confederation paid the companies involved **350 million francs** in compensation. The project costs accumulated by then amounted to about **1.3 billion francs**.

gewusst: Kaiseraugst is also known for the Roman city of Augusta Raurica, which lies partly on its municipal territory.
The occupation of Kaiseraugst is regarded as one of the largest protest actions of the Swiss post-war period.

teile.einleitung: Carl Spitteler was a poet from Liestal. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature and is still the only winner of this prize born in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Carl Spitteler was born in 1845 in Liestal and died in 1924 in Lucerne.
His first works appeared under the name Carl Felix Tandem.
The Nobel Prize was awarded to him for the year 1919.
His best-known work is the long poem “Olympian Spring”.
In 1914 in the speech “Our Swiss Standpoint” he called for unity.
In “The Girl-Haters” he tells of two boys.

abschnitte.text: Carl Spitteler was born in **1845** in **Liestal** in the canton of Basel-Landschaft. He studied law first and then theology. After that he worked for some years as a private tutor in Russia, later as a teacher and as a journalist. For many years he lived in **Lucerne**, where he died in **1924**. In Liestal a museum recalls him.

abschnitte.titel: A poet with a false name
abschnitte.text: Spitteler published his first works under an invented name, a **pseudonym**. He called himself **Carl Felix Tandem**. At first his books were hardly noticed. Only later did he write under his real name and become known.

His best-known work is the long poem **“Olympian Spring”**. A poem that tells a great story is called an **epic**. In it Spitteler tells of **gods** on **Mount Olympus**. He took figures from the Greek legends but invented much that was new. For his work he was awarded the **Nobel Prize in Literature** for the year 1919, and it was presented in 1920.

In the **First World War** German-speaking and French-speaking Swiss argued fiercely. Many German-speaking Swiss sided with Germany, many French-speaking Swiss with France. In 1914 Spitteler gave the speech **“Our Swiss Standpoint”**. He called on people to **stick together** as Swiss and stay neutral. The speech became very well known.

Spitteler also wrote for a wide public. The story **“The Girl-Haters”** is about two boys and their quarrels with a girl. In it he remembered his own **childhood**. The story is funny and closely observed.

gewusst: Hermann Hesse later received the Nobel Prize too, but he was born in Germany.
Spitteler also wrote a work called “Prometheus and Epimetheus”, his first great book.

teile.einleitung: In 1526 scholars met in Baden for a great debate about the right faith. At the Baden Disputation, supporters of the Catholic Church and of the Reformation argued. The Catholic side was declared the winner, but the dispute was not ended by it.
wichtigste: The disputation lasted from 19 May to 8 June 1526 in Baden in present-day Aargau.
A disputation is a public, orderly debate.
The main speaker for the Catholic side was Johannes Eck of Ingolstadt.
The Reformed side was represented mainly by Johannes Oecolampadius of Basel.
Zwingli did not travel there, because he feared for his safety.
In 1528 Bern introduced the Reformation after a disputation of its own.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of the 16th century reformers wanted to renew the Church. In Zurich **Huldrych Zwingli** preached the new teaching. Many other places in the Confederation, however, stayed Catholic. The Confederates argued ever more fiercely over which faith was right. A great debate was meant to settle the question.

In a **disputation**, scholars present their opinions in an orderly debate before an audience. The **Diet**, the assembly of the Confederate places, had a Catholic majority. It invited people to **Baden** and set the rules. Baden was a **common lordship**, ruled jointly by several places, and a usual meeting place of the Confederates.

For the Catholic Church spoke **Johannes Eck** of Ingolstadt. He was a well-known opponent of Luther and Zwingli. Zwingli himself did not travel there. He did not trust the Catholic places and feared being arrested or killed. So **Johannes Oecolampadius**, the reformer of Basel, represented the new teaching. The debate lasted almost three weeks.

The majority of the Diet declared the **Catholic side** the winner. Zwingli and his teaching were condemned. But the Reformation could not be stopped. **Bern** held a debate on faith of its own in **1528** and was Reformed afterwards. Because Bern was a powerful place, this made the Reformed side much stronger.

gewusst: Although the Catholic side “won” in Baden, several important places became Reformed in the following years.

teile.einleitung: Gallus was a monk who lived more than 1,400 years ago. He lived alone in the forest and prayed a great deal. The town of St Gallen is named after him.
wichtigste: Gallus was a monk and lived as a hermit.
According to old tradition he came from Ireland.
He travelled through Europe with the monk Columbanus.
He built his cell by the stream Steinach.
According to legend a bear helped him, and the bear got bread for it.
The coat of arms of St Gallen shows a bear.
St Gall's Day is on 16 October.

abschnitte.text: A **monk** is a man who dedicates his life entirely to God. Old stories tell that Gallus came from **Ireland**. Some researchers today think he could also have come from **Alsace**. Gallus was a companion of the Irish monk **Columbanus**. Together they travelled through Europe as far as **Lake Constance**.

At Lake Constance the paths of Gallus and Columbanus parted. Gallus stayed behind and lived as a **hermit**, that is, alone in the forest. His simple hut, a **cell**, he built by the stream **Steinach**. Today the town of St Gallen stands there. Gallus prayed a great deal and lived very simply.

A famous **legend** tells of a bear. A legend is an old story that need not have happened exactly like that. The bear is said to have fetched wood for the fire of Gallus. As thanks Gallus gave it a **loaf of bread**. After that the bear had to leave the place and was never to show itself again.

abschnitte.titel: Monastery and town of St Gallen
abschnitte.text: About 100 years after Gallus, the priest **Othmar** came to this place. In 719 he founded a **monastery** there and became the first abbot. Around the monastery, the town of **St Gallen** grew over time. The town's **coat of arms** still shows a bear today. It recalls the legend of Gallus.

gewusst: On St Gall's Day, 16 October, people remember the monk Gallus.
The Abbey Library in St Gallen is one of the oldest monastery libraries in the world.

teile.einleitung: The Landsgemeinde is a very old form of democracy. The eligible voters of a canton meet in the open air and vote directly. Today it still exists in Appenzell Inner Rhodes and in Glarus.
wichtigste: At the Landsgemeinde people vote in the open air.
Voting is done by raising hands, which is called the Handmehr.
The eligible voters stand in a circle, the Ring.
The Landammann presides over the Landsgemeinde.
The Glarus Landsgemeinde is usually on the first Sunday in May.
The Inner Rhodes Landsgemeinde takes place in the village of Appenzell.

abschnitte.text: At the **Landsgemeinde** the eligible voters of a canton gather on a large square. There they decide on laws and elect authorities. Anyone who agrees raises a hand. This is called the **Handmehr** (majority of hands). The presiding officer looks at which side has more hands. If it is close, a more careful estimate is made.

The eligible voters stand in a large circle. This circle is called the **Ring**. In the middle stands a stage for the government. The Landsgemeinde is presided over by the **Landammann**. He is the highest representative of the cantonal government. At the beginning an oath is often sworn.

In earlier times there were Landsgemeinden in several cantons of central and eastern Switzerland. Today they exist in only two cantons. In **Appenzell Inner Rhodes** it takes place on the Landsgemeindeplatz in the main town of **Appenzell**, usually at the end of April. In **Glarus** it is usually on the first **Sunday in May**. Both Landsgemeinden take place on a **Sunday**.

In Appenzell Inner Rhodes there is a special custom. Traditionally men show with a **sword** or sabre that they are allowed to vote. Today the **voting card** is also valid. Women in Appenzell Inner Rhodes have been allowed to vote at the Landsgemeinde since 1991. The Federal Supreme Court had decided this.

Many value the Landsgemeinde because people meet directly and decide together. It is also a great festival with a long history. Critics say that the vote is not secret. Everyone sees how the others vote. That is why several cantons abolished the Landsgemeinde and now vote at the ballot box.

gewusst: At the Landsgemeinde people vote without a ballot paper, only with a raised hand.
In Glarus young people from the age of 16 are already allowed to vote at the Landsgemeinde.

teile.einleitung: Aventicum, now Avenches in the canton of Vaud, was the main town of the Helvetii in Roman times. A theatre, an amphitheatre, temples and a long city wall show how large and rich the city once was.
wichtigste: Emperor Vespasian raised Aventicum to the rank of a colony around AD 70.
The amphitheatre had room for 14,000 to 16,000 people.
The city wall was about 5 kilometres long and had 73 towers.
The Cigognier temple complex was probably dedicated to Jupiter and local deities.
The theatre was aligned exactly with the Cigognier temple.
In the late 6th century Bishop Marius moved his seat to Lausanne.

abschnitte.text: After the Roman conquest **Aventicum** became the most important place of the Helvetii. Around **AD 70** Emperor **Vespasian** raised the city to the rank of a **colony**. That was a special honour. The name handed down is Colonia Pia Flavia Constans Emerita Helvetiorum Foederata. Today the place is called **Avenches** and lies in the canton of Vaud near Lake Murten.

From the time of Vespasian comes a **city wall** about 5.2 kilometres long with 73 towers. It enclosed a much larger area than the built-up city. At the end of the 1st century the **amphitheatre** was built. With 33 tiers it had room for 14,000 to 16,000 spectators. Animal hunts and gladiator fights took place there.

The great temple complex of **Cigognier** had a colonnaded courtyard. It was probably dedicated to **Jupiter** and local deities. Its last standing column is about 12 metres high. The **Roman theatre** lay about 140 metres away and was aligned exactly with the temple. Theatre and temple thus formed a shared axis for religious ceremonies.

Aventicum had a **harbour** on the south shore of Lake Murten and another at the end of a **canal**. Via Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Biel the city was connected with the **Aare** and the **Rhine**. This meant heavy goods such as stone, wine or pottery could be transported by ship. That was much easier than on the roads.

In the 3rd century the Roman Empire became unstable, and Aventicum lost importance. In the late 6th century Bishop **Marius** moved his seat to **Lausanne**. With that Aventicum finally lost its role as main town. Today you can visit the ruins and the **Roman museum** in Avenches. In the amphitheatre there are even concerts and opera performances.

gewusst: In 1939 a golden bust of the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius was found in Avenches.
The city wall of Aventicum was so long that it enclosed a lot of land on which houses never stood.

teile.einleitung: War economy is the name for the way Switzerland organised its economy during the Second World War, from 1939 to 1945. The country was surrounded by the Axis powers and needed coal, oil and food from abroad. To survive, the state rationed goods, enlarged the arable land and traded with both sides in the war, which is still discussed today.
wichtigste: In the Second World War Switzerland depended on raw materials and food from abroad.
On 9 August 1940 Switzerland concluded an economic agreement with Germany.
For a clearing credit Switzerland received guaranteed coal deliveries.
From 1940 to 1945 the National Bank bought gold worth about 1.2 billion francs from the German Reichsbank.
Important exports were machine tools, watches and precision parts.
In autumn 1944 Switzerland stopped the export of war material.
In the Washington Agreement of 1946 Switzerland paid 250 million francs to the Allies.

abschnitte.text: Shortly after the outbreak of war in 1939 the federal government introduced **rationing**. Sugar, rice, fat, meat, bread and later also clothes and fuels were available only with **ration cards**. Each person received a fixed quantity, so that the scarce supplies were shared fairly. Rationing was lifted only gradually after the war.

So that Switzerland would have more food of its own, the agronomist **Friedrich Traugott Wahlen** drew up a plan for more arable farming. This **“battle of cultivation”** (Anbauschlacht) began in 1940. Meadows were ploughed up, and even in city parks and on sports grounds potatoes and vegetables were planted. Switzerland never became completely independent of other countries, but it could produce a much larger part of its food itself.

After Germany's victory over France in 1940, Switzerland was almost completely surrounded by the Axis powers. On 9 August 1940 it concluded an **economic agreement** with Germany. Trade ran through **clearing**, in which payments were settled through state bodies without foreign currency flowing directly. For a clearing credit of February 1941 Switzerland received guaranteed coal deliveries.

Among the most important Swiss exports were **machine tools**, watches and precision parts, for example fuses. The share of Swiss arms deliveries in German arms production was at most about 1 per cent. Very important for Germany and Italy was the **Gotthard Railway** as a transit route from north to south. Only in autumn 1944 did Switzerland stop the export of war material.

The **Swiss franc** was freely convertible during the war, so it could be exchanged for other currencies anywhere. Germany needed francs to buy raw materials such as tungsten and oil. From 1940 to 1945 the **Swiss National Bank** bought gold worth about 1.2 billion francs from the Reichsbank. Part of it had been looted by Germany in occupied countries.

abschnitte.titel: Reaction of the Allies and coming to terms with the past
abschnitte.text: The Allies put Swiss firms that traded with Germany on **blacklists**. In 1941 the USA blocked Swiss assets, including a large part of the gold reserves. In the **Washington Agreement** of 25 May 1946 Switzerland paid 250 million francs to the Allies. From 1996 to 2001 the independent **Bergier Commission** investigated Switzerland's role in the war more closely.

begriffe.erklaerung: The state allocation of scarce goods so that everyone gets a fair share.
A settlement system in which two states offset their payments against each other instead of transferring money directly.
Means of payment in another country's currency.
The passage of goods or people through a country.
A group of historians who, on behalf of the federal government, investigated Switzerland in the Second World War.

gewusst: During the battle of cultivation, potatoes even grew on the Sechseläutenplatz in Zurich.
Besides food, soap, shoes and textiles were also rationed in the war.

teile.einleitung: On 26 November 1989 Switzerland voted on whether it should abolish its army. The initiative was rejected, but received a surprisingly large number of yes votes and set off a major debate about the army.
wichtigste: The initiative “For a Switzerland without an Army” came from the Group for a Switzerland without an Army (GSoA).
The GSoA was founded in 1982 and submitted the initiative in 1986.
In the vote on 26 November 1989 turnout was about 69 per cent.
The initiative received 35.6 per cent yes votes.
Only the cantons of Jura and Geneva accepted it.
In the 1990s civilian service was introduced.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland citizens can demand a change to the constitution with a **popular initiative**. To do this they have to collect enough signatures. The **Group for a Switzerland without an Army (GSoA)** was founded in 1982. In 1986 it submitted the initiative **“For a Switzerland without an Army”**. It demanded the abolition of the army and a comprehensive peace policy.

The vote took place on **26 November 1989**. At about 69 per cent, very many people went to the polls. The people and the cantons rejected the initiative. Even so, **35.6 per cent** voted yes. Many observers were surprised by this high share. Only in the cantons of **Jura** and **Geneva** was there a yes majority.

Only a few weeks before the vote, on **9 November 1989**, the **Berlin Wall** fell. With that the **Cold War** between East and West came to an end. Many asked themselves what tasks an army still had. Supporters of the initiative saw a chance for more peace policy. Opponents stressed that the army was still needed for the country's security.

After the vote there was a lot of discussion about the army. One important reform was **civilian service**. Anyone who did not want to do military service had previously been punished. In 1992 the people accepted a constitutional article for a civilian alternative service, and in 1996 civilian service began. A second GSoA initiative received only **21.9 per cent** yes on 2 December 2001.

gewusst: The turnout of about 69 per cent was exceptionally high for Swiss votes.
In civilian service, people work in hospitals, care homes or nature conservation, for example.

teile.einleitung: The Peace Agreement of 1937 was an arrangement between employers and trade unions in the metal and machine industry. It is regarded as the foundation stone of industrial peace in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The agreement was signed on 19 July 1937.
The initiative came from the trade union leader Konrad Ilg.
Ernst Dübi signed for the employers.
Both sides committed themselves to an absolute peace obligation: no strikes, no lockouts.
Conflicts were to be resolved through negotiations and a multi-stage arbitration procedure.
Social partnership grew out of this.
In 1974 the agreement was extended into a full collective labour agreement.

abschnitte.text: In the 1920s and 1930s there were many **labour disputes** in Switzerland. Workers went on strike for better wages, and employers locked workers out. The **economic crisis** of the 1930s hit many firms hard. At the same time the threat from dictatorships was growing in Europe. Many felt that Switzerland had to stick together.

The initiative came from **Konrad Ilg**, president of the Swiss Metal and Watch Workers' Union. He pushed the agreement through even against resistance in his own union. **Ernst Dübi**, president of the employers' association of the machine and metal industry, signed for the employers. On **19 July 1937** they concluded the agreement. The two are regarded as the **fathers** of industrial peace.

The core of the agreement was the **absolute peace obligation**. Both sides gave up combative measures such as **strikes** and **lockouts**. Conflicts were to be resolved by negotiation in **good faith**. If the negotiations failed, there was a **multi-stage arbitration procedure**, up to an arbitration tribunal. In this way disputes could be settled without industrial action.

abschnitte.titel: From agreement to collective labour agreement
abschnitte.text: The original agreement was short. It was **renewed** and extended again and again. In 1974 it was extended into a comprehensive **collective labour agreement**, GAV for short. A GAV regulates, for example, wages, working hours and holidays for a whole sector. Today there are many such agreements in Switzerland.

The cooperation of employers and trade unions is called **social partnership**. With the Peace Agreement it properly began in Switzerland. It shapes the Swiss world of work to this day. It is one reason why, compared with other countries, there are only **rarely strikes** in Switzerland.

gewusst: Konrad Ilg pushed the Peace Agreement through against resistance in his own union.
In Switzerland, compared with many other countries, there are only rarely strikes.

tpyepql.t: Federal Constitution of the Swiss Confederation

teile.einleitung: The Federal Constitution of the Swiss Confederation is the most important law of Switzerland. It sets out how the state is organised, what rights everyone has and what tasks the federal government and the cantons take on. The present version has applied since 1 January 2000.
wichtigste: The first Federal Constitution dates from 1848, when the federal state was founded.
The present constitution was accepted by the people and the cantons on 18 April 1999.
About 59.2 per cent of those voting said yes.
It has been in force since 1 January 2000 and replaced the constitution of 1874.
The preamble begins with the words “In the name of Almighty God!”.
