New is a detailed catalogue of fundamental rights, which begins with human dignity.
Every amendment to the constitution must be accepted by the people and the cantons.

abschnitte.text: A **constitution** is the basic law of a state and stands above all other laws. The Swiss Federal Constitution describes the tasks of the federal government, the cantons and the municipalities. It regulates how the Federal Council, Parliament and the Federal Supreme Court are formed. And it sets out which **fundamental rights** every person in Switzerland has.

So far Switzerland has had three federal constitutions: of **1848**, of **1874** and of **1999**. The constitution of 1874 had become hard to follow because of many amendments. In 1996 the Federal Council therefore presented a draft that it described as an **updating**, that is, a reorganisation of the existing law in clear language. The head of the project was Justice Minister Arnold Koller.

On 18 April 1999 the people and the cantons voted on the new constitution. About **59.2 per cent** of those voting said yes. The **majority of cantons**, by contrast, was narrow: 12 full and 2 half cantons agreed. On 1 January 2000 the new constitution came into force.

The constitution begins with the **preamble**, a solemn introduction. Article 1 lists all the cantons, and Article 4 names the four national languages German, French, Italian and Romansh. Then follow the fundamental rights, the social goals in Article 41 and the tasks of the federal government and the cantons. Further parts regulate the rights of the people and the federal authorities.

An important innovation of 1999 is the written **catalogue of fundamental rights**. It begins in Article 7 with **human dignity**, which is to be respected and protected. Further fundamental rights include equality before the law, freedom of opinion, freedom of religion and the right to help in situations of need. Many of them applied earlier, but were recognised only through rulings of the Federal Supreme Court.

The constitution can be changed at any time, for example through a **popular initiative** with 100,000 signatures. Parliament can also propose changes. Every change needs the **double majority** in a popular vote, that is, the majority of the people and of the cantons. Since 2000 the constitution has been amended many times in this way.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solemn introduction at the beginning of a constitution.
Rights that the state must guarantee to all people, such as freedom of opinion.
The majority of the cantons in a vote.
Reordering and writing down existing law in a more understandable way.
Goals of the state, for example that everyone has access to education and health care.

gewusst: The preamble says that the strength of a people is measured by the well-being of its weakest members.
You can read the Federal Constitution free of charge on the internet, in all four national languages.
Because cantons such as Appenzell count as half cantons, the majority of cantons is sometimes narrower than the popular majority.

teile.einleitung: Gallus was a monk who came to Lake Constance in the early Middle Ages. From his simple cell in the forest, the monastery and the town of St Gallen later grew. We know much about him from old biographies.
wichtigste: Gallus came to Lake Constance as a companion of the travelling monk Columbanus.
Around 612 he stayed behind ill when Columbanus moved on to Italy.
After that he lived as a hermit in the forest by the Steinach.
According to legend, a bear brought him wood for the fire.
Gallus died around the middle of the 7th century in Arbon.
In 719 Othmar founded the monastery of St Gallen at his grave.
St Gall's Day is on 16 October.

abschnitte.text: Gallus belonged to a group of monks around the Irish travelling monk **Columbanus**. They travelled through Europe to spread the Christian faith. At Lake Constance they worked in **Tuggen** and **Bregenz**, among other places. According to the biographies, they destroyed images of the gods of the **Alemanni** there or threw them into the lake. This turned the locals against the monks.

When Columbanus moved on to Italy in 612, Gallus stayed behind. According to the **Vita of Gallus**, his biography, he had a fever and could not travel further. He withdrew into the **Arbon Forest** and built a simple cell on the **Steinach** around 612. A **hermit** is a person who lives alone in order to pray. Gallus died in **Arbon** and was buried in his cell.

The best-known story about Gallus is about a **bear**. Gallus is said to have ordered the animal to put wood on the fire. As thanks he gave it bread. That is why the **coat of arms** of the town of St Gallen still shows a bear today. In many pictures, too, Gallus can be seen together with the animal.

About a hundred years after Gallus, the priest **Othmar** gathered monks at his grave. In 719 he founded the **monastery of St Gallen** and became its first abbot. The monastery became an important place of education with a large library. Later it became a **princely abbey**, which also ruled over land and people. The Grand Council of the new canton of St Gallen dissolved it in 1805, and the church later became the cathedral of the **Diocese of St Gallen**.

Biographies that came into being only after his death tell us about Gallus. Around 833 the scholar **Walahfrid Strabo** of the monastery of Reichenau revised an older version. His version strongly shaped the picture of the saint. Because these texts also contain legends, not everything in them is certain. **St Gall's Day** on 16 October used to be an important date in the countryside for markets and the payment of interest.

gewusst: The town and the canton of St Gallen both bear the name of the monk.
The Abbey District of St Gallen, with its famous Abbey Library, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: The Transmontane Bailiwicks, the “Ennetbirgische Vogteien”, were territories south of the Alps, in present-day Ticino. “Ennetbirgisch” means “beyond the mountains”. The Confederates ruled these territories as subject land until 1798.
wichtigste: Uri ruled the Leventina alone from the 15th century.
In 1478 Confederates and people of the Leventina won the Battle of Giornico against Milan.
From 1512 twelve places jointly administered Lugano, Locarno, Mendrisio and the Maggia valley.
Bellinzona, the Riviera and Blenio belonged only to Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden.
Bailiffs usually governed for two years.
Every year envoys of the places checked the administration in the Syndicate.
In 1803 the canton of Ticino emerged from the bailiwicks.

abschnitte.text: Uri wanted to secure the **Gotthard route** to Italy. So in the 15th century it brought the **Leventina** under its rule. In 1478 the **Battle of Giornico** took place. A small force of Confederates and people of the Leventina defeated a much larger army from **Milan** there. The Leventina remained a subject territory of Uri until 1798.

During the **Milanese Wars** the Confederates conquered further territories. From 1512 **twelve places** jointly administered Lugano, Locarno, Mendrisio and the Maggia valley. **Appenzell** had no share in this, because it became a full place only in 1513. **Bellinzona**, the Riviera and the Blenio valley, on the other hand, belonged only to Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden.

The ruling places took turns sending a **bailiff**, usually for **two years**. He administered justice and collected dues. Many bailiffs used the short time to recoup their expenses for the office. For control, envoys of the places travelled to the bailiwicks every year. This inspection was called the **Syndicate**: the syndics checked the accounts and judged complaints.

After the Reformation there was a Reformed congregation in **Locarno**. In 1555 the Catholic places forced through their expulsion. Most of those expelled fled to **Zurich**, where families such as Orelli and Muralt later became important. In 1755 the Leventina rose against **Uri**, because Uri was interfering with its rights. The uprising failed, and its leaders were punished.

With the end of the Old Confederacy in 1798 the rule of the places ceased. The bailiwicks became free. In **1803** the **canton of Ticino** was formed from them. It became an equal canton of Switzerland. To this day it is the largest Italian-speaking part of the country.

gewusst: “Ennetbirgisch” means “beyond the mountains”, that is, south of the Alps.
The Orelli and Muralt families came to Zurich as expelled Reformed from Locarno.

teile.einleitung: The Perpetual Peace was a treaty between France and the Confederates. It was concluded on 29 November 1516 in Fribourg and lasted almost 300 years.
wichtigste: The treaty was concluded about a year after the Battle of Marignano.
France and the Confederates promised never again to wage war against each other.
The Confederates received money and trade advantages.
They gave up the protectorate over Milan but kept the Ticino bailiwicks.
The Three Leagues were allowed to keep the Valtellina, Chiavenna and Bormio.
In 1521 a military alliance with France followed.
The peace lasted until the French invasion of 1798.

abschnitte.text: In 1515 the Confederates lost the **Battle of Marignano** against France. After that both sides negotiated a peace. On **29 November 1516** the treaty was signed in **Fribourg**. Both sides promised **never again to fight each other**. That is where the name “Perpetual Peace” comes from.

France paid the Confederates large **sums of money** and annual **pensions** to the places. The Confederates also received **trade advantages**, for example in Milan and Lyon. That was very important for the Swiss economy. Many families in the places profited from French money.

The Confederates gave up their claim to protect and direct Milan. France also offered money if they would give up the territories around **Lugano** and **Locarno**. But the Confederates decided to **keep these bailiwicks**. The **Three Leagues** were also allowed to keep the **Valtellina**, Chiavenna and Bormio. Much of what later became the canton of Ticino came from this.

In 1521 a **military alliance** followed. In it the places allowed France to recruit **mercenaries**. Zurich, under the influence of the reformer **Zwingli**, did not take part. France became the most important employer of Swiss mercenaries. Swiss regiments served the French kings until the French Revolution.

The treaty had no **expiry date**. It governed the relationship with France for almost three centuries. Only the **entry of French troops in 1798** ended it. The Perpetual Peace shows how closely the Old Confederacy was tied to France.

gewusst: The Perpetual Peace lasted from 1516 to 1798, so almost 300 years.
The Confederates would have received more money from France if they had given up Lugano and Locarno.

teile.einleitung: The Helvetii were a Celtic people in the area of present-day Switzerland. After their defeat by Caesar they became allies of Rome and lived as the Civitas Helvetiorum, the community of the Helvetii, in the Roman Empire.
wichtigste: The abbreviation CH stands for Confoederatio Helvetica and recalls the Helvetii.
After 58 BC the Helvetii became allies of Rome.
In AD 69 they were severely punished by troops of Vitellius under Caecina.
Tacitus names Julius Alpinus, who was executed as the instigator.
From about AD 85/90 their territory belonged to the province of Germania Superior.
Vespasian's father lived among the Helvetii as a moneylender.

abschnitte.text: In 58 BC the Helvetii wanted to emigrate to Gaul. **Gaius Julius Caesar** defeated them and sent them back. After that he made an alliance treaty with them, a **foedus**. The Helvetii became **foederati**, that is, allies of Rome. They kept their own **self-government** but stood under Roman sovereignty.

For the Romans a **civitas** was a community with its own territory and its own administration. The Civitas Helvetiorum covered a large part of the Central Plateau. Its main town was **Aventicum**, the present-day Avenches in the canton of Vaud. At first the area belonged to the province of **Gallia Belgica**. Under Emperor **Domitian** the province of **Germania Superior** was set up around AD 85/90, and the Helvetii belonged to it from then on.

In AD 69 several men in Rome fought for the imperial crown. The Helvetii sided with **Galba** and clashed with troops of **Vitellius**. Their commander **Caecina** then had their territory laid waste. Many Helvetii were killed or enslaved. According to the historian **Tacitus**, Caecina had the leading Helvetian **Julius Alpinus** executed as the originator of the resistance.

The historian **Suetonius** reports that **Titus Flavius Sabinus**, the father of the later Emperor **Vespasian**, worked among the Helvetii as a **moneylender**. He is also said to have died there. Vespasian became emperor in the same year, 69. Under him Aventicum received the rank of a Roman colony.

The Latin name of the Swiss state is **Confoederatio Helvetica**, the Confederation of the Helvetii. From this comes the abbreviation **CH**, which you see on cars and in internet addresses. **Helvetia** also appears on Swiss coins and stamps. In this way Switzerland still recalls the Celtic Helvetii today.

gewusst: In Avenches you can still visit a large Roman amphitheatre today.
Helvetia is also the name of the female figure who represents Switzerland on Swiss coins.

teile.einleitung: Kulturkampf (“culture struggle”) is the name given to the dispute between the state and the Catholic Church in the 19th century. In Switzerland it reached its peak in the 1870s. Only towards the end of the century did reconciliation begin.
wichtigste: The First Vatican Council declared papal infallibility in 1870.
The Christian Catholic Church arose from the protest against this.
In 1876 Eduard Herzog became its first bishop.
In 1873 Gaspard Mermillod was expelled from Switzerland.
On 12 December 1873 the Federal Council broke off relations with the Holy See.
The diocese article was lifted as the last exceptional article only in 2001.
In 1891 Josef Zemp became the first Catholic Conservative federal councillor.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century the **liberals** wanted a modern state in which the church has less power. The **Catholic Church** wanted to keep its influence, for example over schools and marriage. From this arose a fierce dispute, which is called the **Kulturkampf**. In Switzerland the distrust was especially great because the Catholic places had lost the **Sonderbund War** in 1847. The Kulturkampf also took place in Germany and other countries.

In **1870** the **First Vatican Council** decided the dogma of the **infallibility of the pope**. It declared certain doctrinal decisions of the pope to be free from error. Liberal Catholics and the state saw in this an attack on their **independence**. Catholics who rejected the dogma joined together in a church of their own: the **Christian Catholic Church**. In 1876 a national synod in **Olten** adopted its constitution and elected **Eduard Herzog** as the first bishop.

Rome appointed **Gaspard Mermillod** Apostolic Vicar of Geneva. The Federal Council saw in this an unacceptable separation of Geneva from the Diocese of Lausanne without the consent of the state. In **1873** Mermillod was **expelled**. On **12 December 1873** the Federal Council broke off **relations with the Holy See** and expelled the papal nuncio. Only in **1920** was a nunciature set up again in Switzerland.

In the Catholic **Jura**, which then belonged to the canton of Bern, the dispute was especially fierce. In January **1874** the Bernese government expelled **97 clergy loyal to Rome**. They had refused to recognise the state church laws. Under pressure from the federal government, Bern had to withdraw the expulsion in **1875**. The Federal Constitution of 1874 also contained **exceptional articles** against the Catholic Church, for example the **ban on the Jesuits** and the **ban on monasteries**.

In **December 1891** **Josef Zemp** of Lucerne was elected to the Federal Council. He was the first **Catholic Conservative** in the national government. This tied the Catholic losers of the Sonderbund War into the federal state and is regarded as a sign of **reconciliation**. Mermillod became Bishop of Lausanne after all in 1883. The bans on Jesuits and monasteries fell in **1973**, and the **diocese article** was lifted as the last exceptional article only in **2001**.

gewusst: The diocese article demanded that new dioceses in Switzerland could be established only with the consent of the federal government.
Eduard Herzog led the Christian Catholic Church for more than forty years.

teile.einleitung: From 1564 Charles Borromeo was Archbishop of Milan and a central figure of the Catholic Reform. His diocese also included areas in today's Ticino. He strongly shaped the Catholic places of the Confederacy and was canonised in 1610.
wichtigste: Charles Borromeo was born in Arona on Lake Maggiore in 1538.
His uncle was Pope Pius IV, who made him a cardinal at a very young age.
From 1564 he was Archbishop of Milan.
He took part in the closing phase of the Council of Trent.
In 1579 he founded the Collegium Helveticum in Milan.
He supported the Capuchins, who founded their first German-Swiss monastery in Altdorf in 1581.
In 1610 he was canonised.

abschnitte.text: Charles Borromeo, Carlo Borromeo in Italian, was born in **1538** in **Arona** on Lake Maggiore. He came from a distinguished family. At the end of 1559 his uncle was elected pope as **Pius IV**. He brought his nephew to Rome and made him a **cardinal**. So Borromeo rose to the highest church offices at a very young age.

The **Council of Trent** was a great assembly of the Catholic Church. It was meant to renew the church and answer the Reformation. In 1562 and 1563 Borromeo promoted the last session period and directed the work on the **Roman Catechism**, a textbook of the faith. From **1564** he was **Archbishop of Milan**. There he carried out the decisions of the council consistently and strictly.

The Archdiocese of Milan also included areas in today's **Ticino**. Borromeo also travelled to the Catholic places of the Confederacy. In **1579** he founded the **Collegium Helveticum** in Milan, where young Swiss were to become well-trained priests. He also supported the **Capuchins**, an order close to the people. In **1581** they founded their first monastery in German-speaking Switzerland in **Altdorf**, and Lucerne and Stans soon followed.

The Catholic Reform also had a hard side, which is called the **Counter-Reformation**. In **1583** Borromeo had people accused of **witchcraft** in the **Misox** in Graubünden. Of 108 accused, eleven were executed. The rest were forced to return to the Catholic Church. Today historians view these trials very critically.

During the **plague** from 1576 to 1578, Borromeo stayed in **Milan**. He personally cared for the **sick and the poor**. This effort harmed his health, but increased the veneration for him. He died in 1584. On **1 November 1610** Pope Paul V declared him a **saint**. His feast day is **4 November**.

gewusst: In Arona stands the “San Carlone”, a copper statue about 23 metres high, which you can climb up into as far as the head.
The Golden League of the Catholic places of 1586 is also called the Borromean League after him.

teile.einleitung: With the optional referendum the people can demand a vote on a new law. It was introduced at federal level in 1874 and is an important part of direct democracy in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The optional referendum has existed at federal level since the constitution of 1874.
In 1874 it needed 30,000 signatures.
Since 1977, 50,000 valid signatures have been needed, collected within 100 days.
Eight cantons together can also demand a referendum.
In the vote only the popular majority decides.
The compulsory constitutional referendum has existed since 1848.

abschnitte.text: “Optional” means “voluntary”. An optional referendum takes place only if someone demands it. It is directed against **decisions of Parliament**, above all against new **federal laws**. If it comes about, the **people at the ballot box** decide whether the law applies. In this way the people have the last word.

From 1848 every change to the **Federal Constitution** automatically had to go before the people and the cantons. This is the **compulsory referendum**. With the new Federal Constitution of **1874** the optional referendum was added. It applied to **federal laws and generally binding federal decrees**. At that time it needed **30,000 signatures** from eligible voters.

Since 1977 it needs **50,000 valid signatures**. They have to be collected within **100 days** after the law has been published. Instead of collecting signatures, **eight cantons** can also demand a referendum together. This is called a **cantonal referendum**. It has, however, come about very rarely.

In a vote after an optional referendum only the **popular majority** counts. That means: the majority of those voting decides. The **majority of cantons** is not needed here. For constitutional amendments, by contrast, both majorities are needed.

The referendum also gave minorities a lot of power. The **Catholic Conservatives** used it in the 19th century to bring down many proposals. To include them, **Josef Zemp** was elected in 1891 as the first Catholic Conservative to the Federal Council. To this day Parliament often seeks compromises so that no referendum threatens. This is called **concordance**.

gewusst: Josef Zemp became a federal councillor in 1891 partly because his party put a lot of pressure through referendums.
Eight cantons can demand a referendum together, without any collection of signatures at all.

teile.einleitung: Emilie Kempin-Spyri was the first woman lawyer in Switzerland. In the 19th century she fought for women to have the same rights as men.
wichtigste: Emilie Spyri was born in 1853 in Altstetten, which is now part of the city of Zurich.
The writer Johanna Spyri was her aunt.
She studied law and in 1887 became the first Swiss woman to earn a doctorate in it.
In 1887 the Federal Supreme Court refused to admit her as a lawyer.
In New York she taught women law.
In 1891 she was allowed to teach at the University of Zurich as the first woman.

abschnitte.text: Emilie Spyri was born in 1853 in **Altstetten**. At that time Altstetten was still a village of its own, and today it is a district of Zurich. The famous writer **Johanna Spyri**, who wrote “Heidi”, was her aunt. Johanna Spyri was married to Emilie's uncle. Later Emilie married and was then called Kempin-Spyri.

Emilie Kempin-Spyri studied **law** at the University of Zurich. That was very unusual for a woman at the time. In 1887 she graduated with a **doctorate**. With that she was the **first woman lawyer** in Switzerland. She was not allowed to work as a lawyer, however.

abschnitte.titel: No from the Federal Supreme Court
abschnitte.text: To be allowed to appear in court as a **lawyer**, she turned to the **Federal Supreme Court**. She argued that the constitution gave all Swiss the same rights, including women. In 1887 the Federal Supreme Court said no. It found this interpretation too new and too daring. The decision shows how few rights women had at the time.

Because she could not find work in Switzerland, she travelled to **New York**. There she taught women law and helped to set up a **law school for women**. Later she returned to Switzerland. In 1891 she became a lecturer at the **University of Zurich**. She was the first woman allowed to teach there.

All her life Emilie Kempin-Spyri campaigned for **women's rights**. She wrote texts and gave talks. She wanted women to be able to study, work and be treated equally in court. In her lifetime she did not achieve much of this. Today she is regarded as an important **pioneer** of the Swiss women's movement.

gewusst: Emilie Kempin-Spyri's aunt was Johanna Spyri, the author of “Heidi”.
Emilie Kempin-Spyri taught women law in New York long before women in Switzerland were allowed to work as lawyers.

teile.einleitung: The Golden League (Goldener Bund) was an alliance of Catholic places of the Confederacy. It was concluded in 1586, at a time of great tension between Catholics and Reformed. The alliance deepened the division of the Confederacy.
wichtigste: The Golden League was sworn on 5 October 1586.
Seven Catholic places concluded it.
These included the city places Lucerne, Fribourg and Solothurn.
The name comes from the golden initial letters of the document.
Ludwig Pfyffer of Lucerne drove the alliance forward.
It is also called the Borromean League.

abschnitte.text: Since the **Reformation** the Confederacy had been divided into Reformed and Catholic places. Zurich, Bern, Basel and Schaffhausen were Reformed. After the **Council of Trent** the Catholic Church renewed its faith, which is called the **Catholic Reform**. In this period the Catholic places wanted to hold together more closely. On 5 October 1586 they swore the Golden League.

**Seven** Catholic places concluded the league: the five Central Swiss places Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug, as well as **Fribourg** and **Solothurn**. Three of these were cities, namely **Lucerne, Fribourg and Solothurn**. Later **Appenzell Inner Rhodes** and the Catholic part of **Glarus** also joined. The leading figure was **Ludwig Pfyffer** of Altishofen. The mayor of Lucerne and mercenary leader in France was called the “King of the Swiss”.

The initial letters, the **initials**, of the text of the treaty were decorated with **gold**. This is where the name “Golden League” comes from. It has nothing to do with payments of money. After further territories joined, the saint **Charles Borromeo** was declared patron. That is why the alliance is also called the **Borromean League**.

The partners promised to help each other preserve the **Catholic faith**. If necessary this applied even against other Confederate places. In this way the league placed **loyalty to the faith** above the old obligations of the alliance. This put a heavy strain on the cohesion of the Confederacy. The **confessional division**, that is, the separation by religion, became deeper.

On 12 May 1587 the Catholic places except Solothurn allied themselves with **Spain**. Spain then ruled the **Duchy of Milan** south of the Alps. It received the right to lead troops through their territory. In return the places received grain and **pensions**, that is, regular payments of money.

gewusst: Ludwig Pfyffer was so powerful that he was called the “King of the Swiss”.
Charles Borromeo was Archbishop of Milan and visited Central Switzerland himself.

teile.einleitung: The J stamp was a red “J” in the passports of German Jews. Switzerland and Germany agreed on this marking in 1938. It is one of the dark chapters of Swiss refugee policy.
wichtigste: The J stamp was introduced in autumn 1938.
The trigger was the wave of refugees after the annexation of Austria in March 1938.
Heinrich Rothmund, head of the Police Division, was decisively involved.
Anyone with a passport bearing the J stamp needed a Swiss visa.
The magazine Der Schweizerische Beobachter made Switzerland's role known in 1954.
The Bergier Commission documented over 20,000 rejections at the border.

abschnitte.text: In **March 1938** Austria was annexed to the National Socialist German Reich. This is called the **Anschluss of Austria**. Many Austrian Jews were persecuted and fled, including to Switzerland. The Swiss authorities wanted to limit entry. So they introduced a **visa requirement** for holders of Austrian passports.

Because Austrian passports were soon replaced by German ones, Switzerland looked for a new solution. It threatened Germany with a **visa requirement for all German nationals**. Germany wanted to avoid this because it would also have hit non-Jewish travellers. In **September 1938** both countries agreed: passports of Jews were stamped with a **“J”**. Anyone with such a passport needed a **visa** to enter Switzerland, other Germans did not.

**Heinrich Rothmund** played an important role. He headed the **Police Division** of the Federal Department of Justice and Police and with it the **aliens police**. Rothmund wanted to limit the entry of Jewish refugees severely. With the J stamp, border officials could recognise Jewish travellers at once.

abschnitte.titel: Coming to terms with the past
abschnitte.text: For a long time the public knew little about Switzerland's share of responsibility. In **1954** the magazine **Der Schweizerische Beobachter** published documents on it. After that the Federal Council commissioned an investigation. In 1995 Federal President Kaspar Villiger apologised on behalf of the Federal Council for the J stamp. Later the **Bergier Commission** investigated Switzerland's role in the Second World War.

During the **Second World War** Switzerland did take in many refugees, but also turned many away. The Bergier Commission found evidence of **over 20,000 rejections**, among them many Jews. The actual number was probably even higher. For many of those turned away this meant great danger. Individuals such as the St Gallen police commander **Paul Grüninger** helped refugees despite the strict rules.

gewusst: Paul Grüninger was dismissed and convicted for his help, but fully rehabilitated in 1995.
The Bergier Commission published its final report in 2002.

teile.einleitung: Karl Elsener was a cutler from the canton of Schwyz. He made the Swiss Army knife, which is known all over the world today. From his workshop the firm Victorinox arose.
wichtigste: Karl Elsener was a cutler.
His workshop stood in Ibach near Schwyz.
From 1891 he supplied soldiers' knives to the Swiss Army.
He named his firm after his mother Victoria.
Later “inox” for stainless steel was added: Victorinox.
The typical pocket knife has a red handle with a Swiss cross.

abschnitte.text: Karl Elsener was born in **1860** and learned the trade of **cutler**. In 1884 he opened a **workshop** of his own in **Ibach** near Schwyz in the **canton of Schwyz**. At that time the Swiss Army still bought its knives abroad. Elsener wanted to show that good knives can also be made in Switzerland. For this he joined forces with other cutlers.

From **1891** Elsener supplied the first **soldiers' knives** to the **Swiss Army**. The knife had a blade, a punch, a can opener and a screwdriver. With it the soldiers could, for example, open tins and take their rifle apart. Later Elsener developed a lighter and more elegant knife with more parts. This became the model for many further designs.

When his mother **Victoria** died, Elsener named his firm after her: **Victoria**. Later the word **“inox”** was added. It stands for **stainless steel**, which does not rust. So the name **Victorinox** arose. The firm is still based in Ibach today and is run by the Elsener family.

The typical Swiss **pocket knife** has a **red handle**. On it sits a crest with the **Swiss cross**. It is especially practical that it has **many tools** in one. Besides blades there are often scissors, a saw, an awl, a screwdriver and a can opener. In English it is called the “Swiss Army Knife”.

gewusst: Karl Elsener died in 1918.
The Swiss pocket knife is part of the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. Depending on the region, a different language is spoken. This diversity is one of the special features of the country.
wichtigste: The four national languages are German, French, Italian and Romansh.
Most people in Switzerland speak German.
In Ticino people speak Italian.
Romansh is the smallest national language and is spoken in Graubünden.
Graubünden is the only canton with three official languages.
The abbreviation CH stands for the Latin name Confoederatio Helvetica.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are four **national languages**. About six out of ten people speak mainly **German**. In everyday life they usually speak **Swiss German**, that is, dialect. In the west, in **Romandy**, people speak **French**. The border between German and French is jokingly called the **Röstigraben** (“rösti ditch”).

In the canton of **Ticino**, south of the Alps, people speak **Italian**. Some valleys in Graubünden are also Italian-speaking, for example the Misox and the Poschiavo valley. Italian is the third national language. Many people all over Switzerland understand a little Italian.

**Romansh** is the smallest of the four national languages. It is spoken in the canton of **Graubünden**, for example in the Engadine. Like French and Italian, the language is descended from Latin. There are several forms, which differ from valley to valley. A well-known greeting is **“Allegra”**, which means roughly “Rejoice”. Since 1938 Romansh has officially been a national language.

Most cantons have only one **official language**. In this language the authorities and schools work. Some cantons are bilingual, for example Bern, Fribourg and Valais. **Graubünden** even has three official languages: German, Romansh and Italian. It is the only trilingual canton of Switzerland.

On Swiss cars it says **CH**. This is the abbreviation for **Confoederatio Helvetica**, the Latin name of Switzerland. Latin is none of the four national languages. So no language has to be favoured. On coins, too, it often says “Helvetia”, the Latin name for Switzerland.

gewusst: On Swiss banknotes there are texts in all four national languages.
Because no national language is to be favoured, Switzerland uses a Latin name for its abbreviation.

teile.einleitung: In December 1315 Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden renewed their alliance in Brunnen. In the Federal Charter of Brunnen the allies call themselves Confederates for the first time.
wichtigste: The Pact of Brunnen is dated 9 December 1315.
It renewed the older alliance of the forest cantons.
If one was attacked, the places had to help each other at their own cost.
No place was allowed to accept a foreign lord without the agreement of the others.
Nobody was allowed to buy a judge's office.
The word “Eidgenossen”, Confederates, appears in the charter for the first time.
Brunnen lies on Lake Uri, a part of Lake Lucerne.

abschnitte.text: The **Pact of Brunnen** is dated **9 December 1315**. In it **Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden** renewed their older alliance. Shortly before, in November 1315, they had won the **Battle of Morgarten** against a Habsburg army. Now they wanted to make their unity even firmer. Unlike the older federal charter, this one is written in German.

If one place was attacked, the others had to help it. Each place bore the **costs** of this help itself. In addition, no place was allowed to accept a **foreign lord** or ally itself with outsiders without the agreement of the others. This was meant to prevent one from making agreements alone that harmed the others.

The alliance also regulated life together. Nobody was allowed to **buy a judge's office**. Otherwise rich people could have bent the law to their will. Disputes among the allies were not to be settled by violence. People sought **mediators** or went to court.

In the Pact of Brunnen the word **Eidgenossen**, Confederates, appears for the first time. The allies were bound together by an **oath**, a solemn pledge. That is why they called themselves companions of the oath. From this word the name **Eidgenossenschaft**, Confederation, later came. To this day Switzerland is officially called the Swiss Confederation.

**Brunnen** lies in the canton of **Schwyz** on the shore of **Lake Uri**. This lake is a part of **Lake Lucerne**. From Brunnen you look across the lake to the Rütli. Even then Brunnen was a good place to meet, because it could be reached from all three forest cantons.

gewusst: The Pact of Brunnen is kept today in the Museum of the Federal Charters in Schwyz.
The word “Eidgenosse” is over 700 years old and is still used today.

teile.einleitung: Since the 20th century Switzerland has been an important country of immigration. Many people came to work here, while others fled war and persecution. Immigration has strongly shaped Switzerland's economy, culture and everyday life and has often also been a subject of dispute.
wichtigste: In 1948 Switzerland concluded an agreement with Italy on recruiting workers.
Under the seasonal worker status, many were allowed to work only for a limited time and could not bring their family.
From 1973 seasonal workers were allowed to work in Switzerland for at most nine months a year.
The Schwarzenbach Initiative was rejected on 7 June 1970 with about 54 per cent no.
Max Frisch wrote: “We called for workers, and human beings came.”
With free movement of persons, the seasonal worker status ended for EU citizens in 2002.
On 9 February 2014 the Mass Immigration Initiative was accepted.

abschnitte.titel: From a country of emigration to a country of immigration
abschnitte.text: In the 19th century many Swiss emigrated, for example to America, because there was too little work at home. At the same time workers came from abroad, for example from Italy for the building of the **Gotthard tunnel**. After the Second World War the growing economy needed very many workers. So Switzerland finally became a **country of immigration**.

In 1948 Switzerland concluded an agreement with **Italy** on recruiting workers, and later people also came from Spain, Portugal, Yugoslavia and Turkey. Many worked as **seasonal workers** on building sites, in factories or in hotels. Family reunification was in principle forbidden for them, so children often had to stay in the country of origin or live in hiding. In the **Mattmark** disaster on 30 August 1965, 88 workers, most of them from Italy, died when a glacier broke off on a building site.

In the 1960s fear of **foreign domination** grew in parts of the population. James Schwarzenbach of the National Action party launched an initiative that wanted to limit the share of foreigners in every canton to 10 per cent, with the exception of Geneva. On 7 June 1970 it was rejected with about 54 per cent no. If it had been accepted, hundreds of thousands of people would have had to leave the country.

Besides workers, Switzerland also took in **refugees**, in 1956 for example many people from Hungary. Later refugees came from Tibet, Czechoslovakia, Vietnam and, during the wars in Yugoslavia, in the 1990s. Since 2022 many people from Ukraine have sought protection in Switzerland. Asylum applications are today decided by the State Secretariat for Migration.

abschnitte.titel: Free movement of persons and new debates
abschnitte.text: With the bilateral agreements, **free movement of persons** with the EU has applied since 1 June 2002. Since then EU citizens can live and work in Switzerland if they have a job, and the seasonal worker status was abolished. On 9 February 2014 the people and the cantons narrowly accepted the **Mass Immigration Initiative**. From this came Article 121a of the Federal Constitution on controlling immigration.

Today about a quarter of the people in Switzerland do not have a Swiss passport. Many more have parents or grandparents who immigrated. Immigrants helped build Switzerland, from tunnels and dams to hospitals. You notice it in the food too, and pizza and kebab have long been part of Swiss everyday life.

begriffe.erklaerung: A foreign worker who was allowed to work in Switzerland only for a few months a year.
The right to bring a spouse and children to the new country.
The right to live and work in another country, here between Switzerland and the EU.
When people permanently move their place of residence to another region or another country.

gewusst: The famous sentence by Max Frisch dates from 1965.
Many children of seasonal workers lived secretly in Switzerland and were not allowed to show themselves, and today they are called “hidden children”.
A large part of the construction workers who built motorways and dams after the Second World War came from Italy.

teile.einleitung: Spiritual National Defence was a movement in Switzerland from the 1930s onwards. It wanted to strengthen Switzerland's own culture, democracy and cohesion. In this way Switzerland was to defend itself against foreign ideas from the neighbouring countries.
wichtigste: It was directed above all against National Socialism and Fascism.
Federal Councillor Philipp Etter promoted it in particular.
The Culture Message of December 1938 set out its programme.
In 1938 Romansh became the fourth national language by popular vote.
In 1939 the cultural foundation Pro Helvetia was created.
Films, lectures and the film newsreel spread its ideas.

abschnitte.text: In the 1930s National Socialism ruled in **Germany** and Fascism in **Italy**. Both were dictatorships that also looked for followers in Switzerland. **Spiritual National Defence** wanted to strengthen Swiss values against them: democracy, freedom and diversity. “Spiritual” here means that it was not about weapons, but about ideas and culture. Later the movement was also directed against **Communism**.

Federal Councillor **Philipp Etter** was responsible for culture. On 9 December 1938 the Federal Council presented the **Culture Message**. It described how Switzerland should cultivate and defend its cultural character. From it the foundation **Pro Helvetia** arose in 1939. It supports art and culture from Switzerland to this day.

The movement stressed the **diversity of languages and cultures** as a strength. In February 1938 the people said Yes by a large majority to **Romansh** as a fourth national language. This was also a sign against Italy, which described the language as an Italian dialect. Shared values were also meant to overcome the opposition between classes and parties. The aim was the **cohesion of all parts of the country**.

Films, too, were meant to strengthen cohesion. **“Füsilier Wipf”** of 1938 tells of a young man on active service in the First World War. **“Landammann Stauffacher”** by Leopold Lindtberg came to the cinemas in 1941 and showed the will to freedom of the old Confederates. From 1940 the **Swiss Film Newsreel** was shown before the feature films. It presented Swiss news as a counterweight to foreign newsreels.

In the Second World War the army also played a role. From 1939 the section **Army and Home** informed soldiers and the population. It gave lectures and spread information in order to strengthen the **will to resist**. It was part of the army staff. After the war, ideas of Spiritual National Defence continued to have an effect for a long time.

gewusst: The national exhibition of 1939 in Zurich, the “Landi”, is regarded as the high point of Spiritual National Defence.
Pro Helvetia has existed since 1939, so for more than 80 years.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Constitution of 1848 is the first constitution of the Swiss federal state. With it a loose alliance of cantons became a shared state with a government and parliament. Many principles from then still apply today.
wichtigste: On 12 September 1848 the Diet declared the Federal Constitution accepted.
It replaced the loose Federal Treaty of 1815.
Fifteen and a half cantons agreed, and several cantons such as Uri rejected it.
Following the model of the USA, Switzerland got a parliament with two chambers.
The customs duties between the cantons were abolished.
The federal government became responsible for coins, measures and weights.
At federal level only Swiss men were allowed to vote.
In 1874 the constitution was totally revised for the first time.

abschnitte.text: Before 1848 the cantons were only loosely connected by the **Federal Treaty of 1815**, and there was no real government. Liberal and conservative cantons argued fiercely over the future of Switzerland. In 1847 came the **Sonderbund War**, in which the troops of the Diet under General Guillaume-Henri Dufour defeated seven Catholic-Conservative cantons. The war lasted only a few weeks and cleared the way for a new constitution.

A commission drew up the constitution in the spring of 1848. After that the cantons voted on it, partly through the people, partly through their parliaments. **Fifteen and a half cantons** said yes, while cantons such as Uri, Schwyz and the Valais rejected it. On 12 September 1848 the **Diet** declared the constitution accepted, and in November the new parliament met for the first time.

The constitution created a parliament with two chambers, the **Federal Assembly**. The National Council represents the people and the Council of States the cantons, a two-chamber system following the model of the **USA**. In addition came the seven-member Federal Council as government and a Federal Supreme Court. This basic framework still exists today.

Before, travelling through Switzerland meant paying **customs duties** at many cantonal borders. The constitution of 1848 abolished these internal duties, and duties existed only at the national border. The federal government took over the postal service as well as **coins, measures and weights**. In 1850 the Swiss franc was introduced as a single currency.

The constitution guaranteed rights such as **freedom of the press**, freedom of association and the right of petition. Only Swiss men were allowed to vote, however, and women were excluded. **Freedom of settlement** at first applied only to Christian Swiss, and Swiss Jews received it only in 1866. In addition the constitution banned the order of the Jesuits.

The Federal Constitution of 1848 was **totally revised**, that is, completely reworked, for the first time in 1874. In this the people received more rights and the federal government more tasks. A further total revision led to the present constitution, which has applied since 1 January 2000. The basic structure of 1848 with the Federal Council, National Council and Council of States was preserved, however.

begriffe.erklaerung: The most important law of a state, which sets out the basic rules and rights.
The assembly of the envoys of the cantons in the old Confederation.
A parliament with two parts, in Switzerland the National Council and Council of States.
A fee on goods at borders inside a country.
The complete reworking of a constitution.

gewusst: The Federal Constitution of 1848 was drawn up by a commission in only about two months.
The ban on the Jesuits in the constitution was lifted only in 1973 by a popular vote.
In the canton of Lucerne, eligible voters who did not vote were at that time simply counted as yes votes.

teile.einleitung: In 1536 Bern conquered Vaud, which until then had belonged to the Duchy of Savoy. After that Vaud remained a Bernese subject territory until 1798 and became Reformed.
wichtigste: Officially Bern set out in 1536 to help the hard-pressed city of Geneva.
The Bernese army was led by Hans Franz Nägeli.
In doing so Bern occupied the Savoyard Vaud.
Fribourg also secured territories, for example around Romont and Estavayer.
Bern conquered Chillon Castle and freed François Bonivard.
After the Disputation of Lausanne, Bern introduced the Reformation in Vaud.
In 1537 Bern founded the Academy of Lausanne.

abschnitte.text: The city of **Geneva** was hard pressed and besieged by the **Duke of Savoy**. Geneva was allied with Bern and called for help. In January 1536 a Bernese army set off. It was led by **Hans Franz Nägeli**, who later became Schultheiss of Bern. Bern used the campaign to occupy the Savoyard **Vaud** at the same time.

abschnitte.titel: Bern and Fribourg seize their chance
abschnitte.text: The army moved quickly through Vaud as far as Geneva. Savoy was too weak to resist. **Fribourg** also used the opportunity and occupied lordships near its territory, for example around **Romont** and **Estavayer**. That is why these places belong to the canton of Fribourg today. Through the conquest Bern became the largest city state north of the Alps.

On Lake Geneva the Bernese conquered **Chillon Castle**. **François Bonivard** had been a prisoner there for years because he was an opponent of Savoy. The Bernese freed him. The English poet **Lord Byron** later made him famous with the poem “The Prisoner of Chillon”. Chillon is now one of the best-known castles in Switzerland.

In October 1536 the **Disputation of Lausanne** took place. In it the reformers Farel, Viret and Calvin debated with Catholic clergy. After that Bern introduced the **Reformation** in Vaud by decree. As early as 1537 Bern founded the **Academy of Lausanne** to train Reformed pastors. From it the University of Lausanne later emerged.

Not everything stayed with Bern. In the **Treaty of Lausanne** in 1564, under pressure from Spain and Savoy, Bern gave back the territories around **Gex** and the **Chablais** south of Lake Geneva. Vaud itself remained **Bernese**. Only in 1798 did Bern's rule end. In 1803 Vaud became a canton of its own.

gewusst: The Academy of Lausanne is regarded as the oldest Reformed institution of higher education in the French-speaking world.
Lord Byron made the prisoner of Chillon world-famous with a poem.

teile.einleitung: The Alemanni were a Germanic people. After the end of Roman times they settled in the north and east of present-day Switzerland. Our Swiss German dialects descend from their language.
wichtigste: The Alemanni were a Germanic people from the area of present-day southern Germany.
Before them the Romans ruled the area of Switzerland.
They came across the Rhine and settled on the Central Plateau in the 5th and 6th centuries.
Most of the Alemanni were farmers and lived in small villages and farms.
Many place names ending in “-ingen” recall them.
Swiss German developed out of their language.

abschnitte.text: For a long time the area of Switzerland belonged to the **Roman Empire**. The Alemanni lived north of the **Rhine**. When the power of the Romans grew weaker and they withdrew, Alemanni crossed the Rhine. In the **5th and 6th centuries** they gradually settled on the Swiss Central Plateau. First they settled in northern Switzerland, then further south.

Most of the Alemanni were **farmers**. They kept cows, pigs and sheep and grew grain. They did not like big towns. They preferred to live in **small villages** and on single farms. They built their houses of wood.

Many villages with the ending **“-ingen”** were founded by the Alemanni. The ending means roughly “at the place of the people of ...”. So it shows which family or clan lived there. Examples are **Ermatingen** in Thurgau, Ossingen, Beringen or Hettlingen. Take a look at a map: you will find many names like this.

The Alemanni spoke a Germanic language. From it came the **Alemannic dialects**, which include **Swiss German**. In the west of Switzerland, by contrast, the **Burgundians** settled. They adopted the language of the Romans. That is why French is spoken in western Switzerland today.

gewusst: If you speak Swiss German, you speak a language that goes back to the Alemanni.
In French, Germany is called “Allemagne”, after the Alemanni.

tybbqjh.t: The Charters of Freedom of the Forest Cantons

teile.einleitung: The charters of freedom of the Forest Cantons are documents from kings and emperors of the 13th and 14th centuries. They gave Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden a special position directly under the Empire.
wichtigste: The Uri charter of freedom was issued on 26 May 1231 in Hagenau in Alsace.
With it Uri received imperial immediacy: it was subject directly to the king.
In 1240 Schwyz received a charter of freedom because it had placed itself under the Empire of its own free will.
The Habsburgs did not recognise the Schwyz charter.
In 1309 King Henry VII appointed Werner von Homberg as imperial bailiff over the Forest Cantons.
In 1316 Louis the Bavarian confirmed the freedoms of the Forest Cantons.
Behind the charters lay an interest in the Gotthard route.

abschnitte.text: In the 13th century the way through the **Schöllenen**, the Reuss gorge, became passable. This created a short route over the **Gotthard** to Italy. For the kings and emperors of the house of **Hohenstaufen** this route was very important. No other territorial lord was to control its northern access. So they placed the valleys along the route directly under the Empire.

On **26 May 1231** King **Henry (VII)** issued a document for Uri in the Alsatian imperial palace town of **Hagenau**. With it Uri received **imperial immediacy**. That means: Uri was subject directly to the king, with no territorial lord in between. This did not make it independent of the Empire. But no count could rule over Uri any more.

In 1240 **Schwyz** also received a charter of freedom, from Emperor **Frederick II**. The emperor praised the people of Schwyz for having placed themselves **of their own free will** under the protection of the Empire. In return he took them under his special protection. Legally, however, the situation remained uncertain. The **Habsburgs** continued to claim rights of rule in Schwyz and did not recognise the charter.

In 1309 King **Henry VII** confirmed the rights of the Forest Cantons, now including **Unterwalden**. He appointed Count **Werner von Homberg** as **imperial bailiff**. This put the Forest Cantons under a royal official and not under the Habsburgs. In 1316, shortly after the Battle of Morgarten, King **Louis the Bavarian** confirmed their freedoms. In the dispute over the throne, the Forest Cantons had supported him against the Habsburg Frederick the Fair.

The charters of freedom are among the most important documents of early Swiss history. They show how the Forest Cantons defended their rights against the Habsburgs. Together with the **Federal Charter**, important documents are shown in the **Museum of the Federal Charters** in Schwyz. There you can still see them today.

gewusst: The oldest charter of freedom of the Forest Cantons was issued not in Switzerland but in Hagenau in Alsace.
Having imperial immediacy did not mean being independent, but being subject directly to the king.

teile.einleitung: With the Federal Constitution of 1848 Switzerland went from a loose confederation of states to a modern federal state. Many foundations from then still apply today.
wichtigste: In 1848 the Swiss federal state was founded.
Before that Switzerland was a loose confederation of states.
Shortly before, in 1847, the Sonderbund War took place.
The Diet was replaced by a parliament.
The constitution came into force on 12 September 1848.
Swiss men were allowed to settle in any canton.
Women received the right to vote at federal level only in 1971.

abschnitte.text: Before 1848 the cantons were only loosely connected with one another. This is called a **confederation of states**. Envoys of the cantons met at the **Diet** and had to vote according to the instructions of their cantons. With the new constitution a **federal state** came into being. The cantons stayed important but handed some tasks to the federal government.

In 1847 came the **Sonderbund War**. On one side stood liberal cantons that wanted a stronger federal government. On the other side stood Catholic-Conservative cantons that had joined together in the **Sonderbund**. The war lasted only a few weeks, and the liberals won. After that the new constitution could be drawn up.

The Federal Constitution came into force on **12 September 1848**. In place of the Diet there was now a **parliament** with two chambers, the National Council for the people and the Council of States for the cantons. The government was formed by the **Federal Council** with seven members. In principle this order still exists today.

abschnitte.titel: New tasks for the federal government
abschnitte.text: The federal government took on important tasks. Before, the cantons had had their own postal services, and now the **postal service** became a federal matter. Customs duties and coins also became uniform, and in 1850 the **Swiss franc** came. Swiss citizens were allowed to **settle** in any canton and work there. At first this applied only to Christians, and Jewish Swiss received this right only in 1866.

In 1848 only **men** were allowed to elect and vote. **Women** remained excluded. They received the right to vote at federal level only in **1971**, more than 120 years later. The constitution of 1848 was completely reworked in 1874 and 1999.

gewusst: Switzerland is among the oldest federal states in the world that still exist today.
As early as 1848 the Federal Council had seven members, just like today.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Factory Act of 1877 was one of the first laws in Switzerland to protect workers. It limited working hours, banned child labour in factories and made factory owners responsible for accidents.
wichtigste: The people narrowly accepted the Factory Act in 1877 after a referendum had been called.
A normal working day could last at most 11 hours.
Children under 14 were no longer allowed to work in factories.
Women were no longer allowed to work in factories at night and on Sundays.
Factory owners were liable for accidents to their workers.
Federal factory inspectors checked the businesses.
A model was, among others, the Glarus Factory Act of 1864.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century many **factories** came into being in Switzerland, especially for textiles. The work was long and tiring. Many people worked 13 hours or more a day. **Children** also had to help in the factories. So more and more people demanded rules to protect workers.

Some cantons already had factory laws of their own. The canton of **Glarus**, with its many textile factories, had limited working hours as early as 1864. It was an important model for the federal law. The new Federal Constitution of 1874 allowed the federal government to issue such rules for the whole of Switzerland. In this way the **Federal Factory Act** came about.

A **referendum** was called against the law. So the people decided at the ballot box in 1877. The law was **narrowly accepted**. Many factory owners were against it because they feared higher costs. For many workers, however, it brought a clear improvement.

The law introduced the **eleven-hour day**: a normal working day could last at most 11 hours. Children under **14** were no longer allowed to work in factories, so that they could go to school. **Women** were no longer allowed to work in factories at night and on Sundays, and there were further protective rules for them. For men there were many exceptions to these bans.

The real innovation was **liability**: the factory owner had to be liable for injuries to his workers at work. This rule was extended in 1881 in a liability act of its own. To make sure the law was observed, the federal government appointed **factory inspectors**. They visited businesses and reported abuses. One of the first was the doctor **Fridolin Schuler**.

gewusst: Before the Factory Act, many people in factories worked 13 hours or more a day.
The Glarus doctor Fridolin Schuler was one of the first federal factory inspectors.

teile.einleitung: On 6 December 1992 Switzerland voted on whether to join the European Economic Area, the EEA. The people said no, extremely narrowly. The vote is among the most important in recent Swiss history and shapes the relationship with the EU to this day.
wichtigste: The EEA vote took place on 6 December 1992.
Joining was rejected with about 50.3 per cent no, and the majority of cantons also said no.
Turnout was very high at about 78.7 per cent.
All the French-speaking cantons and the two Basels voted yes, Neuchâtel most clearly.
Uri rejected EEA membership most clearly.
After the no, Switzerland chose the bilateral path with the EU.
Liechtenstein joined the EEA in 1995.

abschnitte.text: The **European Economic Area** links the European Union with some countries of EFTA, the European Free Trade Association. In the EEA there is free movement of goods, services, capital and persons. In return the EEA countries adopt many rules of the EU single market. Of the EFTA countries today, **Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway** belong to it.

As a member of EFTA, Switzerland had negotiated the EEA treaty for years. In May 1992 the Federal Council also submitted an **application for membership** of the European Community. Many took this as a sign that the EEA was meant to be only a first step towards EU membership. The **Campaign for an Independent and Neutral Switzerland** (AUNS) with Christoph Blocher ran a strong no campaign.

On 6 December 1992 about 78.7 per cent of eligible voters went to the polls, as many as rarely before. About **50.3 per cent** voted no, and the majority of cantons also rejected it. All the French-speaking cantons as well as Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft said yes, with Neuchâtel at the top. The canton of **Uri** said no most clearly.

The result showed a clear difference between French-speaking and German-speaking Switzerland. This contrast is jokingly called the **Röstigraben**, the “rösti ditch”, after the German-Swiss dish rösti. Many French-speaking Swiss were disappointed and felt outvoted. Federal Councillor Jean-Pascal Delamuraz spoke of a “black Sunday”.

After the no, Switzerland sought another way to the EU, the **bilateral path**. With sectoral treaties, that is, agreements on individual areas such as transport, research or free movement of persons, it regulated cooperation. The first **bilateral agreements** came into force in 2002. The application for membership of the EC was never pursued further and was officially withdrawn in 2016.

Liechtenstein is closely tied to Switzerland, for example through the franc and a customs union. Even so, shortly after the Swiss no it voted for EEA membership. For this the treaties with Switzerland had to be adapted. Since **1995** Liechtenstein has been a member of the EEA.

begriffe.erklaerung: European Economic Area, a common market of the EU with Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway.
European Free Trade Association, a group of countries that Switzerland also belongs to.
Agreements between two partners, here between Switzerland and the EU.
A joking word for the differences between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland.
The share of eligible voters who take part in a vote.

gewusst: Only about 24,000 votes were missing in 1992 for a yes in the popular majority.
The EEA vote made Christoph Blocher and the SVP known across Switzerland.
In Switzerland people still vote again and again on the relationship with the EU.

teile.einleitung: In the winter of 1871 an entire French army fled into Switzerland. Switzerland took in the exhausted soldiers, looked after them and sent them home again after six weeks.
wichtigste: The army was officially called the Armée de l'Est and was named after General Bourbaki.
On 1 February 1871 General Hans Herzog signed the treaty of Les Verrières.
About 87,000 soldiers and 12,000 horses crossed into Switzerland.
The soldiers were distributed among all the cantons except Ticino.
After about six weeks they returned to France.
France paid about 12 million francs.
The Bourbaki Panorama in Lucerne recalls the event.

abschnitte.text: In 1870 and 1871 France and Germany fought in the **Franco-Prussian War**. The French **Armée de l'Est**, the Army of the East, was encircled near Pontarlier close to the Swiss border. It is named after its first commander, **General Charles Denis Bourbaki**. The soldiers were exhausted, hungry and freezing in the depths of winter.

On **1 February 1871** the Swiss **General Hans Herzog** agreed with the French general Justin Clinchant on the terms of the crossing. This took place in **Les Verrières** in the canton of Neuchâtel. At the border the French had to hand over their weapons and equipment. This is called **internment**: the soldiers stayed in the neutral country until the war was over for them.

Between 1 and 3 February 1871 about **87,000 men** and **12,000 horses** crossed the border. For the young Switzerland this was an enormous task. The soldiers were distributed among about 190 places in all the cantons, except **Ticino**. People did not want to ask them to cross the snowy Gotthard, because there was no tunnel yet. Many people helped with food, clothing and care, including the **Red Cross**.

After the armistice the soldiers were allowed to go back. Between **13 and 22 March 1871** they returned home to France. Many had been nursed and newly clothed beforehand. France paid Switzerland about **12 million francs** for this. The voluntary help of the population was not counted in it.

In **Lucerne** you can see a huge circular painting, the **Bourbaki Panorama**. It shows the crossing of the border at Les Verrières. It was painted by the Genevan **Édouard Castres**, who had accompanied the army as a helper at the time. Anyone standing in the middle feels as if they were in the midst of the action.

gewusst: The taking in of the Bourbaki army is regarded as one of Switzerland's first great humanitarian actions.
A panorama is a circular picture that surrounds the viewer completely, a little like a film without movement.

teile.einleitung: In the Appenzell Wars at the beginning of the 15th century, the people of Appenzell resisted the rule of the Abbot of St Gallen. With victories at Vögelinsegg and at the Stoss they became largely independent and moved closer to the Confederates.
wichtigste: The people of Appenzell first fought against the Abbot of St Gallen.
The name Appenzell comes from the Latin “abbatis cella”, the abbot's cell or estate.
In 1403 the people of Appenzell won the Battle of Vögelinsegg.
In 1405 they repelled a Habsburg army at the Stoss.
Schwyz took Appenzell into its law of citizenship in 1403 and supported it.
The League above the Lake collapsed in 1408 after a defeat at Bregenz.

abschnitte.titel: Under the Abbot of St Gallen
abschnitte.text: The **Abbey of St Gallen** was the landlord in the Appenzell region. That means it owned a lot of land, and the farmers had to pay **dues**. The name **Appenzell** comes from the Latin “abbatis cella” and means the abbot's cell or estate. As the dues kept growing, the people of Appenzell resisted. So around 1401 the Appenzell Wars began.

On **15 May 1403** the people of Appenzell put the army of the abbot and his allies to flight at **Vögelinsegg**. After that **Habsburg** came to the abbot's aid. In **1405** the people of Appenzell successfully repelled the Habsburg army in the battle **at the Stoss**. The fighters from the mountains knew the terrain well. That helped them against the knights.

As early as **1403** **Schwyz** took Appenzell into its **law of citizenship**. With that Schwyz promised protection and support. Schwyz then led Appenzell politically and militarily. It also promoted an alliance against the princes. Later the people of Appenzell bound themselves even more closely to the Confederates.

After their victories the people of Appenzell founded the **League above the Lake** with allies. It included the city of St Gallen and other places around **Lake Constance**. The league became very powerful for a time. After a defeat at **Bregenz**, however, it collapsed in **1408**. Appenzell nevertheless remained largely independent.

There is a well-known **legend** about the battle at the Stoss. **Uli Rotach** is said to have leaned against a hut and fought alone against many enemies. He is said to have defeated several opponents before he himself fell. Whether everything happened exactly like this is not known. In Appenzell Uli Rotach is regarded as a **folk hero** to this day.

gewusst: In 1513 Appenzell became the 13th place and a full member of the Confederation.
The canton of Appenzell still carries the abbot in its name, although it freed itself from the abbey.
